substrate temperatures of 470 -500 ◦ C, with atomic flux ratios of 1.5 -3. After  InAs  growth,  the  samples  were  quenched to room temperature with the arsenic cell valve open down to 350 ◦ C. For the fabrication of InAs-Al nanowire hybrids, the InAs samples thus prepared were subsequently cooled to ~0 ◦ C for the deposition of an Al full shell at a rate of 0.3 Å.s 1 . The morphology of the as-grown samples was examined with the aid of a high-resolution field-emission scanning electron microscope (FEI Nova NanoSEM 230), working at 50 V-30 kV and equipped with an EDX detector (EDAX Genesis XM2i) for quantitative analysis.

## 3. Results and discussion

Several approaches can be employed to fabricate Au nanodiscs on GaAs via lithography. In this work, the unmasked Au film was removed using a non-selective, high-power CF ₄ reactive ion etching (RIE) process, with the SiO ₂ -ARC nanopillars serving as a hard mask. After the LIL process, large-area arrays of photoresist nanopillars with the designed pitch and diameter covered the exposed sample surface uniformly. Fig. 1 (b) shows a cross-sectional view of a sample after LIL exposure. From bottom to top, the GaAs substrate is visible, followed by the thin (bright) 10 nm Au layer. Above it lies the ARC layer with a measured thickness of 191 nm. The SiO ₂ layer can be observed in certain regions above the ARC, while the photoresist nanopillars form a regular square array. The poly-L-lysine and photoresist adhesion layers are not visible in the image due to their negligible thickness (ideally monolayers).

The photoresist nanopillar pattern was transferred into the underlying layers through a sequence of RIE steps. An initial O ₂ -plasma with 30 sccm and 50 W etch for 1 min removed organic residues from the SiO ₂ surface and reduced the nanopillar diameter slightly. Subsequently, a CF ₄ RIE process with 30 sccm and 50 W for 5 min was used to etch the 20 nm SiO ₂ layer using the photoresist as the etch mask, thereby forming SiO ₂ nanodiscs partially capped with photoresist. A subsequent O ₂ RIE step with a gas flow of 30 sccm, 50 W of power for 4 min, selectively etched the ARC layer beneath, with the SiO ₂ nanodiscs acting as the hard mask.  After  this  step,  the  resulting  nanostructure  consisted  of  ARC nanopillars  capped  with  SiO ₂ nanodiscs  and  residual  photoresist,  as shown in Fig. 2(a). Some residual ARC material was observed on the Au surface;  although  a  longer  O ₂ etch  could  remove  it  completely,  the process was intentionally stopped to prevent excessive undercutting of the  nanopillars.  These  organic  residues  are  not  expected  to  interfere with the subsequent high-power etching process.

The SiO ₂ -ARC nanopillars obtained at this stage were used as a hard mask for transferring the pattern into the underlying Au layer. A nonselective, primarily physical CF ₄ RIE process was employed to etch the 10 nm Au film. The sample was subjected to a 150 W, 30 sccm CF ₄ plasma for increasing periods of time. Due to the granular nature of the Au film, etching proceeded faster along grain boundaries. To ensure complete removal of Au between nanopillars, a total etching time of 7 min was selected. As a result, Au nanodiscs remained on top of the GaAs pedestals,  as  shown  in  Fig.  2(b).  The  image  confirms  that  the  surrounding GaAs surface was completely free of Au. A contrast variation along the pillar sidewalls was observed: the top darker region corresponds  to  residual  ARC  and  possible  redeposition,  the  intermediate bright layer corresponds to the Au nanodisc, and the lower darker region corresponds to the GaAs pedestal. The etch rates determined for this process were 1.93 nm min 1 for Au and 14.62 nm min 1 for GaAs.

As a final cleaning step, a 50 W O ₂ RIE treatment was performed for 5 min to remove the remaining ARC from the top of the Au nanodiscs. This was followed by immersion in a 1 N HCl solution with ultrasonic agitation for 1 min to eliminate redeposited material from the etching process. The final result is shown in Fig. 2(c), which presents a top-view SEM image of the clean array of Au nanodiscs. The inset shows a closeup of an individual nanodisc with a measured diameter of 119 nm. The height of the GaAs pedestal was approximately 100 nm.

Examination of the growth morphology by high-resolution SEM after 20 min InAs deposition on the Au/GaAs(111)B substrates showed that the selectivity and yield of the growth process as well as the nanowire density  and  morphology  depended  strongly  on  the  type  of  cleaning procedure  applied.  The  exposure  to  an  O3-UV  ambient  followed  by atomic H irradiation in ultra-high vacuum appeared to hinder the formation  of  nanowires,  while  leading  to  the  non-selective  growth  of elongated 2D nanoplatelets in different crystallographic directions, as depicted in Fig. 3(a). The presence of chemisorbed H on the GaAs surface has been shown to reduce the diffusion length of group III adatoms and decrease the energy barrier for nucleation [19], which accounts for the high density of 2D nanostructures formed under these conditions. The preferred formation of (110) nanoplatelets relative to (111)B oriented nanowires, on the other hand, points to an 1:1 As/In stoichiometry, which favors growth on the (110) surface [20]. This tendency can be corrected by simply lowering the atomic V/III flux ratio. By contrast, J. Bravo et al.

cleaning of the Au/GaAs substrates with a 1:1 HCl/H2O solution prior to epitaxy contributes to enhance selective growth of vertical (111)B InAs nanowires, as shown in Fig. 3(b). However, the image evidences that the growth yield, i.e. percentage of Au nanodots that catalyze the growth of InAs nanowires, is not optimal, most likely due to the partial elimination of the poly-L-lysine coating that keeps the Au dots attached to the substrate  during  the  cleaning  process.  A  shorter  HCl/H2O  rinse  would therefore  be  more  convenient  for  preserving  the  integrity  of  the  Au nanodot mask and thus optimize growth yield in future experiments.

Under the experimental conditions here studied the estimated axial growth rate of the InAs nanowires ranges between 4.5 and 6.0 μ m/h, with the rate value increasing with As2  flux. The high-resolution SEM image in Fig. 3(c) depicts a row of InAs nanowires, where the uniformity in diameter (~ 90 nm) and height (~1 μ m) can be appreciated. These nanostructures were grown for 20 min on the Au/GaAs(111)B substrate at 500 ◦ C with a V/III flux ratio of 3. Real-time monitoring of the sample crystal structure during InAs growth was carried out by RHEED. The RHEED pattern recorded at different times of the growth experiment showed only transmission spots corresponding to the wurtzite phase. Fig. 3(d) corresponds to the RHEED pattern taken along the [11 -20]WZ direction at the end of growth.

In order to fabricate InAs-Al nanowire hybrids, InAs growth was first carried out for 20 min under the same conditions described above. A RHEED pattern corresponding to the wurtzite phase was also observed throughout the growth run. Subsequently, the temperature of all cells, except that of Al, was lowered overnight until the background pressure J. Bravo et al.

The  substrate  temperature  was  then lowered to 0 ◦ C to deposit a nominal 20 nm-thick Al coating around the InAs nanowire at a rate of 1.6 nm min 1 . The SEM micrograph depicted in Fig. 4(a) shows a general view of the as-grown InAs-Al hybrids. Most nanostructures grow in the (111)B direction and exhibit average heights and diameter values of 1 μ m and 170 nm, respectively (Fig. 4(b)). The surface  of  the  nanowires  appears  uniformly  coated  by  Al  grains,  as shown  in  Fig.  4(c),  This  figure  corresponds  to  a  high-magnification micrograph of a nanowire sidewall acquired with normal e-beam incidence to facilitate the estimation of the grain size, s . An average value of s = 11 nm was rendered from a minimum of 10 measurements of the grain diameter carried out randomly on the nanowire side wall in six different nanowires.

New experiments are underway to improve the growth yield of InAs and InAs-Al nanostructures on the fabricated Au/GaAs(111)B patterns. Notwithstanding, these preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of  applying  laser  interference  lithography  to  grow  epitaxial  InAs-Al nanowire arrays on large areas with the uniformity in size and crystal phase uniformity required in the fabrication of topological qubits based on this material system.

## 4. Conclusion

This work demonstrates a scalable and reproducible strategy for the site-controlled growth of InAs and InAs -Al hybrid nanowires through the combination of laser interference lithography (LIL) with molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). The use of LIL enabled the fabrication of largearea,  periodic  arrays  of  Au  nanodots  on  GaAs(111)B  substrates  with high spatial precision, which served as effective catalysts for nanowire nucleation via the vapor -liquid -solid (VLS) mechanism. Surface preparation prior to growth proved critical, with HCl-based cleaning markedly  improving  selectivity  and  promoting  vertical  alignment  of  InAs nanowires.  Subsequent  Al  shell  deposition  yielded  uniform  hybrid nanowires with the desired morphology and wurtzite crystal phase, as confirmed  by  scanning  electron  microscopy  (HRSEM)  and  reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED). Although further optimization  of  parameters  is  required  to  enhance  growth  yield,  the  results validate  LIL  as  a  cost-effective  and  high-throughput  approach  for deterministic nanowire integration over large areas. This methodology represents a significant step toward the scalable fabrication of hybrid superconductor -semiconductor nanowire networks, paving the way for the  realization  of  topological  qubits  and  future  quantum  computing technologies.

## Laser direct lithography of large-area three-dimensional integrated photonics: Technological challenges and advances

Lijing Zhong 1,* , Yuying Wang 2 , Xuhu Han 2 , Jiacheng Hu 2 &amp; Jianrong Qiu 2,*

1 Institute of Light þ X Science and Technology, College of Information Science and Engineering, Ningbo University, Ningbo 315211, China 2 State Key Laboratory of Extreme Photonics and Instrumentation, College of Optical Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China

* E-mails: zhonglijing@nbu.edu.cn (Lijing Zhong), qjr@zju.edu.cn (Jianrong Qiu)

Cite as: Zhong, L, Wang, Y, Han, X, Hu, J, Qiu, J. Laser direct lithography of largearea three-dimensional integrated photonics: Technological challenges and advances. Chip 4 , 100157 (2025).

[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chip.2025.100157](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chip.2025.100157)

Received: 26 February 2025

Accepted: 10 June 2025

Published online: 14 June 2025

Integrated optics have been stuck in two-dimensional (2D) topologies for decades until the femtosecond laser direct writing (FLDW) technique enables direct lithography of three-dimensional (3D) geometries and nanoscale structures with rapid prototyping and large-scale manufacturing capabilities in a variety of transparent substrates. The 3D capability of FLDW makes diverse lightwave remapping geometries possible, thereby realizing ef fi cient interconnection of optical systems at different spatial scales, offering a 3D integrated-optics footprint capable of scaling a benchtop optical system down to a 3D glass chip. This work summarizes the history and important milestones in developing FLDW waveguides. Basically, all revolutionary improvements in waveguide key performance, including low propagation loss and small bending radius, were accompanied by the discovery and development of new mechanisms for laser-induced refractive index modi fi cation. At the same time, advanced laser beam-shaping methods for tightly focused spatiotemporal fi elds have been technically grafted onto the fi ne control of laser -matter interaction in FLDW, notably achieving variable cross-section, arbitrary refractive index and mode- fi eld distribution, thus providing new degrees of freedom beyond the limitations of traditional 2D planar waveguides for more complex photonics circuit design. In this work, we present a comprehensive review of the fi eld, encompassing fundamental mechanisms (such as refractive index modifi cation) as well as key technological advances that enable true 3D integration. On the basis of this, we summarize the basic integrated waveguide components fabricated by FLDW and point out the prospective challenges and future research directions. Tentative routes towards large-area, ultra-broadband, hybrid, multifunctional, all-optical system integration in 3D glass chips are also suggested.

Keywords: Femtosecond laser, Optical waveguide, 3D photonic circuits, Glasses, Refractive index change, Laser micromachining

## INTRODUCTION

Looking into the next decade, the key highlighting trends in photonics include integrated quantum photonics and quantum computing, topological/non-Hermitian photonics, AI-empowered nanophotonics, and photonic machine learning 1 . These cutting-edge areas are closely interrelated and greatly bene fi t from a monolithic integrated-optics approach 2,3 . It is a well-accepted truth that integrated optics are always anticipated to drive signi fi cant advancements in the fi eld of photonics over the coming era 4,5 . In comparison with traditional electronic chips, photonic circuits have signi fi cant advantages in high speed, broad bandwidth, and low power consumption 6 , which can transmit and process data at extremely high speeds and generate very low heat dissipation 7 , making them ideal for applications such as bigdata centers, high-performance computing, and quantum information 8,9 . In general, integrated optics may allow interconnects to continue to scale to match the processing ability of future chips, but this will innovative compact optical components con fi gured in three dimensions (3D) 10 .

Dating back to the past decades, great progress has been made in two-dimensional photonic integrated circuits (2D PICs) on the platforms of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) 11 -21 , silicon nitride (Si3N4) 22 -28 , and lithium niobate (LiNbO3) 29 -36 ; while three-dimensional architecture photonic integrated circuits (3D PICs) have been stuck in the simple stacking of multiple layered 2D PIC structures 10 , and have not been developed as rapidly as wished. In fact, 3D PICs with controllable 3D path arrangements and arbitrary cross-sectional shapes remain out of reach. More recently, the explosive growth of PICs has boosted the technological iteration and revolution of manufacturing technology of rapid prototyping, large-scale, true three-dimensional 3D PICs 37 -40 . However, traditional fabrication techniques, including optical lithography 41 , and energetic ion beams 42 are based on two-dimensional planar etching and deposition processes, which limits their functional diversity and fl exibility. The remarkable limitation of the 2D structure makes 2D PICs dif fi cult to implement hybrid optical signal processing tasks, especially when integrating multiple functional components including passive and active units 38 . Alternatively, femtosecond laser direct writing (FLDW) technique has irreplaceable prospects for 3D fabrication capability in various transparent substrates, including glass 43 -45 , crystal 46 -48 , and polymer 49 enabling direct lithography of 3D geometries and nanoscale structures 50 -52 .

<!-- image -->

Eliminating the need for masks, etching, and cleanroom environments, FLDW utilizes femtosecond laser pulses to locally modify the refractive index within the substrate, allowing direct ' writing ' of photonic components. The 3D capability of FLDW makes diverse waveguide remapping geometries possible, thereby enabling the ef fi cient interconnection of optical systems at different spatial scales, such as connecting micron-scaled silicon-based photonic chips with kilometerscaled few-mode 40,53 or multi-core fi bers 54 -56 systems to achieve a record-breaking one petabyte per second switching node 55,56 . Besides its importance in conventional optics, the 3D light modulation capability of FLDW waveguides is of particular signi fi cance in cutting-edge experimental physics, including the experimental veri fi cation of 3D nonlinear topological phenomena 57,58 , as well as the implementation of 3D quantum photonics circuits 9,59,60 . Therefore, beyond 2D light manipulation achieved in conventional optics based on free-space optics 61 and planar light-wave circuits (PLC) 62 , FLDW offers a 3D integrated-optics footprint capable of manipulating light fi elds in the 3D spatial domain, thus providing a promising route to scale a benchtop optical system down to a 3D glass chip.

During the development of FLDW, many representative review articles have time lined its progress and growing importance in various cutting-edge scienti fi c fi elds, especially its application in 3D integrated photonics. In 2008, Gattass and Mazur 43 fi rst described the core principles and mechanisms behind femtosecond laser micromachining in transparent materials. They highlighted FLDW ' s potential to manufacture 3D photonic devices more ef fi ciently than photolithography, predicting rapid growth and great prospects beyond photonics. After nearly a decade of rapid development, in 2015, Gross and Withford 39 summarized FLDW ' s applications, particularly its success in astronomical photonics, optical communications, quantum photonics, opto fl uidics, and sensing. Over the next decade, FLDW technology expanded signi fi cantly in the fi eld of quantum photonics, leading to several scienti fi c breakthroughs; Corrielli et al. 60 have published a very timely review focused on FLDW ' s potential in quantum photonics, emphasizing the technology ' s great promise. In 2021, Tan et al. 63 systematically reviewed the landmark technological advances, refractive index change mechanisms, and prospective applications of FLDW waveguides. Although these reviews each provide valuable insights -whether focused on mechanisms (e.g., refs. 64,65 .), or application-level summaries (e.g., refs. 39,60,63 .) -they generally treat mechanisms, technologies, and applications in isolation. However, FLDW fundamentally depends on the intricate interplay between laser parameters and material response, requiring both precise beam control and a solid understanding of underlying physical mechanisms. Here, this review is attempting to systematically present recent advances from an integrated perspective -covering the evolution of waveguide formation mechanisms, the laser innovations they have driven, and the expansion of application domains they have enabled.

On the other hand, recent years have witnessed signi fi cant breakthroughs in FLDW technology, particularly in fabrication techniques that enable arbitrarily tailorable refractive index (RI) distributions 37 and variable cross-sections 66,67 . Notable innovations include the development of naked-eye-invisible PICs by suppressing light scattering 68 and by the discovery of new RI modi fi cation mechanisms 69 , control of microcracks in the cladding to enhance index contrast and overcome bending radius limitations 70 , and the waveguide cross-section conformal transformation method for large-area and large-depthchange PICs 71 , as outlined in Fig. 1. These impressive progresses achieved in FLDW technology are expected to create a new era of manufacturing high-performance 3D integrated waveguide optical devices that are comparable to traditional planar waveguide devices. Here, we carefully summarize these breakthroughs in FLDW waveguide technology, especially delignate the key technological challenges for laser direct lithography of large-area 3D PIC in glass.

Speci fi cally, this review focuses on the emerging direction of largearea 3D PICs in glass enabled by FLDW. By ' large-area, ' we refer to photonic circuits with centimeter-scale lateral spans, extended depth ranges reaching hundreds of microns, or multilayered 3D con fi gurations -attributes critical for scaling up integration density, implementing complex optical routing, and enabling hybrid functional architectures. Such large-area 3D PICs are essential for next-generation applications, including high-density optical interconnects 72,73 , chiplevel quantum photonics 74 , recon fi gurable photonic systems 7,75 , and integrated sensors (including examples of mechanical 76 , refractiveindex 77 , chemical 78,79 , and biological 80 sensing modalities). Meanwhile, recent technological advancement of FLDWs provides a foundational framework for high-throughput 3D laser micromachining with applications in large-scale integrated 3D photonic chips 74,81 , volumetric optical interconnects 82,83 , and glass-core optoelectronic co-packaging platforms 10,84 . Achieving these capabilities requires mastering key challenges such as maintaining low propagation and bending loss over extended paths, precise 3D spatial control of waveguide trajectories, and tailoring waveguide geometry and index pro fi les to meet systemlevel demands. This review organizes the state-of-the-art progress in FLDWtechnology around these technical requirements, with the aim of providing a coherent foundation for future innovation in large-area 3D glass photonic chips.

Background: mechanism, technology, and applications When femtosecond laser pulses are focused beneath the surface of glass, the light is absorbed nonlinearly, resulting in a permanent and localized change in the refractive index 85 . Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain this laser-induced refractive index change in glass, including heat accumulation 86,87 , thermal diffusion 88 , structural modifi cation 89 , color center formation 90 , shock wave propagation 68,91 , and nanograting formation 92,93 However, recent studies have highlighted the crucial role of ion migration in this process 64 . In general, by carefully controlling the mechanism by which the refractive index changes, researchers can create bespoke photonic devices. At the same time, the discovery and development of new mechanisms of laser-induced refractive index modi fi cation have driven revolutionary improvements in the waveguide ' s key performances, as discussed in Section 2 . Femtosecond laser micromachining involves a range of experimental parameters, primarily dependent on the laser itself and, to a lesser degree, the material. The factors that in fl uence the number of generated photoelectrons and the temperature within the focal volume are outlined in Fig. 1 and Table 1.

History: at sprout time In Fig. 2, we summarized the roadmap charting the development of the FLDW waveguide during its fi rst few years; roadmap depicts landmark studies on the formation mechanism of FLDW waveguides, highlighting key discoveries while citing seminal work.

The history of FLDW of waveguides began in 1996 when Miura ' s group fi rst demonstrated the technique 97 . They utilized focused femtosecond laser pulses to create optical waveguides in glass, marking a signi fi cant advancement in the fi eld of laser microfabrication. Initially, the available ultrafast laser sources were limited, primarily relying on high-energy ampli fi ed Ti:Sapphire lasers with pulse durations around 100 fs to achieve the necessary peak intensity for nonlinear absorption in glasses. Following this pioneering work, Miura and Qiu were among the fi rst to propose that the observed refractive index changes were associated with laser-induced structural modi fi cations and local densifi cation of the glass matrix 98 . The fabricated single-mode waveguide exhibits the optical properties close to those of single-mode glass optical fi ber in terms of geometric diameter and mode- fi eld distribution, thus enabling low-loss coupling with optical fi ber communication systems. Besides, higher-order modes, such as LP11 and LP21, were intentionally excited and observed in this waveguide, paving the way for its subsequent applications in mode conversion and multimode fi ber interconnects. Notably, the research contributions from Prof. Jianrong Qiu ' s group have spanned the full spectrum of FLDW-related investigations -from the discovery of waveguide formation mechanisms and advances in direct-writing techniques to the development of practical photonic applications. In this review, we aim to convey the methodology and scienti fi c logic that has emerged from the Qiu group ' s sustained research over nearly three decades. By tracing the interconnections between fundamental discoveries, technological innovations, and emerging applications, we seek to present a comprehensive framework that re fl ects the evolution of the fi eld and provides valuable insights for future researches in 3D integrated photonics.

Over the years, researchers explored various laser systems and con fi gurations to improve the ef fi ciency and capabilities of waveguide writing. Schaffer et al. 99 later demonstrated that lower energy, highrepetition-rate femtosecond laser oscillators could also effectively form optical waveguides 101 , which opened up new possibilities for the technique. Speci fi cally, Mazur ' s group achieved microfabrication of smooth waveguides at a high-repetition rate of 25 MHz and nanojoule energy using an unampli fi ed seed laser. This result inspired subsequent researches on the thermal effect of high-repetition-rate femtosecond lasers on waveguide formation.

As technology progressed, high-repetition rate bulk solid-state and fi ber femtosecond lasers providing higher pulse energies were developed, allowing for more versatile and effective waveguide writing. This evolution enabled true three-dimensional processing while maintaining nearly circular waveguide cross-sections and mode shapes, facilitating ef fi cient coupling with external fi bers. The advancements in FLDW technology have led to a wide range of applications in integrated optics, sensing, and photonic devices. From the application prospect, an important advantage of using femtosecond nonlinear materials processing for device fabrication is the ability to create 3D structures 100 , which enables higher densities and more complex devices through mode coupling in multiple dimensions, signi fi cantly expanding the range of possible devices.

## NEW REFRACTIVE INDEX MODIFICATION MECHANISM

The general mechanism for FLDW of waveguides involves the nonlinear absorption of laser light, which leads to localized heating and subsequent refractive index changes in the glass 43 . This mechanism is primarily based on the concept of multiphoton absorption, where multiple photons are absorbed simultaneously by the material, resulting in a signi fi cant increase in temperature at the focal point of the laser. As the temperature rises, it can cause structural modi fi cations in the glass, such as densi fi cation or the formation of defects, which ultimately lead to a change in the refractive index. This localized modi fi cation creates regions of higher or lower refractive index, forming the waveguide structure. The initial studies focused on understanding the interplay between the laser parameters (such as pulse duration, energy, and repetition rate) and the resulting refractive index changes, laying the groundwork for further advancements in the fi eld of femtosecond laser micromachining. The material origins of laser-induced refractive index change in glass have been summarized in literatures 64,65 . In this section, from the perspective of device performance optimization, we reviewed the remarkable results of the laser -matter interaction mechanisms affecting the waveguide characteristics in FLDW. Clarifying the prin- ciples of FLDW and reviewing its current technique challenges are both urgent and signi fi cant, as they will provide valuable guidance for future researches and development. Fig. 3 charts landmark studies on the formation mechanism of FLDW waveguides, highlighting key discoveries while citing seminal work.

FLDW in thermal regime and non-thermal regime Thermal effects include heat accumulation and thermal diffusion effects 102,103 . As the temperature of the material increases due to heat accumulation from successive laser pulses, the material undergoes thermal expansion. This expansion can lead to a change in density, which directly affects the refractive index. Generally, an increase in temperature results in a decrease in density, which can lead to a decrease in the refractive index 104 . In some materials, localized heating can cause a densi fi cation effect where the structure becomes more compact. This is particularly relevant in glasses, where rapid cooling from a molten state can lead to an increase in density and, consequently, an increase in the refractive index. The viscosity of the glass decreases signi fi cantly with increasing temperature. Lower viscosity allows for easier fl ow of the glass melt, which can facilitate ion migration and structural rearrangements that contribute to changes in the refractive index. Heat accumulation can create conditions that promote the migration of ions within the glass matrix 105 . This migration can lead to changes in the local composition and charge distribution, which can alter the refractive index. In some cases, the heat generated can induce phase changes in the material, such as crystallization or the formation of new phases, which can have different optical properties compared to the original material 106 . The temperature gradient created by the laser can induce thermal stress in the material, leading to mechanical deformation 107 . This deformation can also affect the refractive index by altering the material ' s microstructure. Overall, the interplay of these factors due to heat accumulation results in a modi fi cation of the refractive index, enabling the creation of waveguides and other optical structures through femtosecond laser processing. The insight of Eaton et al. 87 highlighted the relationship between repetition rate, heat accumulation, and waveguide performance 108 . A higher repetition rate leads to more cumulative heating, which expands the modi fi ed region and improves waveguide quality by reducing scattering losses. Speci fi cally, waveguides written at a 1-MHz repetition rate have a propagation loss of about 0.2 dB/cm in glass 87 . Notably, preheating the glass sample to several hundred degrees Celsius has proven to be an effective method to greatly extend the heat diffusion area and also waveguide diameter 109 .

Within the waveguide cross-section written in the cumulative heating regime, there have been identi fi ed with two distinct thermal stability regions, including heat-accumulation core and thermal diffusion cladding 110 -112 . Arriola et al. 110 applied a differential thermal annealing process, which takes advantage of the varying thermal stability across the refractive index pro fi le, and erases the outer cladding while preserving a high-index contrast Gaussian-like core, resulting in waveguides with signi fi cantly improved bend loss characteristics compared to non-annealed waveguides. The annealing process re fi nes the index pro fi le, leading to improved light con fi nement and reduced scattering in curved waveguide sections. This approach leverages the thermal properties of different regions to fi ne-tune the waveguide structure, enhancing performance, especially in applications where low bend loss is critical.

By studying the behavior of glass components in response to ultrafast laser exposure across 14 commercially available silicate glasses with varying compositions, Fernandez et al. found that key factors infl uence the production of waveguides with high circularity and significant refractive index changes include the glass ' s viscosity, the ratio of aluminum-to-alkaline earth and alkali metals, and the total silicon content 113 . The aluminum-to-alkaline earth and alkali ratio emerged as the key factor in controlling the formation of circular waveguide cores

with a positive refractive index. Aluminum, the only glass intermediate in all the silicate glasses studied, acts as a glass former in peraluminous compositions, where it migrates toward the densi fi ed, positive-index core. In contrast, in peralkaline compositions, aluminum behaves differently. It was also identi fi ed as the crucial element for maintaining both a positive-index core and waveguide circularity. The study further revealed that the presence of alkaline earth elements, along with alkalis, promotes densi fi cation in the core region. Heavier alkaline earths enhance the refractive index, while ensuring a peraluminous glass composition helps preserve the circular morphology of the waveguide core. Additionally, a peraluminous composition in silicate glass prevents phase separation or crystallization during waveguide inscription. Drawing on this knowledge, the deliberate incorporation of speci fi c atomic elements into custom-designed glass enables unprecedented control over the morphology and refractive index changes in ultrafast laser-written circular waveguides.

In principle, the thermal and athermal modi fi cations refer to different mechanisms for inducing refractive index changes in materials 64 . Thermal modi fi cation involves the formation of defects such as non-bridging oxygen hole centers to effect a positive refractive index change, which is typically induced by localized heating of the material due to the absorption of laser energy, leading to structural changes and the formation of defects, and exhibits relatively higher thermal stability compared to athermal modi fi cations. Athermal modi fi cation involves induced ion migration, leading to compositional change, and the formation of non-bridging oxygen hole centers (among other defects) to effect a positive refractive index change, which is less reliant on localized heating and is more related to the induced compositional changes in the material and exhibits reduced thermal stability compared to the thermal regime. In the context of the recent study 103 , the athermal regime was shown to exhibit reduced thermal stability compared to the thermal regime. The study demonstrates that these two mechanisms can be triggered sequentially for improved index contrast, and the fabrication parameter space was optimized to maximize athermal refractive index contrast. The differences between these two modi fi cation regimes are crucial for understanding the fabrication process and the resulting properties of the composite laser-written 3D waveguide.

Shock wave propagation and cumulative stress The intense pressure generated by the laser can create shock waves that modify the material ' s structure and density, leading to changes in the refractive index 114 . When a focused laser pulse generates a shock wave, it creates a rapid increase in pressure within the material. This pressure can lead to localized changes in density. Since the refractive index is generally proportional to the density of the material, an increase in density due to shock wave propagation can result in an increase in the refractive index. The shock wave can create regions of lower density or even voids within the material 115 . These voids can signi fi cantly alter the local refractive index, as the refractive index of air (or vacuum) is much lower than that of the surrounding material. The presence of these voids can lead to a decrease in the overall refractive index in the affected regions. The shock wave can also induce thermal effects, leading to localized heating and subsequent cooling 116 . This thermal cycling can cause changes in the material ' s structure, such as densi fi cation or the formation of defects, which can further in fl uence the refractive index.

The mechanical stress from the shock wave can lead to microstructural changes, such as local densi fi cation 117 , the formation of nanocracks or other defects 70 . These changes can affect how light propagates through the material, leading to variations in the refractive index. The intense conditions created by shock wave propagation can lead to nonlinear optical effects, where the refractive index becomes dependent on the intensity of the light. This can result in phenomena such as self-focusing or self-defocusing, which can complicate the relationship between the shock wave and the refractive index 114 . In some materials, shock wave propagation can induce phase changes, such as transitions from amorphous to crystalline states 118,119 . Different phases can have distinct refractive indices, and the transition from one phase to another can result in signi fi cant changes in the overall refractive index 120 . Overall, shock wave propagation can lead to complex changes in the refractive index through mechanisms involving pressure and density changes, void formation, thermal effects, microstructural alterations, nonlinear optical effects, and phase transitions, making it a critical factor in laser processing and photonic applications.

A comprehensive study of how stress affects the refractive index pro fi le and the usage of cumulative stress to enhance waveguide refractive index contrast and suppress losses was recently done by Sun et al. 70,121 They demonstrated that the refractive index distribution is affected by accumulated stress during the multiscan FLDW 121 , and the sequence of laser scan lines determines the direction of stress accumulation and also the change of refractive index correspondingly 70 . Building on this knowledge, they proposed a novel approach to control stress accumulation in order to fi ne-tune the refractive index pro fi le for high-performance diffractive optical elements. Asymmetric stress accumulation, however, can result in uneven refractive index distributions and even lead to crack formation. By deliberately inducing a strong asymmetric stress pattern in silica glass, uniform cracks with predetermined dimensions can be created and directed along a fi xed path. For example, 90  curved waveguides with microcracks on the outer bend edge were inscribed to improve modal con fi nement, setting a record for a bending radius of 10 mm (radiative bending losses as low as 1 dB/cm) without introducing additional scattering.

Thermodynamic analysis of FLDW waveguide formation Highrepetition-rate laser irradiation can rapidly raise the local temperature above 2000 K within the focus area 122 , leading to localized melting of the material. The molten fl uid is con fi ned within the laser-modi fi ed zone and is subjected to periodic thermomechanical shock waves initiated by the absorption of pulsed laser energy. The fl uid continues to oscillate as long as the absorbed energy is suf fi cient to counteract the dissipation from fl uid viscosity. On the other hand, the quenching time is de fi ned as the time required to move the sample by half the waveguide width and ranges from hundreds of μ s to tens of ms, which is more than an order of magnitude larger than the cooling time of static exposure (about 10 μ s for silicate glasses 123 ). Thus, as the sample moves away from the laser ' s focal point, the molten fl uid undergoes rapid cooling, and the shock wave within the molten pool similarly freezes instantaneously in its position.

Rapid cooling of the material after being heated by the laser can lead to structural changes that affect the refractive index 124 . After the laser pulse heats the material, the rapid cooling (quenching) that follows can lead to a change in the material ' s structure. This quick transition from a high-temperature molten state to a solid-state can ' freeze ' the atomic arrangement, potentially leading to a denser structure or the formation of defects. During thermal quenching, the material may undergo densi fi cation, where the atomic or molecular structure becomes more compact. This increase in density typically results in an increase in the refractive index, as the refractive index is generally proportional to the density of the material. The rapid cooling process can create defects such as non-bridging oxygen hole centers or other color centers in glasses. These defects can alter the electronic structure of the material, affecting its optical properties and leading to changes in the refractive index. In some materials, thermal quenching can induce phase changes, such as crystallization or the formation of amorphous regions. These changes can have different refractive indices compared to the original material, contributing to an overall change in the effective refractive index. The rapid temperature drop can create thermal stresses within the material, leading to mechanical deformation. This deformation can alter the local refractive index due to changes in the material ' s microstructure.

The signi fi cant thermal effects observed in high-repetition-rate FLDW suggest that the dynamic process of the formation and evolution of the waveguide morphology, namely the thermodynamic process, plays a crucial role at high-repetition rates 116 . Interestingly, under focusing conditions with a damped intensity gradient, Zhong et al. reported that the waveguide cross-section follows a similar morphological evolution in different commercial glasses (boroaluminosilicate, aluminosilicate, borosilicate, and silica), despite the large differences in the glass composition 68 . Based on this fi nding, they proposed a novel physical model to explain waveguide formation based on a frozen-in shock wave diffusion process. In this model, the molten fl uid generated during the laser irradiation exhibits a uniform viscosity distribution, resembling a homogeneous Newtonian fl uid. Photo-thermal excitation of the molten liquid leads to standing wave oscillations, and when the laser is turned off, these oscillations rapidly solidify in situ. The resulting frozen shock wave closely aligns with the refractive index or density distribution across the waveguide ' s cross-section. This work introduced a groundbreaking perspective by focusing on the dynamic process of waveguide formation and presenting an empirical physical model. This approach allows for precise control over waveguide mode diameter and effective suppression of visible light scattering. The careful suppression of visible light scattering is of great signi fi cance in activating ever-passive screen glass by embedding multifunctional photonic circuits, paving the way for mobile and wearable transparent devices. This advancement has the potential to enhance a wide range of transparent screens, including those found in smartphones, computers, AR/VR glasses, car windshields, and electronic dashboards.

Structural modi fi cation and laser-induced band-gap shift The laser can induce changes in the atomic or molecular structure of the material 125 , such as densi fi cation or the formation of new phases, which alters the refractive index. When a material is subjected to laser irradiation, the intense energy can cause localized melting and subsequent rapid cooling. This process can lead to densi fi cation, where the atomic structure becomes more compact. An increase in density typically results in a higher refractive index, as the refractive index is generally proportional to the material ' s density. Laser irradiation can induce the formation of defects within the material, such as vacancies, interstitials, or non-bridging oxygen hole centers in glasses. These defects can alter the electronic structure and local bonding environment, leading to changes in the optical properties and, consequently, the refractive index.

Structural modi fi cations can lead to phase transitions, such as crystallization or the formation of new amorphous regions. Different phases can have distinct refractive indices, and the transition from one phase to another can result in a signi fi cant change in the overall refractive index of the material. The laser can induce changes in the microstructure of the material, such as the formation of nanograins or nanostructures 126 . These changes can affect light propagation through the material 127 -129 , leading to signi fi cant changes in the refractive index through mechanisms involving periodic structures, density changes, birefringence, altered polarizability, nonlinear optical effects, and the ability to control optical properties 130,131 . The energy from the laser can break and reform chemical bonds within the material, leading to changes in the bonding characteristics. This alteration can affect the polarizability of the material, which is a key factor in determining the refractive index. Overall, structural modi fi cations induced by laser irradiation can lead to signi fi cant changes in the refractive index through alterations in density, defect formation, phase transitions, and changes in bonding characteristics, which are crucial for applications in photonics and integrated optics.

Laser-induced structural modi fi cations locally alter the material ' s bandgap, resulting in a shift in electronic resonance 132 . Lapointe et al. 69 introduced the concept of femtosecond laser-induced bandgap shift (FLIBGS), which enables the inversion of refractive index contrast, facilitating the creation of smooth waveguides with a positive refractive index change in crystals. Remarkably, this technique allows for the fabrication of waveguides that are completely invisible under a microscope by selectively modifying the refractive index at certain wavelengths -especially in the telecommunications bands -while leaving it unchanged at others. FLIBGS holds signi fi cant promise for overcoming the challenges of fabricating tightly curved waveguides, particularly in addressing the bending radius limitations of FLDW waveguides. Notably, they experimentally achieved waveguide bends with a radius of curvature as small as 363 μ m (1 dB/cm loss cut-off), representing a tenfold improvement over previous results. Despite its promise, the wavelength range over which invisibility is realized for FLIBGS waveguides is typically narrow, often less than 50 nm. Furthermore, the materials suitable for this application are currently limited to those with absorption bands in the visible spectrum, which constrains their broader applicability.

In summary of this section, the general mechanisms of refractive index change induced by laser irradiation include thermal effects of heat accumulation and thermal quenching 103 , structural modi fi cation 69 , color center formation 133 , shock wave propagation 68 , nanograting formation 70 , and ion migration 64 . These mechanisms can act independently or in combination, depending on the laser parameters and the material properties. Meanwhile, the discovery and development of new mechanisms of laser-induced refractive index modi fi cation have driven revolutionary improvements in the waveguide performances.

## ADVANCES OF FABRICATION TECHNOLOGIES

Technological advances for 3D light manipulation in FLDW waveguides are driven by numerous technological innovations such as multifoci-shaped pulses 95,134 and improved multiscan schemes 67,70,135 which enable higher refractive index (RI) contrast and variable cross-section that allow for ef fi cient conversion of beam polarization state and mode rotation along the light propagation direction 135,136 . These advancements are bene fi cial for many emerging integrated photonic applications 60,63,137 -139 , by developing on-chip light manipulation components such as rotating waveplates 138 and mode converters 139 . Fig. 4 lists the milestones in FLDW technology, highlighting the most widely adopted processing methods while citing the latest technological advances.

Laser beam-shaping techniques The laser beam intensity distribution plays a crucial role in laser micromachining of transparent materials. The way in which the intensity of the laser beam is distributed at the focus affects various aspects of the machining process, including the precision, ef fi ciency, and quality of the resulting waveguides. Advanced laser beam-shaping techniques for tightly focused spatiotemporal fi elds have been successfully integrated into the precise control of laser -matter interaction in FLDW 134,140 . Here, we present a concise summarization of remarkable optical fi eld-shaping strategies adopted for revolutionizing waveguide performances of low scattering loss 68 , high mode circularity 95 , controllable birefringence 138 and variable refractive index pro fi le 37 .

Fig. 4 | Roadmap depicts landmark studies in FLDW waveguides on laser beam-shaping methods and fi ne control of light-matter interactions, while summarizing recent technological breakthrough .

<!-- image -->

Astigmatism beam Transforming the input laser beam into an astigmatic one, fi rstly demonstrated by Osellame et al. 141 and Ams et al. 142 using cylinder lens pair or slit shaping, respectively, has been widely used to improve the longitudinal and transverse symmetry of the cross-section to achieve a circularly symmetric mode distribution. Recently, Zhong et al. 68 identi fi ed a commonality among these beamshaping methods. They found that different intensity fl attening designs -such as those utilizing astigmatic cylindrical telescopes 51,141,143,144 , combinations of cylindrical lenses and slits 145 , and multi-focus techniques 95 -share the same mechanism of intensity-gradient damping. Among these, slit shaping is noted as the simplest method to implement.

Adaptive aberration correction A limitation of FLDW is its sequential nature, where three-dimensional structures are fabricated by moving the focal spot within the material on a motorized stage. Unlike lithographic techniques, which expose entire areas simultaneously, FLDW writes structures one at a time using a focused laser. As a result, higher fabrication speeds are needed for FLDW to become viable for industrial manufacturing or the production of larger devices. To address this, parallel processing techniques have been proposed and demonstrated 146 -148 . Additionally, spherical aberration caused by the refractive index mismatch between the immersion medium of the microscope objective and the fabrication substrate, alters the energy intensity of the laser focus with increasing depth 148 , limiting the ability to fabricate continuous 3D structures with high consistency. To address these issues, a holographic optical system using a spatial light modulator (SLM) is typically employed to apply compensatory phase adjustments, correcting depth-dependent spherical aberration. Additionally, it helps minimize zero-order diffraction in holograms while maintaining parallelization. However, SLM has a low refresh rate (typically 60 Hz), which makes it dif fi cult to adapt in time when direct writing involves rapid depth changes. In other words, SLM-based aberration correction is inherently discrete and cannot continuously compensate for light fi eld distortion in the depth direction, making it dif fi cult to process complex 3D structures that have high requirements for continuity and smoothness, such as optical waveguides 71 . Therefore, dynamic aberration correction with high refresh rate, or holographic phase algorithms that support rapid light fi eld switch 149 , are the key to achieving cross-depth, multi-layer integrated device manufacturing in the future.

Multi-focus beam shaping Astigmatic beams can only create circular waveguides in speci fi c directions. For writing wide-angle bending waveguides, the cylindrical telescope or slit needs to rotate along the tangent of the curved waveguide. To address this issue, Li et al. 95 developed a more ef fi cient method using multi-foci-shaped femtosecond pulses to write circular cross-section waveguides. This approach utilizes a phase-only SLM to modulate the laser beam, eliminating the need for complex spherical aberration compensation algorithms. The waveguide cross-section shapes varied based on the foci distribution, achieving circularity of up to 96.0% and an optimal birefringence of 1.14 × 10 5 .

In another way, a ring-shaped cladding waveguide has eigenmodes with axially symmetric distribution 150 . The annular ring-shaped focal intensity distribution in the transverse plane can be easily achieved using a hollow vortex beam 151,152 . However, generating a longitudinal annular ring-shaped focal intensity distribution along the laser propagation axis is more challenging due to the absence of an analytical expression describing this focal fi eld, necessitating the use of iterative methods to address the issue 153,154 . Exemplarily, a longitudinal multifocus beam, composed of discrete spots arranged in a ring pattern, was employed to inscribe depressed cladding waveguides through a single laser scan 155,156 . However, the uniformity or consistency of energy distribution of longitudinal multi-focus is still a problem, and real-time feedback optimization is necessary 154 .

High-order laser mode Higher-order laser modes, like the LaguerreGaussian mode, Bessel beam, and Airy beam, have different intensity distributions from the fundamental-mode Gaussian beam, and are also the eigenmodes of free-space propagation 157 . These high-order laser modes have been widely employed as light-shaping tools for ultrafast laser micromachining of special-shaped or ultra-high aspect ratio structures 158 -160 . However, the in fl uence of laser light fi eld distribution on the cross-sectional morphology, optical loss, and birefringence characteristics of FLDW waveguides under highrepetition-rate pulsed laser irradiation remains relatively unexplored. This is primarily due to the fact that, at high-repetition rates, ultrafast laser irradiation induces signi fi cant thermal effects 124 , which, in combination with the light fi eld distribution, govern the evolution of the waveguide ' s cross-sectional morphology. Almost published at the same time but independently, Sun et al. 161 and Han et al. 71 systematically studied the dependence of the focused light fi eld distribution on the waveguide cross-sectional morphology, considering the longitudinal light fi eld distribution (optical axis plane) and the transverse light fi eld distribution (focusing plane), respectively.

Sun et al. 161 conducted a systematic study on the impact of phase aberrations on refractive index modi fi cation and proposed a hypothesis model for glass waveguide formation. Their model suggests that the formation process results from a sequence of regional index modi fi cations caused by varying laser focal shapes. By repositioning the focal intensity distribution toward the bottom of the laser focus using a phase retrieval algorithm -integrating primary and higher-order spherical aberrations -they developed a method to prevent longitudinal elongation and splitting of the focus. This approach enabled the creation of a single high-contrast refractive index modi fi cation region, which was further extended through multiple scans to sequentially stitch these regions together, forming waveguides with variable cross-sections 66,162 .

At the same time, Han et al. 71 studied the morphological evolution of waveguide cross-sections written by various laser modes including TEM00 mode and high-order modes of TEM11, LG01, TEM21 and LG02 modes, revealed that the key factor that affects the cross-sectional morphology of the waveguide is not the intensity distribution, but the laser-induced thermal fi eld distribution, or more speci fi cally the gradient of the temperature fi eld. Thereby, it is proposed to tune the cross-section of waveguides by manipulating the intensity distribution at the focal plane. On the basis of this, a femtosecond cylindrically polarized vortex laser beam (LG02 mode) with MHz repetition rates was chosen for conformally transforming waveguide cross-sections at arbitrary bending angles of 0 to 90  and across a large depth change over 500 μ m. The reason for selecting the vortex beam is due to its inherent property of mathematically rotationally invariance, namely, the intensity projection of the vortex beam in all directions is completely consistent, allowing the waveguide to be bent arbitrarily while maintaining the cross-sectional shape. In applications, they demonstrate a one-layer 12-core waveguide circuit with a variable cross-section (diameter 5 to 11.5 μ m) while maintaining a high mode ellipticity &gt;0.974, as well as a more complex three-layer 36-core connector in which the waveguide dives continuously from 50 μ m to 550 μ m with a small loss difference of &lt;0.1 dB. Therefore, this work represents a substantial technological progress, overcoming the challenge of traditional LDW technology of uncontrollable waveguide cross-sectional shape deformation under large bending angles and depth changes, and is of great signi fi cance in constructing large-area, multilayered circuits, thereby offering a pathway for 3D imprinting of large-area photonic circuits in glass and other transparent materials 163 .

Multiple scans FLDW As discussed earlier, the formation of FLDW waveguides is a complex multiphysics process involving optical fi elds, thermal dynamics, fl uid mechanics, and material phase changes. The interplay of these physical fi elds complicates both the waveguide formation and the precise control of its cross-sectional shape. Since the pioneering work of Nasu et al. 164 in 2005, the primary strategy to tackle these challenges has been the adoption of multiple scanning techniques. Below, we summarize key technical advancements in multiple scan strategies for achieving arbitrary cross-sectional shapes, including rectangles 40,128 , hexagons 165 , rings 67 , and transformable shapes 66,67 , as well as complex refractive index distributions 37 .

In-situ multiscan Generally, the multiscan technique has strong processing robustness against external disturbances, which can offset the in fl uence of laser power fl uctuation and environmental vibrations on the uniformity of the waveguide 164 -166 , thereby reducing the generation of scattering centers and suppressing propagation loss 167 . Besides, multiple scans in situ, as schematically shown in Fig. 5a, also allow the accumulation of laser-induced effects, including thermal expansion and convection 116 , leading to higher refractive index modi fi cation and smaller bending radii 168 . The in-situ mutiscan process triggers complex thermodynamic effects due to matter melting and quenching in laser writing with high frequency pulses, resulting in complex changes in the cross-sectional material structure and refractive index distribution (Fig. 5b, c). A thermodynamic model promoted by Mermillod-Blondin et al. 116 , is suitable for interpreting waveguide formation at in-situ multiscan, as summarized in Fig. 5d. The ultrafast injection of energy generates high temperatures at the focal point, breaking atomic bonds and causing materials to melt and ionize 85 . This creates a sharp temperature gradient and propagates a pressure wave, driving rapid mechanical expansion and structural reorganization as the temperature changes 112 . Consequently, molten and ionized material is expelled from the hot, pressurized core to surrounding regions, forming a densi fi ed ring around a central zone with a lower-density structure. In waveguide structures, rapid stress relaxation along the direction of laser pulse propagation triggers a convention of material fl ow from the core and expanded cladding towards the tops of the densi fi ed cladding, promoting densi fi cation at these points.

Fig. 5 | In-situ multiscan FLDW. a, In-situ multiscan scheme. b, Typical crosssectional microscope and corresponding near- fi eld mode pro fi le of fabricated waveguide. Reprinted with permission from ref. 112 . © 2020 Optical Society of America. c, Raman mapping on the waveguide cross-section at 487 and 604 cm -1 . Reprinted with permission from ref. 112 . © 2020 Optical Society of America. d, Qualitative description of thermomechanical processes in FLDW. Reprinted with permission from ref. 116 . © 2008 American Physical Society.

<!-- image -->

Displacement multiscan and stress management In another strategy, by displacing the central position of adjacent scanning tracks and carefully arranging the overall cross-sectional shape formed by rastering closely spaced scanlines, one achieved arbitrary cross-sectional shapes, including rectangles 40,128,169 , hexagons 165 , rings 67 , and transformable shapes 66,67 . Moreover, strategic scanline placement and stress control allow for precise manipulation of both refractive index and crack propagation (Fig. 6a, b), which can be exploited to improve optical waveguide performance, especially in curved geometries (Fig. 6c). Notably, the sequence of scanlines signi fi cantly in fl uences the stress pattern. When consecutive scanlines are closely spaced, their stress fi elds overlap, causing cumulative stress 121 . Each scanline is affected by the stress distribution of the previous one, resulting in an asymmetric stress pro fi le with a non-central peak skewed towards the fi nal scanline (Fig. 6d). This stress buildup directly impacts the refractive index distribution. Typically, the multiscan leads to an asymmetric stress distribution and even crack formation, and a multiscanned waveguide generally forms a gradient index change. By applying different scanning strategies and inducing an appropriate stress pattern, Sun et al. demonstrated to control the refractive index distribution. Furthermore, by inducing a strong asymmetric stress pattern, uniform cracks with set dimensions can be created within the substrate and propagated along a fi xed path 70 . A strong asymmetric stress pro fi le can also generate uniform cracks within the substrate that propagate along predictable paths. To ensure controlled crack propagation without spontaneous formation, at least one end of the waveguide must be lapped. During lapping, surface fl aws act as stress concentrators, triggering crack nucleation, followed by propagation through the path with the highest stress, following a ' weakest-link ' model 170 . Building on these insights, Lee et al. 70 developed a repeatable method for fabricating precision microcracks, which they utilized as waveguide cladding to overcome challenges posed by the low refractive index contrast between core and cladding. They successfully inscribed 90  curved waveguides with microcracks along the outer edge of the bend, enhancing modal con fi nement. This approach signi fi cantly reduced bend loss to as low as 1 dB/cm for a bend radius of 10 mm at a 1.55 μ m wavelength; It has also been recently demonstrated by Skryabin et al. to reduce the propagation losses to 0.07 dB/cm in silica glass 169 . In summary, by carefully controlling scanline order and stress patterns, researchers have not only improved the refractive index distribution but also introduced novel solutions like microcrack cladding to enhance waveguide performance.

Fig. 6 | Displacement multiscan and stress management. a, Displacement multiscan schemes with scanline order from the right, center and left, and b, the corresponding waveguide cross-sections. Reprinted with permission from ref. 70 . © 2021 The Author(s).

Overlap-controlled multiscan and GRIN waveguide While multiscan techniques offer some capability of tailoring waveguide diameter and refractive index contrast compared to single-pass direct-writing methods, creating FLDW waveguides with arbitrarily variable crosssections remains an unmet challenge. Current FLDW waveguides lack the precision necessary for fi ne mode- fi eld manipulation, as there is no effective way to achieve precise control over the refractive index pro fi le with high spatial and refractive index resolution. Achieving waveguides with fully customizable cross-sections will require precise management of the refractive index pro fi le, including both its distribution and cross-sectional shape. However, neither insitu multiscan nor displacement multiscan methods currently provide the level of control needed. This limitation arises from the absence of techniques capable of spatially selective refractive index modi fi cation with high resolution, posing a signi fi cant barrier to achieving precise control over mode- fi eld distribution and mode coupling.

To overcome this limitation and push FLDW-based waveguide devices towards broader practical applications, Wang et al. 37 proposed a general waveguide fabrication strategy that spatially selectively changes the overlap ratio (OR) of adjacent written scanlines, i.e. overlapcontrolled multiscan (OCMS), as schematically illustrated in Fig. 7a, which for the fi rst time allows customizing both refractive index distribution and cross-section morphology of FLDW waveguides at a high resolution, enabling fi ne control over mode- fi eld distribution and intermode coupling and achieving high-purity higher-order mode conversion. The underlying mechanism of OCMS changing the refractive index is based on a well-established fact in the multiscan FLDW technique that the OR of adjacent scanlines are positively correlated with the obtained index distribution 166 . In the writing process, by closely stacking scan lines at speci fi c OR distribution, the OCMS method creates waveguides with designed index distribution. To verify this method, they design several centrosymmetric waveguides by tailoring pro fi les as step and gradient index (GRIN) distributions (Fig. 7b), exhibiting single-mode operation with tunable mode- fi eld diameters (8 to 18 μ m) and high mode circularity reaching 99.5%, enabling excellent fi ber-waveguide interconnection with record low insertion loss of 0.29 dB. With OCMS, they present the fi rst arbitrary refractive index fabrication process that achieves submicron spatial resolution and refractive index change resolution on the order of 10 -5 .

The proposed approach for precise refractive index control through careful management of thermal accumulation effects can be applied to a range of transparent materials, including commercially available screen glasses like Eagle XG, Gorilla 3, and fused silica glass FS-7980 (Fig. 7c). Notably, the OCMS method enables both positive and negative refractive index adjustments, as seen in alkali-rich glass K9. Furthermore, OCMS allows for highly customizable degrees of laserinduced thermal modi fi cations with exceptional resolution, offering an ef fi cient way to produce submicron or nanoscale structural changes in glass that surpass the capabilities of current thermal FLDW techniques 44,68,124 .

Fig. 7 | Overlap-controlled multiscan and GRIN waveguide. a, Overlap-controlled multiscan scheme. b, Design diagram of scanline schemes (upper) for four types of fundamental-mode waveguides with measured index distributions (down). c-e, Optical micrographs of four fundamental-mode waveguides (left), four higher-order mode waveguides (middle) in three typical glasses (Eagle XG, Gorilla 3, and fused silica FS 7980), as well as Raman mappings of four higher-order mode waveguides (right). Reprinted with permission from ref. 37 . © 2024 The Author(s).

<!-- image -->

Designing glass ingredients The composition of glass is essential for optimizing waveguide performance across several critical factors 111,171 . Firstly, it directly in fl uences the refractive index, where a higher contrast between the waveguide ' s core and cladding improves light con fi nement and minimizes the losses, boosting the optical ef fi ciency. Additionally, speci fi c elements in the glass affect waveguide morphology; for example, the aluminum-to-alkaline earth and alkali ratio determines the shape, with a circular morphology proving advantageous for reducing coupling losses and enhancing light propagation. Glass composition also impacts viscosity during the laser inscription process -high viscosity provides better control over ion migration and waveguide formation, allowing for consistent waveguide characteristics. Moreover, the choice of elements affects optical quality; adding aluminum, for instance, can enhance transparency by reducing scattering and absorption losses, avoiding unwanted absorption from other elements. Finally, the material consistency and continuity of the glass substrate is critical for processing low-loss, high refractive index contrast waveguides 171 -173 ; therefore, common commercial glasses, made by sintering in large sizes, including display glass, cover glass and optical lens glass, are widely chosen; however, designing the glass composition to achieve a more circularly symmetrical cross-sectional morphology and higher refractive index contrast, making glass specifically for LDW waveguides, is a game-changing approach 111,174 . Carefully selecting and optimizing glass composition is key to achieving waveguides with optimal optical properties, morphology, and stability, all fundamental to high-performance photonic devices 175 .

Fernandez et al. have examined 14 different commercial silicate glasses (Fig. 8a, b), focusing on four main families: borosilicate, aluminosilicate, boroaluminosilicate, and sodalime silicate glasses 111,174,176 . Borosilicate glasses are valued for their thermal resistance and low thermal expansion, making them ideal for optical applications. Aluminosilicate glasses, which include aluminum oxide, offer enhanced mechanical strength and thermal stability. Boroaluminosilicate glasses combine the strengths of both borosilicate and aluminosilicate, providing a balance of thermal and mechanical properties. Sodalime silicate glasses, which are commonly used in everyday products, are cost-effective and possess good optical properties, though they may suffer from iron contamination affecting optical quality. The study analyzed the variations in the aluminum-to-alkaline earth and alkali ratio (Al:[AE + Alk]), total silicon content, and other modi fi ers the in fl uence viscosity and refractive index. The role of aluminum as an intermediate element and alkaline earths like calcium and barium in enhancing refractive index contrast was particularly emphasized. Additionally, designer glasses with a speci fi c formula of 57SiO2 - 25Al2O3 -9Na2O - 9MO (wt.%), where M represents either calcium (CaO) or barium (BaO). Among them, SiO2 serves as the primary glass former, Al2O3 enhances mechanical and thermal properties, Na2O lowers the melting point and improves workability, and MO tailors the refractive index and performance. The research emphasizes the importance of maintaining an optimal Al:[AE + Alk] ratio (where AE represents alkaline earths and Alk represents alkalis) to achieve desirable waveguide characteristics. A ratio close to 0.5 is suggested to ensure good morphology and refractive index contrast.

## PARAMETER CONTROL AND PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION IN 3D PHOTONIC OPTICS: TECHNICAL ADVANCES

and loss dynamics in integrated photonic systems. This section highlights the transformative impact of FLDW on integrated optics, exploring its capabilities in fabrication, optical property control, component integration, and advanced applications.

Avariety of optical parameters can be fi nely controlled to create highperformance waveguides and photonic circuits. Key parameters include the refractive index contrast, which is crucial for effective light guiding by ensuring a clear distinction between the waveguide core and cladding; Waveguide morphology, such as shape and cross-sectional dimensions, is adjustable to control mode- fi eld distribution and coupling ef fi ciency with fi bers; mode- fi eld diameter is tailored to match the modes of optical fi bers, reducing insertion losses; Birefringence can be induced and managed through stress control during fabrication, which is bene fi cial for polarization-sensitive applications; Propagation loss is minimized by optimizing laser parameters like pulse energy and repetition rate, and by post-processing techniques such as thermal annealing; Numerical aperture, in fl uencing light con fi nement and collection, is adjustable based on the refractive index contrast created during writing; Finally, alignment and spacing between waveguides can be precisely controlled, which is critical for integrated photonic circuits to reduce cross-talk and enhance device performance.

FLDW is a versatile method, allowing the fabrication of waveguides in 3D and enabling the creation of complex optical circuits, with waveguides that can curve, cross, and connect in ways that are not possible with traditional 2D fabrication techniques. FLDW is also a powerful method that allows the fabrication of complex, high-performance photonic devices with potential applications in fi elds like telecommunications 73,82,177 -179 , sensing 77,180 -184 , astrophotonics 185 -192 , topological 193 -205 and non-Hermitian physics 206 -209 , and quantum technologies 74,210 -212 . FLDW waveguides in glass have also been used to realize Zeno control 213,214 , a signi fi cant mechanism for optical manipulation, enabling precise control over light propagation Especially, the propagation loss, referring to the attenuation of the light signal as it travels through a waveguide, which is often caused by scattering, absorption, or other imperfections in the waveguide material or structure, is among the most critical performance metrics for evaluating the feasibility and scalability of large-area PIC applications. These losses directly impact signal fi delity, device footprint, and integration density. Here, we summarize the key data in a table (Table 2), providing a comparative overview across commonly used glass substrates such as fused silica, borosilicate, Eagle XG, and soda lime glass. The comparison also considers the operating wavelength regimes, ranging from the visible spectrum to the telecom bands. This overview aims to provide practical insights into materialspeci fi c performance trends relevant to large-area 3D PIC development.

In this section, from an application perspective, we focus on the key approaches of parameter control and performance optimization in FLDW waveguides, to tackle challenges of integrated optics, such as high-precision optical state manipulation or large-scale 3D photonic integration, where the FLDW approach may add novel functionality.

3D capabilities in FLDW waveguides 2D integrated waveguides are typically created through etching processes on a fl at, two-dimensional substrate, where extending the design to three dimensions still remains challenging. Planar waveguide circuits, produced by the conventional methods like optical lithography and focused ion beam etching, rely on de fi ning two-dimensional patterns on a surface. The core design elements of these planar waveguides are simple shapes -rectangular and trapezoidal ridges or grooves -that are con fi gured through sizing, spacing, and Boolean combinations 222,223 . However, these top-down fabrication methods face limitations. They restrict the ability to adjust cross-sectional shapes and dimensions along the waveguide ' s length while maintaining a low-loss pro fi le. This rigidity hinders complex 3D control, which is increasingly necessary in applications requiring high precision, intricate geometries, and customizable waveguide characteristics, such as those in quantum photonics or advanced telecommunications.

From a manufacturing technology perspective, integrated optics have been stuck in 2D topologies for decades until the femtosecond laser micromachining technique enables direct lithography of threedimensional (3D) geometries and nanoscale structures in transparent substrates 43,44,50 . The 3D capability of FLDW makes diverse waveguide remapping geometries possible, thereby enabling the ef fi cient interconnection of optical systems at different spatial scales 40,53,56 , and also has demonstrated its particular signi fi cance in cutting-edge experimental physics applications, including 3D nonlinear optical topology 57,58 . and 3D quantum photonics 9,59,60 . Here, we argue that FLDW waveguide ' s 3D capability has three connotations: arbitrary variable cross-sectional shape, tailorable refractive index distribution, and arbitrary 3D path bending, which not only means the expansion of spatial dimensions, but also innovates new degrees of freedom in the design of optical waveguides and photonic optical paths.

3D variable cross-section Using multiple scan strategy (see Section 3.2 ), FLDW enables a wide variety of cross-sectional shapes and sizes, and the ability to arbitrarily transform the cross-section along the waveguide with high resolution 66,67 . Ultra-wide tuning of waveguide mode diameters from 4.9 to 26.5 μ m has been demonstrated 68 , while a tapered waveguide with continuous variation of waveguide diameter can achieve mode- fi eld diameter reduced from 10 μ m to 5 μ m 136 . Besides, transforming the cross-section along the waveguide, such as circular to annular transformation, twisted shape, can achieve vortex mode conversion 68 and polarization state manipulation 66 on a glass chip. Although variable-section waveguides based on negative-index modi fi cation have been widely reported before 46,150 , which con fi ne the light fi eld within an unmodi fi ed core (type-II cladding waveguide), the fi rst variable-section waveguide utilizing positive-index modi fi cation 224 , where light is guided between modi fi ed wires, was recently demonstrated by Wang et al. 67 (Fig. 9a). Shortly thereafter, Sun et al. advanced this concept further by demonstrating the application of arbitrary variable-section waveguides in diverse areas, including mode conversion and polarization control (Fig. 9b) 66 .

3D refractive index control The refractive index of a waveguide core and cladding determines light con fi nement, propagation characteristics, and mode- fi eld distributions, and it can be manipulated through various methods. Adjusting material composition, such as doping glasses with elements like germanium or phosphorus or using polymers with tunable refractive indices 225 , provides fl exibility in design 226 . Thermal processing, including heat treatments, can alter the refractive index by relieving stress 110 . Ultraviolet (UV) or femtosecond laser exposure enables permanent refractive index changes, particularly in photosensitive materials like doped silica 217,227 . Additionally, mechanical stress can induce anisotropic variations in the refractive index 70 , further expanding the range of optical property adjustments for waveguides.

However, whether based on traditional planar lithography or current FLDW technology, fi ne control over the refractive index distribution of waveguides remains out of reach, primarily due to the absence of a universal technical mean that can space-selectively change the refractive index of the material, leading to great dif fi culties in the control of mode- fi eld distribution and optical coupling. This capability of tailoring refractive index is essential for the control of chromatic dispersion, presenting signi fi cant potential for applications in photonic devices.

Fig. 9 | FLDW waveguide with variable cross-section. a, Gaussian mode to doughnut-like mode converter with hexagonal-shaped input and ring-shaped output.
