Reprinted with permission from ref. 66 . © 2022 The Author(s). Schematic representations of multi-scans of the laser spot at the waveguide facets provide further insight into the precise structuring and fabrication of the waveguide geometry.

<!-- image -->

To address this problem, Ocier et al. 225 introduced a novel lithographic method to control the refractive index in three dimensions at a submicron scale using FLDW. This method involves selectively exposing nanoporous silicon and silica scaffolds fi lled with photoresist to a laser beam. By adjusting the laser exposure parameters, they achieve precise control over the polymer density in these scaffolds, tuning the refractive index with a range exceeding 0.3, achieving lowloss fi ber-waveguide- fi ber interconnect of 2.14 dB, and reporting 15 and 30 μ m radii microrings with quality factors of 27,000 and 77,000 and bending losses of 6 dB/cm and 3 dB/cm, respectively 226 . In terminology, single-step additive manufacturing of gradient index optical elements was achieved by introducing a spatially selective variation of the refractive index as an additional dimension in 3D laser writing, which Porte et al. 228 called (3 + 1)D writing.

However, the above multiphoton polymerization and additive manufacturing methods are not suitable for 3D refractive index modifi cation inside glass materials. Wang et al. 37 present a major step forward in solving this long-standing optical problem by developing a precise FLDW method, namely OCMS method (see Section 3.2.3 and Fig. 7), which for the fi rst time allows customizing both refractive index distribution and cross-sectional morphology of 3D waveguides at the sub-diffraction-limited spatial resolution and a high accuracy of ~5.6 × 10 -5 in the control of index change. Besides, amazingly, this approach is applicable to various glasses regardless of their chemical composition.

3D path design and conformal bending 3D paths are essential in photonic circuits, enabling compact, complex, and ef fi cient designs that are crucial for advanced optical applications in communication, sensing, modulating, and lasing 10 . Unlike 2D layouts, where components are con fi ned to a single plane, 3D paths allow for vertical layering and greater integration density, making it possible to pack more functionality into a smaller footprint 229 . This architecture also provides enhanced design fl exibility, as optical signals can be routed in any direction, reducing the need for complex crossings and minimizing signal loss and cross-talk. By spatially separating waveguides, 3D paths prevent unwanted interactions, improving overall signal quality. Furthermore, the freedom of 3D design supports the development of sophisticated optical functions, such as multiplexing and demultiplexing, while maintaining a compact form. This dimensional expansion not only improves circuit performance but also enables new applications in areas like quantum computing, optical neural networks, and integrated biosensors, where complex operations and data handling are essential 38 . In short, 3D paths are fundamental for advancing photonic circuit capabilities by increasing integration density, fl exibility, and performance, all of which are essential for the next generation of compact, high-speed, and multifunctional optical devices 229 .

FLDW is a powerful technology that enables the precise inscription of 3D paths within transparent materials. By delivering ultrashort laser pulses lasting only femtoseconds, this technique concentrates energy within an extremely small volume, inducing localized changes in the material ' s structure or refractive index through nonlinear absorption 229 . In essence, FLDW is an ideal tool for fabricating 3D optical waveguides, lenses, and other photonic elements directly within the bulk material 43 . The fl exibility of this approach enables the design of intricate optical circuits, such as splitters 230 , couplers 231 , mirrors 232 , and resonators 233 , which are essential in integrated optics. Widely used in photonic chips 74 , micro fl uidic devices 234 , and lab-on-chip systems 235 , FLDW facilitates complex path design in 3D integrated photonic chips and hybrid packaging schemes 236 .

Nevertheless, constructing large-area and multilayered circuits using FLDW waveguides still remains challenging due to uncontrollable shape deformation of the waveguide cross-section under largeangle bending and signi fi cant depth variations 71 . The shape deformation can cause issues such as asymmetric mode conversion, increased propagation loss 112 , and anisotropic coupling coef fi cients 231 , while also impacting phase and polarization states 237 -239 . The primary issue stems from spherical aberration caused by the refractive index difference at the air-material interface, which causes the cross-sectional size and circular symmetry to deteriorate rapidly with depth 148 . The self-focusing effects further disrupt the cross-sectional shape and refractive index distribution as writing depth increases, typically limiting depth variations to within 200 μ m 67,240 . Although SLMs can correct spherical aberration, their low refresh rates (about 60 Hz) make them less effective for rapid depth adjustments 241,242 . It is still dif fi cult to achieve depth changes over 500 μ m with FLDW techniques and large-scale photonic circuits require waveguides to bend at large angles in 3D space while maintaining cross-sectional shape. Laser beam-shaping techniques, as summarized in Section 3.1 including slits, cylindrical lenses, and multi-foci-shaped beams have been employed to improve circularity by modulating energy or thermal gradients at the focus plane. Conventional methods, such as cylindrical telescopes or slits, can only fabricate circular waveguides along speci fi c directions, requiring the apparatus to rotate tangentially to the curved waveguide for wide-angle bending waveguides. In contrast, centrosymmetric square quadrifocal femtosecond pulses generated via an SLM enable the fabrication of circular crosssection waveguides with enhanced precision (Fig. 10a, b). This approach achieves a circularity of up to 96.0% (Fig. 10c), a birefringence of 1.14 × 10 5 , and a minimal coupling coef fi cient difference of 0.01 mm -1 between vertical and horizontal coupling directions. However, these beam-shaping methods lack true rotational invariance, resulting in signi fi cant cross-sectional shape deformation when the waveguide is bent sharply or inscribed at different depths.

To achieve conformal mapping of waveguide cross-sections across large bending angles, Han et al. proposed using a femtosecond cylindrically polarized vortex laser beam with MHz repetition rates (Fig. 10d -g), which allows for consistent waveguide cross-section transformation at arbitrary bending angles (0 to 90  ) (Fig. 10d) and depth changes exceeding 500 μ m 71 . The vortex beam was chosen for its inherent rotational invariance (Fig. 10e), meaning its intensity projection remains consistent in all directions, allowing waveguides to bend freely while maintaining a stable cross-sectional shape. In their work, they demonstrated a one-layer, 12-core waveguide circuit with a variable cross-section (diameter 5 to 11.5 μ m) (Fig. 10f) that preserved a high mode ellipticity (&gt; 0.974) (Fig. 10g) and a more complex, threelayer, 36-core connector that smoothly transitioned from depths of 50 μ m to 550 μ m with minimal loss (&lt; 0.1 dB). This advancement addresses a major limitation in traditional LDW, where waveguide cross-sectional shapes tend to distort under large bending angles and depth variations. Han et al. ' s approach represents a signi fi cant technological step forward, paving the way for 3D imprinting of large-area photonic circuits in glass and other transparent materials. This breakthrough has potential applications in high-ef fi ciency photonic computing, multidimensional quantum networks, and 3D optical topology.

Manipulation of optical properties of FLDW waveguides Manipulating the optical properties of FLDW waveguides involves tailoring their physical, chemical, and structural characteristics to in fl uence how light propagates through them. These properties include mode con fi nement, polarization state, phase delay, dispersion, loss, and coupling. Below are the key methods to achieve such manipulations.

Mode-field distribution (MFD) control Mode control in waveguides involves managing the number and type of modes they support to meet speci fi c application requirements. Single-mode waveguides are designed with small cores relative to the wavelength to con fi ne light to the fundamental mode, ensuring minimal interference and optimal performance in applications like optical communications. Adjusting the waveguide mode diameter while maintaining high mode circularity, such as the 4.9 to 26.5 μ m diameter variation reported by Zhong et al. 68 , can fl exibly achieve mode matching with various optical fi bers at different wavelengths, thereby realizing low coupling loss interconnection of waveguide and optical fi ber systems 71,73 . In terms of industrial applications, Psaila et al. 73,84 with Intel Corporation developed a pluggable optical connector designed for the co-packaging of multi-core optical fi bers and planar light-wave circuits (PLCs). This innovation was driven by the explosive demand for high-density, high-speed optical information transmission in the big-data era. The pluggable connector aims to enhance the integration of optical interconnects in data centers and high-performance computing systems, enabling more ef fi cient and scalable data transfer.

By combining the high-bandwidth capabilities of multi-core fi bers with the compact, ef fi cient design of PLCs, this solution addresses the need for faster, more reliable optical communication systems that are crucial for handling the massive data throughput in modern computing and telecommunications infrastructures.

In contrast, multimode waveguides are created by increasing the core size or enhancing the refractive index contrast, enabling them to support multiple modes for multiplexing applications 177 . High mode conversion using a directional coupler structure can realize the generation of vector vortex beams inside a photonic chip 139,243 . Meanwhile, mode fi ltering techniques, such as introducing mode-speci fi c perturbations like gratings 244 , can suppress higher-order modes, providing greater control over light propagation within the waveguide. However, the most noteworthy advantage of FLDW is that it can continuously transform the cross-section of the waveguide along the direction of light propagation, achieving adiabatic mode conversion 66,67 . Additionally, Wang et al. 67 demonstrated the fi rst lattice-like waveguide based on positive refractive index modi fi cation in silicate glass, which has also been extended to polymer substrate 224 , where the arrangement of modi fi ed lines slowly changes from regular hexagons to rings, and light is guided between the modi fi ed tracks to achieve mode conversion from Gaussian beams to hollow beams.

Coupling dispersion control Controlling the coupling of waveguides involves managing how light transfers between adjacent waveguides or other optical components. This process depends on the physical proximity of the waveguides, their refractive index pro fi les, and external modulations 245,246 . Controlling waveguide coupling relies on precise manipulation of waveguide geometry and the introduction of grating structures 247 . The shape and structure of waveguides signi fi cantly in fl uence light transfer. For example, asymmetric couplers are designed with differing core sizes or refractive indices to create directional coupling 177 , enabling selective light transfer for speci fi c wavelengths or modes. Similarly, mode-speci fi c coupling is achieved by tailoring waveguide dimensions to couple only particular modes 37,248 , such as the fundamental or higher-order modes. Another effective method is grating-assisted coupling, which involves embedding periodic gratings within or between waveguides 249 -251 . This approach allows for wavelength-selective coupling, where gratings enable phase-matching of guided modes to transfer speci fi c wavelengths ef fi ciently. Additionally, dispersion engineering using chirped or customized grating pro fi les broadens spectral coupling control, enabling precise manipulation of light behavior across a wider wavelength range 252 . Together, these strategies provide robust tools for designing waveguide systems with tailored optical properties.

Signi fi cant progress has been made in developing methods to precisely control the mode fi eld and optical coupling within glass photonic chips. Recent advances in FLDW technology (summarized in Section 3), including precise 3D con fi guration capability and the characteristics of arbitrarily varied cross-sectional shape and refractive index distribution 37 , have enabled more freedom in designing waveguide mode coupling and dispersion, which is vital in achieving ef fi cient light propagation and manipulation within photonic circuits. As a result, the interplay of tailored waveguide geometries and refractive index pro fi les leads to improved performance in optical coupling and reduced loss during signal transmission. Speci fi cally, the rapid prototype nature of direct-writing approach makes it easy to con fi gure and recon fi gure the coupling coef fi cient 253,254 , which is used to non-volatile reset the directional coupler for high- fi delity photonic integrated chips 238 .

Moreover, Wang et al. 37 demonstrated that glass photonic chips serve as a broadband and low-dispersion integration platform. The broadband response arises from two intrinsic factors: the low dispersion of glass in the near-infrared region and the operation of 3D waveguides in a weak coupling regime with a millimeter-scale coupling length. Speci fi cally, the fi rst intrinsic factor contributing to the broadband response of glass photonic chips is the inherent low dispersion of glass materials 255 , particularly in the near-infrared region. The dispersion characteristics of glass allow for minimal variation in refractive index with changing wavelength, which leads to less pulse broadening and distortion during transmission. This property is crucial in photonic applications where maintaining pulse integrity is essential for effective communication and information processing 256 . Furthermore, the low propagation loss associated with glass ensures that signals can travel longer distances without signi fi cant attenuation, strengthening its viability as an integration platform. The second intrinsic factor is the operation of 3D waveguides in a weak coupling regime 194,199 , which is characterized by a coupling length on the millimeter scale. This weak coupling condition improves the performance of mode conversion and reduces the potential for coupling losses that typically occur in more strongly coupled systems 222 . The design of 3D waveguides, enabled by advanced fabrication techniques such as FLDW, allows for complex waveguide architectures that can manipulate light more effectively than traditional planar waveguides. Exemplary, as shown in Fig. 11, they demonstrate dispersionless LP21-mode conversion of supercontinuum pulses with the largest deviation of &lt;0.1 dB in coupling ratios on 210 nm broadband. Thus, this work presents a 3D glass photonic circuit that exceptionally enables high-purity high-order mode conversion, dispersionless laser pulse transmission, and ultra-broadband operation with centered wavelengths covering visible and near-infrared spectrums. Overall, it offers a general approach that deliberately manipulates the spatial entities of the temporal optical fi eld in an integrated 3D glass chip at will.

Furthermore, Wang compared the FLDW-waveguide-based coupling devices with conventional 2D planar waveguide coupling structures based on SOI 11 -19 , silicon nitride (Si3N4) 22 -27 , and lithium niobate (LiNbO3) 29 -32 platforms. Table 3 summarizes key performances, including coupling ratio variation, operating bandwidth, and operating wavelength, as well as underlying mechanisms. It is obvious that the coupling devices based on glass 3D waveguides, including their work and the earlier work from the Withford group 177 , outperform even state-of-the-art 2D planar waveguide coupling devices, with an order of magnitude lower coupling ratio variation and operating wavelength covering visible and near-infrared spectrum. It shows the overall advantages of glass integrated devices, which simultaneously achieve broadband, high coupling ratio, as well as high robustness and low insertion loss.

In summary, the advancements in controlling mode fi elds and optical coupling, combined with the favorable properties of glass materials, position glass photonic chips as key players in the development of broadband and low-dispersion integration platforms. The unique combination of low-dispersion and fl exible 3D waveguide designs sets the stage for technological advancements across multiple applications in modern photonics. The future of glass photonic chips appears promising, supported by ongoing research aimed at further enhancing their performance and expanding their applications. Efforts to optimize the fabrication techniques and re fi ne the mode control methods will likely lead to even lower losses and higher ef fi ciency in these integrated systems. Moreover, as the demand for high-performance photonic devices grows across telecommunications, biomedical applications, and quantum computing, glass photonic chips are poised to play a vital role in driving innovation in these fi elds.

Phase customization and waveguide phase shifter In astronomy applications, customizing the phase difference of waveguide-based photonic lanterns is particularly important in astronomy applications. In fact, two key issues limiting the performance of the current generation of photonic nullers are phase variations within the beam combiner and chromaticity 257 . These challenges impact the accuracy and stability of fringe measurement in optical interferometry, particularly in applications like astronomical imaging and highprecision sensing. To address these limitations, the use of a triple coupler based on an FLDW waveguides array has been proposed 192,258 . This approach provides a broadband, achromatic null, overcoming chromatic dispersion across a wide range of wavelengths 257 . Additionally, the FLDW waveguide enables precise phase measurement 237 , which is essential for fringe tracking, improving the overall stability and performance of photonic nullers 259 . By effectively mitigating both phase variations and chromaticity, this solution enhances the accuracy and robustness of interferometric systems, making them more reliable for complex, high-resolution measurements 191,260 .

Phase shifters are crucial components in photonic integrated systems. Traditional passive phase shifters, which rely on path length differences or refractive index variations, are limited in broadband applications due to their inherent wavelength dependence. For the fi rst time, Douglass et al. 237,239 introduced FLDW waveguides to create passive achromatic phase shifters. Their design incorporates adiabatic

These tapers are carefully engineered to maintain a consistent differential phase shift across a broad spectrum, playing a crucial role in phase shifters by reducing losses, maintaining a consistent differential phase shift, and enhancing broadband performance 261 . Firstly, by gradually transitioning between regions of different widths 177 , these tapers minimize abrupt changes that can cause signal degradation, and therefore, these tapers are implemented to reduce losses within phase shifters. Secondly, the use of adiabatic tapers contributes to the broadband performance of phase shifters. They enable wide-bandwidth ef fi cient coupling, which is essential for applications needing high instantaneous bandwidth or multi-frequency operation 262 . For example, in multimode submicron tapers, they permit the simultaneous adiabatic transmission of multiple higher-order modes, which can be used in multimode nonlinear optics and quantum optics 263 . Using this method, a 3.6 mm long 180 

achromatic phase shifter was fabricated, and measured to have a phase shift of 171.5 ± 4  from 1440 to 1640 nm (Fig. 12c), and the phase performance of the achromatic phase shifter was further tested within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer (Fig. 12b) 237,239 .

Cross-talk suppression and reconfigurable 3D photonic circuit Optical waveguides inscribed inside a transparent, hard, lowthermal-conductivity dielectric (e.g., glass in this work) are insensitive to external modulation signals, including mechanical, thermal, electrical, and magnetic waves, preventing them from building ef fi cient waveguide light modulators and thus programmable photonic circuits. A straightforward solution proposed by Flamini et al. was to bring up the waveguide to the glass surface (e.g., 25 μ m depth) so that it can be modulated by the thermal gradient of the surface thermoelectrode 7 . The underlying principle involves the generation of waveguides whose properties can be altered by thermal stimuli. When localized heat is applied to speci fi c sections of the waveguide, changes in the refractive index occur due to thermal expansion and stress, allowing for the tuning of optical characteristics such as propagation loss and birefringence. This capability enables the recon fi guration of light pathways within the circuit, making it adaptable for thermally recon fi gurable quantum photonic circuits 210,211,264,265 . However, thermal cross-talk occurs when the heat generated by one component in fl uences the operation of adjacent components within a circuit. In photonic circuits, this can lead to unintended phase shifts, signal degradation, and operational instability, particularly in systems with densely integrated components. Effective suppression of this phenomenon is essential to maintain high performance and reliability in quantum devices 162,266 .

Implementing structural designs to minimize heat transfer is essential for reducing thermal cross-talk in photonic circuits. One effective approach is the use of thermal isolation trenches (Fig. 13a) 137 , which act as physical barriers within the substrate to con fi ne heat generated by individual actuators and prevent it from in fl uencing neighboring components. Additionally, optimizing the layout and spacing of actuators plays a crucial role in thermal management. By strategically increasing the distance between actuators and re fi ning their geometric arrangement, the pathways for thermal conduction are minimized, signi fi cantly reducing the risk of heat interference and improving the overall performance of the circuit. Using the suspended waveguide as the modulation arm of the waveguide interferometer, Memeo et al. 179 developed an optical phase and intensity modulator in glass, working in the megahertz range (Fig. 13b). The operational mechanism relies on the elasto-optic effect, where the refractive index of the glass changes in response to mechanical stress. When these microstructures are actuated -typically at megahertz frequencies -they induce phase shifts in the light traveling through the interferometer. The device utilizes resonance conditions to achieve signi fi cant modulation effects, enabling changes in both the phase and intensity of the transmitted optical signal. This capability allows the interferometer to effectively control and manipulate light at high speeds. Designed to operate in the megahertz range, these interferometers can modulate optical signals quickly, ideal for high-bandwidth applications, including data transmission and real-time signal processing. With optical losses as low as 0.04 dB, these devices maintain signal integrity even at high frequencies. The low-loss characteristics ensure that the modulation and transmission of signals are ef fi cient. Moreover, the design of these interferometers allows seamless interfacing with optical fi ber networks, expanding their applicability in existing communication infrastructures and sensing technologies.

In another way, Yang et al. 267,268 suggested on-chip light modulation based on low-loss skimming waveguides that can be directly integrated into FLDW 3D photonic circuits in glass and compatible with optical fi bers (Fig. 13c and d), and has the advantage of controllable mode leakage over traditional waveguide modulators, including Microfi ber and D-shaped fi ber 183,269 . In details, by integrating low-loss skimming waveguides using femtosecond laser pulses, they report a general strategy to signi fi cantly enhance the nonlinear response of glass photonic circuits based on the evanescent-coupling of 2D material thin fi lm (an ENZ material as an example) and skimming waveguides (Fig. 13c). On basis of this, an application of skimming waveguides combined with magnetron-sputtered indium tin oxide (ITO) thin fi lm with well-controllable deposition conditions are fabricated, exhibiting fl exible tuning of absorptive optical nonlinearity between saturable absorption and reverse saturable absorption and also high-density integration. Through evaporation coating, a controllable interval between the waveguide and the coated material is achieved. Compared to the physical sticking, the magnetron sputtering deposition method takes the advantage of the tunable optical nonlinearity of indium tin oxide for optical switching, delineating its prospects for its enhanced nonlinear modulation in the fi eld of high-power optical switches or modulators as well as a potential solution for future photonic devices in dynamic performance. This work overcomes the dif fi culty in achieving ef fi cient nonlinear optical modulation in ordinary silicate glass substrates and provides a micro-sized optical platform with high compactness and versatility, which can be used for rapid testing and development of new materials and can also be applied to nonlinear optics, optical sensors, atomic optics, and fi ber lasers. It is worth noting that similar nonlinear absorption characteristics have been veri fi ed more concisely and clearly in the D-shaped fi ber system 270 .

In summary, the suppression of thermal cross-talk in actuators involves a multifaceted approach, combining structural design, advanced control strategies, material selection, and passive cooling methods. By implementing these solutions, the reliability and ef fi ciency of thermal actuation processes in integrated photonic circuits can be signi fi cantly enhanced, thereby ensuring optimal system performance. Research continues to evolve in this fi eld, potentially unveiling new methods for even greater thermal management and cross-talk suppression. A ' gamechanger ' solution for zero-cross-talk circuits is to use leaky oscillating structures instead of leaky modes, such as those borrowed from designs in silicon-based photonic circuits using anisotropic perturbations of subwavelength gratings 271 .

Birefringence control and polarization management The polarization dependence in glass waveguides originates from the unique structural modi fi cations induced by femtosecond laser pulses. The primary polarization effects arise from two contributions to birefringence: form birefringence, primarily from asymmetry in transection 145,253,272 -276

and nanogratings 277 -279 , and stress-induced birefringence 280,281 , resulting from mechanically induced stresses during the laser-writing process. This duality allows for the customization of optical responses in glass waveguides and signi fi cantly enhances their functional capabilities in various applications.

Tailoring birefringence in glass waveguides offers several signi fi cant bene fi ts that enhance their utility in various applications within photonics science. One of the primary bene fi ts of tailoring birefringence is the ability to achieve precise control over the polarization state of light. This property is crucial for applications such as telecommunications, where polarization management is necessary for signal integrity and separation. By engineering the birefringence, designers can manipulate the propagation of different polarization states, creating more ef fi cient waveguides suited for polarization-dependent operations. This control allows for the development of components such as on-chip manipulation of light polarization state that can be packaged with larger photonic systems which usually needs input and output fi ber connections 138,282 . In quantum technologies, birefringent waveguides play a pivotal role by preserving the polarization state integrity required for quantum systems 9,59,60,211,212,283 .

Scattering center suppressing and invisible photonic circuit Embedding naked-eye-invisible electronic and optical elements within transparent panels is pivotal for developing mobile transparent accessories, enabling the creation of see-through smart screens including cell phone and computer screens 77 , AR/VR glasses 284 , car windshields 285 , and various electronic dashboards. Meanwhile, the development of highly see-through photonic circuits in glass has emerged as a signi fi cant advancement in the fi eld of integrated optics 69 . These innovative circuits leverage the unique properties of photonic structures to facilitate ef fi cient light transmission while maintaining aesthetic transparency. The visibility of photonic elements inscribed in glass primarily arises from scattering caused by scattering centers 51 . In FLDW waveguides, such scattering signi fi cantly affects loss performance, as any discontinuities in the glass matrix induced by laser irradiation can scatter guided light, increasing propagation loss. In previously reported FLDW waveguides, the cross-section typically features a densi fi ed ' guiding core ' surrounded by irregular rare fi ed regions 79,110,286 -289 , including cracks, nanopores, and ripple structures 115 . These less dense zones, often located in the cladding, contribute to light leakage via the evanescent fi eld, leading to substantial scattering losses.

To address the scattering issue, Zhong et al. 68 introduced a novel manufacturing strategy utilizing a damping effect on the laser intensity gradient. This approach relies on synergistic control of thermodynamic and dynamic behaviors of the matter fl uid within the laser-irradiated con fi ned region, enabling precise tuning of waveguide cross-sections and suppression of scattering center formation. This strategy not only facilitates the writing of waveguides but also ensures low scattering and minimal defects, which are pivotal for achieving high transparency and ef fi cient performance, thereby effectively reducing light leakage covering different wavelengths, covering blue, green, red, and infrared, and making it highly see-through at bright illumination of &gt; 100 lux. In principle, the magnitude of the refractive index change signi fi cantly in fl uences the invisibility of waveguides. Ideally, for a cylindrical waveguide with a step-index pro fi le illuminated by parallel light, geometrical ray tracing estimates that a maximum refractive index change of approximately 5 × 10 -4 is undetectable to the naked eye, given the human eye ' s visual resolution of 0.02  290,291 . Thus, waveguides with a refractive index change below 5 × 10 -4 , such as those in Gorilla glass 78 , are entirely invisible to the naked eye. However, Eagle glass waveguides exhibit a higher refractive index change, ranging from 1.6 to 3.2 × 10 -3 as revealed in this study and up to 3 × 10 -3 in previous reports 77 , yet remain undetectable even under a 5 × objective. This phenomenon can be attributed to the illumination by diffuse light, where light refraction caused by the waveguide ' s refractive index change is overshadowed by light arriving from multiple incident directions, a scenario common in practical applications such as phone screens.

As an intriguing demonstration, Fig. 14a presents a 3D schematic of a laser light fi eld display stack utilizing a FLDW glass chip 292,293 . This stack incorporates a photonic integrated circuit comprising thousands of precisely fabricated, low-loss optical waveguides, which enable microscale control of laser light. These waveguides are interfaced with nanoimprinted micro-optics to produce a uniform and collimated light source. Such a source serves as an illumination device for liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS)-based augmented reality (AR) projectors in smart glasses or as a backlight for liquid crystal display (LCD) panels in virtual reality (VR) systems (Fig. 14b) 294 . Furthermore, combined with the scatter suppression method, Fig. 14c -h conceptually shows the integration of the highly see-through (HST) photonic circuits into the mobile phone screen cover glass proposed by Zhong et al. 68 . Both normal and HST waveguides are barely visible to the naked eye when exposed to a bright background due to their small size and moderate refractive index variation (Fig. 14c). However, scattered light leakage can reveal the waveguides ' locations and create visual artifacts (Fig. 14d). This issue is exacerbated in dense waveguide arrays or photonic circuits, where excessive scattered light may overwhelm the background, causing the glass plate to appear overly bright or dazzling (Fig. 14e). When the screen is illuminated with blue (Fig. 14f), green (Fig. 14g), or red (Fig. 14h) background images, the HST photonic circuits embedded within the cover glass enables visible light to transmit ' invisibly, ' ensuring that the screen ' s color display remains unaffected. Therefore, one of the primary advantages of HST photonic circuits is their ability to maintain high optical performance while being aesthetically pleasing. This characteristic makes them ideal for applications where visual integrity is crucial, such as in augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) devices. Additionally, the transparent nature of these circuits promotes their integration into advanced consumer electronics, automotive displays, and architectural elements, enabling innovative lighting and communication systems.

Minimum bending radius and compact integration Bending loss in FLDW waveguides arises when optical power radiates out of the core due to inadequate mode con fi nement at curved segments. This loss becomes more signi fi cant as the bend radius decreases, constraining the compactness of integrated photonic circuits. Early FLDW waveguides in silica exhibited large minimum bend radii (&gt; 20 mm at 1550 nm) due to limited refractive index contrast 173 . Recent advancements, however, have enabled substantial improvements. Waveguides fabricated in boroaluminosilicate glass with composite morphology and a refractive index contrast of ~1.7% have demonstrated minimum bend radii as low as 4 mm at 1550 nm -a 2.5 × enhancement over earlier systems. Techniques such as microcrack formation at the bend ' s outer edge and multi-pass laser inscription further reduce bending losses by enhancing optical con fi nement. State-of-the-art LDW waveguides now achieve a 1.0 dB/cm bending loss threshold at 4 mm radius 103 , compared to 10 mm previously 70 . In optimized silica-based systems, post-annealed waveguides support high normalized throughputs (~80%) at 16.6 mm radius with minimal bending loss, suitable for practical integration. Besides, a new refractive index modi fi cation mechanism of fs laser-induced bandgap shift (FLIBGS) achieved waveguide bends with a radius of curvature as small as 363 μ m (1 dB/cm loss cut-off), representing a tenfold improvement over previous results 69 . Despite its promise, the wavelength range over

Advancements in FLDW have signi fi cantly reduced bending loss and enabled tighter waveguide routing through a combination of material and process innovations. Microcrack-induced con fi nement at the outer bend edge introduces a high refractive index contrast (e.g., 1.45 vs. 1.0), enhancing mode con fi nement and minimizing radiation loss 70 . Composite waveguide morphologies in boroaluminosilicate or other high-index glasses increase the numerical aperture, supporting tighter bends with lower loss 103 . Multi-pass and hybrid inscription strategies, combining thermal and athermal regimes, further enhance index contrast and enable dense 3D photonic integration. Thermal postprocessing, such as selective annealing, eliminates non-essential index changes, suppressing multimode propagation and ensuring ef fi cient single-mode performance at small radii 110 . Additionally, direct writing in high-index materials like specialty glasses 79,286,288,295 supports submillimeter bend radii with moderate losses, greatly expanding the design space for compact, high-performance photonic circuits.

Bending loss in laser-direct written waveguides is governed by a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic factors related to material, design, and fabrication (Table 4). A key determinant is the refractive index contrast between the waveguide core and its surroundings -higher contrast enhances optical con fi nement and reduces loss, particularly at small bend radii. The operating wavelength also plays a critical role, as longer wavelengths (e.g., 1550 nm) alter modal con fi nement, in fl uencing both minimum bend radius and overall loss behavior. Waveguide geometry, including core diameter, shape, and refractive index pro fi le (e.g., single-mode versus multimode), directly affects the ability to sustain low-loss bending. Fabrication quality, encompassing interface smoothness, induced stress, and material inhomogeneity from the writing process or post-processing, signi fi cantly impacts scattering and con fi nement. Additionally, innovative structural designs such as composite cores, air-clad regions, and micro-engineered peripheries can further enhance con fi nement and mitigate bending losses by locally modifying the refractive index distribution.

## 3D WAVEGUIDE-BASED DEVICES FOR 3D INTEGRATED OPTICS

Traditional photonic circuits relied on planar lithography, which restricted device layouts to a single plane. FLDW overcomes this limitation by allowing direct fabrication of optical waveguides inside transparent substrates, enabling fully 3D photonic architectures 39 . This advancement allows for the fabrication of arbitrary 3D waveguide geometries, multi-layer photonic circuits with reduced footprint, and enhanced light routing, leading to compact optical interconnects 71 . By enabling monolithic 3D photonic chips, FLDW transforms bulky optical setups into compact, high-performance systems 37 . This rapid prototyping capability supports diverse materials such as glass 111 , polymers 49 , and crystals 150,296 , making it possible to create buried optical structures with minimal material removal. The signi fi cant reduction in fabrication costs and the facilitation of on-demand, customized photonic device manufacturing underscore FLDW ' s advantages. Beyond fabrication, recent technological advances have made it possible for FLDW to have precise control over refractive index modi fi cations, optimizing waveguide performance for various applications. Tailoring refractive index contrast for low-loss waveguides 70 , engineering waveguide mode pro fi les 37 , and achieving ultra-low propagation loss 169 and small bending radii signi fi cantly enhance photonic circuit performance 66,69 . These capabilities contribute to high-quality optical interconnects 73 , polarization-maintaining devices 273 , and mode converters 66,67 . The ability to create 3D waveguides with customizable 3D geometries and refractive indices has made FLDW a revolutionary technique in integrated optics. In this section, we provide a concise review of FLDW 3D waveguide devices and their applications in 3D photonic optics (Fig. 15), a concept fi rst conceived by Nolte et al. 230,297 FLDW has emerged as a powerful tool for fabricating optical waveguides with high precision and fl exibility.

FLDW facilitates the seamless integration of passive components such as waveguides, micro-ring 233 , Bragg-gratings 232 , couplers 139,177,231,272 , and splitters 230 with active photonic elements like lasers 298 -300 , ampli fi ers 301 -303 , and nonlinear components 267,268 . This integration enables monolithic all-optical processing systems, reducing the need for external components and improving circuit ef fi ciency. The technology also plays a crucial role in quantum 59 and nonlinear photonics 267 , fostering the development of entangled photon sources 304,305 , modulator 7,306 , and quantum processors 9,307 . By enabling integrated quantum circuits for photon entanglement and computation, tailoring nonlinear interactions for frequency conversion, and creating ultra-low-loss circuits for quantum applications 162,308 , FLDW is advancing scalable quantum computing and secure optical communications.

Compatible with various transparent materials, FLDW supports large-scale photonic circuit manufacturing through hybrid integration 309 , underscores its versatility in constructing multifunctional devices such as integration of FLDW waveguides in a lab-on-chip 184,235 . Hybrid material integration further enhances multifunctional photonic chip performance, facilitating future breakthroughs in biophotonics, high-power laser systems, and ultra-broadband communication networks. Meanwhile, as FLDW technology matured with the introduction of advanced laser beam-shaping techniques (as discussed in Section 3.1), precise control over the spatiotemporal characteristics of the laser pulses enables the creation of complex 3D waveguide geometries and multimode waveguides 139,243 , expanding the range of applications in integrated optics. In more recent developments, FLDW has enabled the fabrication of hybrid and multifunctional devices by combining waveguides with other photonic components of different sizes, including sub-micrometer-scale planar waveguides 74 , centimeter-scale interconnector 71,84 , and meter-scale astronomical detectors 259,310 . These advances enable the integration of both active (ampli fi ers, modulators, detectors) and passive components within the same 3D waveguide structure, paving the way for ultra-broadband, high-capacity photonic systems 37 . This seamless incorporation enhances the functionality of waveguide-based devices, unlocking new possibilities for next-generation integrated-optics and high-performance optical communication networks 179 .

Fig. 15 | Roadmap charting the remarkable progression of the FLDW waveguide devices, emphasizing pivotal 3D integration techniques while referencing signi fi cant technical breakthroughs .

<!-- image -->

Despite the signi fi cant advancements in FLDW technology, there still remain several challenges, including the need for better control over the material properties and more reliable large-area and high-speed fabrication techniques. An innovative approach, inspired by fi ber grating writing technology, involves combining a femtosecond laser with a phase mask to enable high-speed, long-distance direct writing of low-loss waveguides using low-repetition-rate femtosecond lasers 217 . Future research may focus on overcoming these limitations to enable the development of fully integrated optical systems. Furthermore, continued exploration into new materials and hybrid integration techniques will likely drive the next generation of FLDW-based optical devices.

## PERSPECTIVES AND OUTLOOK

FLDW has emerged as a transformative approach in photonic integration, uniquely enabling the fabrication of three-dimensional (3D) optical circuits with submicron precision in a wide range of transparent substrates. In contrast to traditional 2D photonic platforms, FLDW supports truly volumetric integration of optical waveguides and devices, allowing for compact, complex, and multifunctional photonic systems within a single glass chip. This capability is critical for realizing large-area PICs, which require high-density, multi-layer interconnects to support advanced applications such as optical computing, quantum communication, and photonic-electronic co-packaging. Compared to traditional glass-based PLCs, including SOI 11 -19 and ion-exchange 311 waveguides, 3D FLDW waveguide offers key advantages in its fabrication processes, particularly its ability to create complex, multilayered structures and integrated functionalities that traditional PLCs may struggle to achieve. Potential synergies exist where 3D FLDW chips could complement traditional PLCs by enabling advanced integration, such as high-density multifunctional components and enhanced optical interconnects that traditional PLCs may not easily support. Additionally, hybrid systems combining both 3D FLDW and traditional PLCs could be utilized for applications requiring different performance characteristics, such as low loss and high scalability, which are critical in fi elds like telecommunications and quantum computing.

This review has highlighted the key technological advances that underpin the progress toward large-area 3D PICs, including innovations in refractive index modi fi cation mechanisms, waveguide morphology control, spatial beam shaping, and low-loss laser-writing techniques. These developments have enabled substantial reductions in propagation and bend losses, more accurate mode- fi eld tailoring, and the creation of novel device geometries not achievable with planar processes. Importantly, recent breakthroughs -such as conformal waveguide shaping, high-precision stress management, and the ability to engineer arbitrarily tailored index pro fi les -are unlocking new degrees of freedom in 3D photonic design.

However, there still remain several challenges. The relatively low index contrast in glass limits the miniaturization and bend compactness compared to semiconductor-based platforms, which poses signi fi cant constraints for dense routing in large-area layouts. While strategies such as stress-induced con fi nement, subwavelength structuring, and highindex doping offer promising solutions, they often introduce tradeoffs in fabrication stability, uniformity, and optical losses. Furthermore, insertion and coupling losses -particularly at chip -fi ber and chip -chip interfaces -still require innovative coupling structures and alignment schemes. Standardization of packaging and alignment for large-area systems is another pressing need, particularly as system-scale integration becomes more practical.

To fully realize the potential of FLDW for large-area PICs, future efforts should prioritize the convergence of advanced fabrication methods (e.g., adaptive beam shaping, OCMS, and multi-focus writing) with material innovations (e.g., custom glass compositions, hybrid substrates). Additionally, the integration of FLDW with active elements, nonlinear components, and programmable photonic devices will be essential for broadening the functional scope of 3D photonic systems. Incorporating arti fi cial intelligence and machine learning into fabrication work fl ow optimization may also enable higher reproducibility and throughput.

In conclusion, the path forward for large-area 3D PICs in glass lies in synergizing precise 3D waveguide writing with scalable fabrication and packaging strategies. Continued progress in understanding laser -matter interaction, improving material platforms, and developing system-level design principles will be key to overcoming current limitations and unlocking a new era of versatile, deeply integrated, and multifunctional 3D photonic systems.

## Laser Repair and Clean of Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography Photomasks

Tod Robinson *a , Jeff LeClaire a , Iacopo Mochi b , Ricarda Maria Nebling b , Yasin Ekinci b , Dimitrios Kazazis b

a Bruker BNSM RMRBU (United States), 430 S. Congress Ave., Ste. 7, Delray Beach, FL, USA 33445; b Paul Scherrer Institute (Switzerland) ODRA/119, Forschungsstrasse 111, 5232 Villigen PSI, Schweiz

## ABSTRACT

This publication is a continuation of a prior work on the process space available for the repair and localized cleaning of extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL) photomasks with the fpIII femto-pulsed deep ultraviolet (UV) repair tool.  This next  phase  of  work  was  done  in  partnership  with  the  Paul  Scherrer  Institute  (PSI)  to  provide  a  more  systematic examination of  the  process  space.    In  these  tests,  specialized  cells  were  produced  to  systematically  test  the  effect  of variations in the fpIII laser parameters with both carbon and HSQ (hydrogen silsesquioxane) absorber material pin dots on multilayer fields, according to design of experiments (DOE) methodology. Blank (no pin dot) test cells and pin dots were  inspected  both  with  nmVI  AFM  and  PSI  RESCAN  EUV-actinic  lensless  metrology  before  and  after  laser processing.  This data was then analyzed with full-factorial DOE, and less structured techniques, to provide insights into the capability of a modelled optimal fpIII laser process.

Keywords: Photomask, repair, clean, contamination, particle, laser, EUV, sub-resolution.

## 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 Background

In  prior  work,  proof  of  concept  was  shown  for  the  application  of  ultrashort  (femtosecond)  pulse  DUV  laser  repair systems  to  the  removal  of  small,  high  aspect,  contaminates  from  EUV  photomasks  with  no  detectable  impact  on printability 1 .  The capability of the laser system was shown on both multilayer and absorber for defects with a number of different compositions, including metal, silicon, carbon, and unknown material (see top panel of Figure 1).

The  bottom  panel  of  Figure  1  shows  initial  work  to  determine  laser  parameter  thresholds  for  detectable  (by  EUV printability)  multilayer  damage.    These  parameter  values  and  ranges  were  then  compared  to  those  used  in  the demonstration repairs (top panel of Figure 1) where there was a successful repair yield of 77% for a total of 73 defects.

The next phase of work was done in partnership with the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) to provide a more systematic examination  of  the  process  space  available  for  the  repair  and  localized  cleaning  of  extreme  ultraviolet  lithography (EUVL) photomasks with the fp-III femto-pulsed deep ultraviolet (UV) repair tool.  In these tests, specialized cells were produced to systematically test the effect of variations in the fp-III laser parameters with different absorber material pin dots on multilayer fields and were inspected both with Merlin AFM and PSI RESCAN EUV printability inspection.

*tod.robinson@bruker.com; phone 1 561 330-0411; fax 1 561 330-0896; bruker.com

Figure 1.  Prior  proof  of  concept  demonstration  repairs  of  real  particulate  defects  on  an  EUV  photomask  (top  panel).    Initial testing of laser parameter thresholds for printable multilayer damage (bottom panel). 1

## 2. METHODOLOGY

## 2.1 Apparatus and overall test procedure

The apparatus for this work is summarized in Table 1.  The first step of the overall process was to produce a test sample (and adaptor chucks to allow the sample to be loaded in mask repair toolsets) designed specifically for systematic laser repair process testing.  A standard test sample was produced by PSI that consisted of repeating cells of different pin dot type absorber defects on multilayer (see Figure 3).  This sample was then to be inspected with the RESCAN apparatus for EUV printability of the defects before laser repair and then shipped to Bruker RMR for AFM inspection before laser repair.  After these AFM scans, laser repairs are performed on each of the pin dot defects in the targeted test die using varying laser parameters determined from pre-planned full factorial design of experiments.  Once these test repairs are performed, the same sites were AFM scanned to determine the topographic changes (if any) of each of these defects.  In the final stage, the sample was shipped back to PSI where it was once again inspected with the RESCAN apparatus for EUV printability.    Other  dies  were  also  inspected  for  additional  (originally  unplanned)  tests  as  well  as  to  provide  a supplement of pre repair defect data (there were indications in AFM scans that defect variations were similar for the same sub die location).

Table 1, summary of the apparatus used in this work

| Purpose                    | Apparatus                           |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Laser Photomask Repair     | Bruker RMRfp-III                    |
| EUV Printablity Inspection | PSI RESCAN                          |
| AFM Inspection             | Bruker RMRMerlin Nanomachining Tool |

## 2.2 Apparatus review: RESCAN EUV metrology

RESCAN is a lensless microscope dedicated to EUV mask inspection operating at the Swiss Light Source synchrotron. 2 The microscope relies on coherent diffraction imaging (CDI) to reconstruct the complex amplitude of the mask surface. A coherent EUV beam is focused on the sample surface with an angle of incidence of 6 degrees. The sample plane is scanned, and a pixel detector records the diffracted light for each position of the object. The complex amplitude of the sample is reconstructed using ptychography 3 , a noise-robust CDI technique that makes it possible to retrieve the phase and the amplitude of the object under investigation. RESCAN can detect amplitude defects as small as 50x50 nm 2  and characterize  the  phase  of  buried  structures  with  an  uncertainty  of  2%. 4 In  the  current  experiment,  each  of  the reconstructed  images  has  a  pixel  size  of  32.5  nm  and  a  spatial  resolution  of  45  nm.  Each  corresponding  dataset  is constituted by 141 diffraction patterns, covering a sample area of about 450 μm 2 .

## 2.3 Apparatus review:  fp-III Femtosecond Laser Photomask Repair System

The fp-III photomask repair tool employs a deep ultraviolet (DUV) 258 nm wavelength, femtosecond pulsed laser with high numerical aperture (NA) objectives.  Compared to prior toolsets, the fp-III has increased stability, reliability, and a smaller cleanroom footprint.  Repairs are performed with one of two different objective lenses.  The 50X objective is most often used for through-pellicle repairs and dry cleaning (due to its longer working distance) and typically shows thin film removal beam burn diameter around 300 nm in diameter.  The 150X, or highest magnification objective, is used when there is no pellicle mounted on the mask (this is automatically detected at mask load, and if a pellicle is present, this objective is locked out or disabled from being selected).  The nominal beam burn diameter for the 150X on most photomask absorbers is approximately 200 nm.  Another unique feature of the fp-III is that it has integrated features to support  particle  and  surface  clean  processes  that  allow  for  EUV  photomask  defect  selective  repair  and  clean  with potentially no detectable mask damage.

Figure 2, fp-III advanced laser photomask repair system

<!-- image -->

## 2.4 Sample for RESCAN EUV Metrology

Figure 3 shows a summary of the test defect matrix pattern for the sample specifically made for the RESCAN apparatus. The sample's substrate was a silicon wafer cut to 2 x 2 cm with a testing pattern in the center and two reference patterns in the upper corners.  All repairs and AFM scans were performed on the center test pattern only which included a 4 x 4 array  of  die  with  identical  patterns  and  defects.    Each  die  (labelled  0-9  then  A-F  as  shown  in  Figure  3)  was  then comprised of a 3 x 3 array of sub die (referred to by row and column number, for example row1 column 2, or R1C2). Each sub die was even further comprised of 3x3 um square cells, each of which could contain up to 50 defects.  With this very large number of defect sites, most of the repairs were focused on one die (die B as seen in Figure 3), additional test repairs were performed in R1C3 sub die of die F as well as some pre repair referencing metrology performed in dies A and C.

Figure 3, sample pattern layout for RESCAN EUV metrology

<!-- image -->

There were two different defect sizes (and aspects) evaluated and two different material compositions for the pin dots. These two materials were hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and carbon (C).  The former material (HSQ) was the same material as the absorber material for all of the surrounding patterns and had a maximum height equal to the nominal absorber thickness of approximately 200 nm.  These were high aspect pin dot defects found only in row 3 of the 3x3 sub die matrix shown in Figure 3.  Although the HSQ defects were processed, it should be noted that results for HSQ and a third  laser  cleaning  process  are  not  included  here,  but  will  be  reviewed  in  a  future  publication,  and  some  promising results of a new process that provides an even more complete EUV repair and clean solution will be shown.

The other defect material, the carbon (C) pin dots, came in two different sizes and aspect ratios as shown in Figure 4.  In the first row of the 3x3 sub die were the high aspect pin dot defects as shown in the left panel of Figure 4.  As shown in the figure inset table, there were 91 of these C defects in die B with a z height range from 27.7 to 204.6 nm (mean 91.6) and a full-width half-max (FWHM) ranging from 131 to 306.5 nm (mean of 221.1).  The low aspect c-pin dots in sub die row 2 had a z height range from 12.5 to 19.7 nm (mean 13.8) and a FWHM range of 499.5 to 682.5 nm (mean 578.6). Calculating the aspect ratios from these numbers (AR = z-height/FWHM) we get a range of 0.15 to 1.08 (mean 0.43) for the high aspect, and a range of 0.02 to 0.03 (mean 0.02) for the low aspect carbon pin dot defects.

Figure  4.    AFM  inspection  results  for  carbon  pin  dot  defects  in  die  B  prior  to  laser  test  repairs.    All  units  shown  are  in nanometers.    A  conceptual  schematic,  an  example  AFM  scan,  and  raw  AFM  topographic  measurements  are  shown  for  high aspect (left panel) and low aspect (right panel) defects.

<!-- image -->

In doing a large number of pre-repair AFM scans of die B, and other dies there were a couple of observations of interest that helped to define how the test procedure developed.  The first observation was that although there was a large range in C defect sizes and aspect, there was some general groupings in the values.  Thus, when the full factorial tests were defined for the laser processing parameters, the test sites were grouped so that their sizes were as close as possible to each other for that test.  This meant that none of the tests were performed sequentially in placement on the sample but were scattered throughout the sub die row.  It should be noted that for this work there are broad generalizations being made here in the defect  sizes  (high  aspect  versus  low  aspect  defects).    However,  with  further  differentiation  in  these clusters, it may be possible to improve and clarify the analyses and modeling of the process data.

The second observation was that the variations in the high aspect carbon defects had a correlation to their location by, and within, each sub die.  This feature of the test substrate was used to obtain comparable pre-data for those die where testing was performed, but no AFM pre-repair scans were collected.

Once the defect types were classified and grouped, the next consideration for test planning was the laser repair processes to be applied.  Three different processes (parameters are not necessarily in order) with 2x different value ranges were evaluated.    The  first  was  the  spot  process  where  the  laser  beam  is  indexed  to  a  location  on  the  mask  surface corresponding to the (DUV imaging) visual center of the defect.  is the defect site is then exposed with a defined laser energy  for  some  period  of  time  and  intensity.    This  process  has  three  critical  parameters  for  DOE  tests  (which  for purposes here will be referred to as parameters A, B, and C).  The second process is the area process where the beam is moved over the mask surface in a defined region according to a programmed series of movement vectors in the XY plane (of the mask surface).  This process was tested with five defined critical processing parameters (parameters A through E).    The  final,  and  third,  process  was  a  new  process  still  currently  in  development.    A  systematic  DOE  was  not performed with this new process.  Instead, a best of breed set of parameter values, determined from prior demonstration repairs were used.  For the third process, the primary objective was to determine what the removal efficiency was for the high aspect carbon pin dot defects and whether there were any detectable effects on multilayer EUV printability.

In total, there were at least six different laser processing parameters which were targeted as being critical in DOE testing. These  parameters  included  spot  overlap,  number  of  laser  pulses  exposed  to  the  surface,  motion  vector  speed,  focus offset, vector spacing, and mean laser pulse energy.

## 3. RESULTS

## 3.1 High Aspect C-Defects (AFM) Repaired with Spot Process

Looking first at the results from testing the high-aspect carbon defects, one sees a representative example of the AFM result before (left side) and after (right side) laser test repair (using the spot process) in Figure 5.  As seen in this case, there was a significant reduction in the maximum z-height of the defect (from 76 to 10 nm) and full width half max (FWHM, from approximately 206 to 74 nm) with less than 3 nm of topographically-resolved affect to the multilayer substrate.    It  should  be  noted  that  the  overall  slope  seen  in  these  scans  are  an  artifact  of  thermal  drift  in  the  AFM scanning tool.  This example shows what was observed over the hundreds of AFM scans manually examined; there was a clear variation in the amount of material removed according to the laser parameters applied in each test.

Figure 5. Typical AFM results for a high aspect (HAR) carbon pin dot defect pre (left side) and post (right side) laser test repair. In this example, there was a significant reduction in the maximum z-height (from 76.5 to 10.1 nm) and FWHM (from approximately 206 to 74 nm) with less than 3 nm topographic damage to the substrate.  The overall slope to the surrounding surface seen here is an artifact of thermal drift in the AFM scanning tool.

<!-- image -->

Once the testing was performed, and all of the pre and post repair data was collected, it was first critical to determine what the best (or most physically representative) single measurement was to use in the DOE analysis.  For the EUV imaging produced by RESCAN inspection, this step is trivial since the EUV amplitude attenuation (and later separate analysis, the relative phase shift) with respect to the surrounding references can be readily seen as the relevant measured response.    With  AFM  topographic  measures,  however,  the  single  best  measure  can  be  a  little  less  clear.    Figure  6 graphically reviews the raw measurements performed on the AFM scans.  It also shows that all of the pin dot defects were  generalized  to  be  three  dimensional  Gaussian  shapes.    Maximum  z-height,  full  width  half  max,  and  even  the minimum  height  (to  characterize  any  topographically  measured  affect  to  the  multilayer  Ru  cap  or  multilayer)  all characterize the defects size.  However, all of these parameters can be correlated, possibly to variable degrees, in their impact on removal of the defect.

<!-- image -->

Figure 6. Schematic to define AFM measurement parameters on pin dot defects before (left panel) and after (right panel) laser repair processing.

Table 2 summarizes four different measures evaluated for use with the HAR carbon pin dots, and all of the other defects measured  with  AFM.    These  measures  included  z-difference,  z-difference  percent,  volume  difference,  and  volume difference percent.  Refer to Table 2 for the equations used to calculate each of these  measures.  Full factorial DOE analyses were then separately run for each result and the consistency of the top three (highest impact) parameter across all  of  the  HAR  and  LAR  carbon  pin  dot  tests  for  all  interaction  orders.    As  seen  in  the  table,  the  volume  difference percent  had  the  most  consistency  across  all  of  these  tests.    The  volume  difference  percent  can  also  be  viewed conceptually as the best measure of defect removal, since it included both the z height and the FWHM and accounted for variations in both of these parameters for the defects before repair.

Table 2. Volume Difference Percent was best measure (in red box, applied to area DOE's).

## 3.2 Low Aspect C-Defects (AFM) Repaired with Spot Process

Figure 7 shows an example of the pre (left panel) and post (right panel) spot process repair AFMs of a low aspect carbon defect.    Whereas  the  high-aspect  defect  removal  primarily  met  expectations,  the  low  aspect  defect  results  were significantly more complex.  As the aggressiveness of the laser removal process was increased, the main body of the defect remained, for the most part, unchanged.  There was, however, the appearance of new peaks on top of the defects that  often  had  the  appearance  of  regularly  spaced  surface  texturing.    This  texturing  appeared  to  coincide  with  some combinations of parameter values while other defects were not visibly affected as seen in the AFM.

Figure 7. Low Aspect C-Defects (AFM) (right panel).

<!-- image -->

As seen in Figure 6, the AFM manual measurement methods developed for the high aspect, fairly 3D gaussian shaped, carbon defects would have difficulty measuring some of these textured post repair defects.  The volume of these defects was approximated by using the peak height defined by the smaller peaks but adjusting the FWHM to accommodate for the reduced material volume.

## 3.3 Spot Process Analyses

The  first  stage  in  the  overall  spot  process  analysis  was  to  apply  full  factorial  design  of  experiments  techniques  to determine  what  were  the  pareto  principle  parameters  for  this  process.    The  collected  best  metric  (percent  volume difference) data from all of the DOE's was applied to the full factorial design of experiments methodology as shown in Table 3.  These results were then compared and contrasted for the two different parameter ranges (low range versus high range) for the two different defect size domains (high aspect versus low aspect).

For the high aspect carbon defects (AR~0.4), as seen in Table 3, parameters A and C appear to be the primary variables. At higher parameter A ranges, parameter C appears to become more dominant.  Looking at the low aspect (AR~0.02) carbon defects in Table 3, the first order parameter interaction AxC appears to be the most important input at low ranges of parameter A.  At higher ranges of A, parameter B becomes the more significant influence on the low aspect carbon defects.

These  significant  differences  in  the  dominant  input  parameters  suggests  that  one  may  be  looking  at  four  distinct processes  in  these  four  DOE  tests.    This  further  suggests  that  it  may  be  required  to  separately  model  each  of  these regimes separately in their topographic changes with laser repair.  This is unsurprising for the high versus low aspect carbon defects given the complexities in characterizing the post AFM scans of the latter.

Table 3. FFDOE Analyses of C pin dot AFM results.

<!-- image -->

In  analyzing  the  carbon  pin  dot  defect  data  from  spot  process  repairs  with  RESCAN  EUV  inspection,  the  amplitude attenuation results are the primary focus.  Since the laser processes applied was intentionally highly variable, the defect that experienced the greatest change in reflectivity (referred to here as the best of breed repair) is of most interest.  In this high aspect carbon defect repair, the actinic EUV relative reflectivity (referenced to untouched blank multilayer) went from 12% to 100%.  Looking at the AFM results from this same repair, one sees that the maximum z-height went from 71 to 6 nm and the FWHM went from 234 to 148 nm with approximately 3.4 nm in Ru cap layer affect.  For the rest of the test defect repairs, due to gaps in each of the full factorial DOE data sets in the EUV results, a FFDOE parameter response slope analysis was not possible.  Instead, a search was performed for an analytical model to correlate to the data which was obtained (see Figure 8). As seen in Figure 8, which shows the current state of the empirically based analytical model search process, the high parameter range for both the high and low aspect carbon defects has a better correlation to the data.  It is currently believed this is due to the lower signal to noise ratio for the lower input parameter ranges (Test 1). One curious observation is that both HAR and LAR models make significant use of the modulo ('mod'), and to a somewhat lesser degree, the logistic functions.

Figure 8. Analytical Empirical Fit Functions of C-Defects (RESCAN EUV) Repaired with Spot Process.

<!-- image -->

## 3.4 Area Process 2 (New Process)

Towards the end of the laser repair testing period, a novel process was used for proof of concept for (i.e. demonstration) contamination selective repairs.  Initial results with this new process were obtained on DUV lithography optical masks, some  examples  of  which  are  shown  in  Figure  9.    As  may  be  seen  in  this  figure,  this  new  area  clean  process  was developed in response to the challenge of selectively removing very low aspect unknown (possibly organic or carbonrich) contaminates that have become distributed over large areas (multiple microns in scale) across sensitive patterns on a DUV optical photomask.  The existing area repair and clean process could potentially recover these areas.   However, it would  be  very  slow  and  arduous  for  the  tool  operator  to  accomplish  this  with  possibly  incomplete  removal  of  the contaminates.    Thus,  a  new  approach  was  considered  which  would  significantly  speed  up  and  simplify  for  complete removal of these contaminates.

Looking further at Figure 9, one may see that (as seen in the SEM as shown) the dark, spread out, contaminate regions appear  to  be  completely  removed.    This  was  confirmed  in  DUV  imaging  on  the  laser  tool  both  before  and  after processing.  The only visible contaminates left after this treatment appear to be more discrete (possibly denser, possibly metallic or otherwise inorganic) nanoparticles which are typically easily and rapidly removed with the laser spot process on both absorber and substrate materials.

Figure 9. SEM proof of concept results for novel area clean repair process (area process 2) as performed on a DUV optical photomask.  Large, low aspect (i.e. spread out) contamination.

<!-- image -->

Due  to  the  dramatically  successes  in  the  proof  of  concept  testing  reviewed  above  with  a  DUV  photomask,  it  was speculated that this same process could also be of significant utility to EUV photomask repair and clean.  EUV masks can be easily contaminated with volatile organic compounds (VOC's) which can significantly absorb EUV wavelengths even when they are very thinly spread out over the surface.  A test with this new area process was performed in sub die row 1, column 3 of die F as shown in Figure 10.  This was not a pre-planned test so the subsequent AFM and RESCAN EUV results were compared to the same measurements in the same sub die in die A.  As one may see in the left panel, these high aspect pure carbon pin dot defects were clearly visible in the fp-III laser repair tool's DUV imaging with both the 50X and 150X objectives prior to laser processing.  This contrasted with the same imaging conditions of the same sub die after processing as is shown in the right panel.  The pin dot defects in the centers of the test cells are no longer clearly discernable.  This sub die was analyzed with AFM, and ultimately RESCAN EUV, post repair metrology.

One may see in the comparison of these histograms that the mean, maximum, and minimum of the distribution were reduced by the area repair as well as the variance of the distribution.  The difference is significant and  clearly  discerned.  However,  the  reduction  is  qualitatively  less  than  what  was  observed  with  the  lower  aspect contamination removed in the demonstration repairs in Figure 9.

The middle panel is the comparable sub die after repair with area process 2.  In these images to EUV actinic amplitude is denoted by the  greyscale  shading  (with  darker  regions  showing  lower  reflected  amplitudes  and  thus  more  absorption)  while  the phase shift is shown by a shift in the RBG values relative to the surrounding reference areas.  In the reference sub die image the high aspect carbon pin dots are visible as a region of darker greyscale shading in the center of the test.  In the repaired sub die, these darker shading regions are no longer visible and there is no clear color shift, which indicates no significant  phase  damage.    Almost  as  important  is  that  the  repaired  cells  do  not  appear  darker  than  the  surrounding multilayer reference areas which indicates the selectivity of the high aspect defect reduction in actinic EUV printability.

In the far-right panel of Figure 12, the histogram distributions for the relative amplitude (i.e. EUV reflectivity) are shown as it was for z-heights in Figure 11.  As with the z-height histograms, the repaired defects (in green in the far-right panel of Figure 12) show discernable improvement than the unrepaired reference defects (in orange for die A and blue for die D).    The  repaired  defects  show  increased  EUV  reflectivity  in  all  of  their  statistics  and  a  decreased  variance  in  their distribution.    It  appears  that  the  repair  increased  the  mean  reflectivity  from  56  to  83%  while  reducing  the  standard deviation from 12 to 7%.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS

For carbon pin dot repairs using the established spot repair process, AFM pre and post laser repair data was analyzed in distinct regimes of defect aspect (high 0.4 AR, versus low 0.02 AR) and laser parameters (low and high ranges).  No removal enhancement was observed for carbon defects of less than or equal to 0.02 AR in the range of laser parameter values generally safe for use on EUV photomasks.  Parameter slopes clarified which laser parameters were most crucial to  affecting  pin  dot  defect  percent  volume  change  (AxC  for  high  aspect  and  B  for  low  aspect  defects).    This  was confirmed in the prevalence of the parameters in the empirically based analytical models and modelling using neural networks (the latter not being shown in this work).  These same empirically based analytical and neural network models with correlation to testing results were established for ongoing process for topological and EUV print optimization.

A  novel  area,  laser-based  process  for  low-aspect  carbon/organics  repair/clean  was  first  introduced  in  demonstration repairs on a DUV optical photomask (Figure 9).  The new process was successfully used in a complementary process ensemble with the spot process in this demonstration where the former removed low aspect (i.e. spread out) contaminates over  large  areas  and  the  latter  process  was  most  effective  with  small  particles.    From  the  experience  of  this demonstration, it was believed this new process could be the final piece to complete the laser repair and cleaning solution for  EUV  photomasks,  so  it  was  initially  tested  on  high  aspect  carbon  pin  dots  on  the  sample  to  be  sent  to  PSI  for RESCAN EUV metrology.  There was significant reduction in these  defects seen in  both AFM  and  RESCAN  EUV amplitude although the degree of cleaning and removal was not as dramatic as was observed in the prior demonstration repairs  of  very  low  aspect  contaminates.  This  reduction for possibly  non-optimal defects, along with  the lack of any detectable (non-selective) damage, reinforces the belief that this new low aspect and low density area process has the potential to be highly complimentary with the more established spot process which works best with dense (metallic), compact high-aspect nanoscale contaminates.
