## 3.3.2. Cross-Linking Gradients in Stimuli-Responsive Materials based Microstructures

DLL can be used to tune the stiffness of specific sections of a microstructure, where the cross-linking gradients are locally predefined by varying the writing parameters (e.g., laser power, speed, and so on). This technique allows to overcome the drawbacks related to the multimaterial process, such as interlayer adhesion issues, that can arise at the micrometer scale.

<!-- image -->

[www.advancedsciencenews.com](http://www.advancedsciencenews.com/)

However, it has to be considered that materials with very low cross-linking densities can achieve large deformations but can be too soft to be self-standing in 3D architectures. On the contrary, high cross-linking densities allow the fabrication of complex structures but with reduced deformability. Therefore, a trade-off is mandatory.

In recent years, because of the lack of active materials suitable for being processed by DLL, many custom-made photocurable materials have been developed having an instrinsic sensitivity to specific external stimuli such as pH (i.e. PAAc, PAAm), temperature (i.e. PNIPAAm), and light (i.e. azobenzene). Once the structure has been fabricated with such kind of materials, its 3D architecture can be further modified by changing the surrounding environment conditions in a 4D-DLL approach (i.e., application of a specific stimulus such as change in temperature or pH). [105 -112] For example, self-propelled microrobots with microgripping and drug release capabilities are developed by combining pH- and photoresponsive materials. [106]

The sensitivity of these materials to the external stimulus changes in dependence of the cross-linking density, and complex actuation and sensing capabilities can be obtained. For example, in the study by Rekstyte et al. [113] the hybrid inorganic -organic photoresist SZ2080 is used for the fabrication of micromechanical structures that can be swelled by ethanol. The amount of solvent-induced deformation is based on the cross-linking density. The structures are composed of more rigid and densely cross-linked regions that are not subjected to swelling and thin deformable lines obtained with fewer scan passages of the laser for having a lower cross-linking of the material. In the presence of different amounts of ethanol in a water solution, the lines are able to deform and rotate around the rigid structure, forming different angles in dependence of the ethanol concentration in solution. Thus, the deformation can be used for microactuation or for sensing the proportion of ethanol and water. Thus, 4D DLL associated with variable stiffness microstructures opens the possibility to fabricate new generations of on-demand reconfigurable and self-morphing untethered microdevices and micromachines for applications in complex biological microenvironments (e.g., remotely minimally invasive operations, targeted drug delivery, cell manipulation, etc.). Indeed, coupling layers of the same material but different cross-linking density provides complex but controlled deformations. Bilayers can be assembled in 3D geometries forming the building blocks of more complex reconfigurable microstructures. Larger, complex, and continuum 3D to 3D shape transformations can be addressed through the assembly of these building blocks endowed with active deforming layers, rigid layers, and hinge joints, by following a programmable smart modular design. [105] In a very recent work, Jin et al. [110] develop a pH-sensitive photocurable material by adding both N -isopropyl acrylamide (NIPAAm; 98%) and acrylic acid functional monomers to an ethyl lactate solution. Then, PVP is used to adjust the photoresist viscosity, dipentaerythritol pentaacrylate (DPEPA) is added as cross-linker, triethanolamine (TEA) is used as a photosensitizer, and 4,4,0-bis(diethylamino)benzophenone (EMK) photoinitiator serves as gel precursor. Once exposed to the laser, the polymerized material shows shrinking and swelling behavior in acid and alkaline solutions, respectively. The sensitivity of the material to pH is tuned with the cross-linking level, and in particular lower sensitivity is observed at higher www.advintellsyst.com densities (i.e., lower and higher levels of pH are required for shrinking or swelling respectively). Then, coupling layers of the same material but different density/crosslinking level, enables bending or rolling of the bilayered structure in response to pH variation because of the coupling of shrinking/swelling reactions. In the same work, a hollow microball with ten stripes distributed along its longitude is fabricated, with each strip divided into two layers: the outer one printed with high laser power (40 mW) and the inner one with a smaller laser power (12 mW) at the same velocity (8 mm s ␀ 1 ). The variation of pH switches in a few seconds the microball shape back and forth between a spherical structure (swelling state) and a slender cylinder (shrinking state) because of the heterogeneous swelling and shrinking degree between the outer and inner layers of strips ( Figure 11 a). In the study b Huang et al., [105] the same approach is used but, in this case, bilayers are assembled in 4D (i.e., timedeformable) building blocks (Figure 11b). Very complex deformable structures are then obtained by assembling such 4D building blocks in a modular mock-up that can change shape, e.g., a microscale race car transforming in a humanoid microrobot (Figure 11c).

<!-- image -->

This kind of self-shaping mechanism is very useful for fabricating innovative self-morphing machines at the microscale because their modification can be actuated and controlled wirelessly and on-demand. Also, the method does not require a manual assembly, which is not trivial at that scale. For example, in the study by Hu et al. [112] a pH-responsive hydrogel is used for the 4D printing of complex microcages developed to capture microparticles. Indeed, increasing the pH over the ionization threshold (pH ¼ 9) causes the swelling of the polymer microparticles, which are captured because of the pore size change in the expanded/contracted states of the hexagonal microcages. When not swollen, the cage size is lower with respect to the microparticles size; the increase in pH causes pore expansion allowing microparticles to enter the cage. Then, by reducing pH the structures shrink again to their initial state, and the particles are trapped inside. The application of magnetic coatings allows for the transportation and remote targeted release of microparticles in a controlled way.

The use of sensitive materials with specific internal structure can also trigger color changes in addition to shape. As an example, in the work of del Pozo et al., [111] 4D photonic microactuators with submicron resolution are fabricated with DLL using supramolecular cholesteric liquid crystalline (CLC) photonic photoresist. After base treatment, the structures show structural color and shape changes when exposed to a variation of humidity or temperature. Indeed, CLC network has a self-organized helical photonic structure that can selectively reflect light. Base treatment acts cleaving hydrogen bonds among specific molecules, resulting in a charged hygroscopic photonic polymer sensitive to changes in humidity and temperature. A variation of humidity causes the change of water vapor in air, directly inducing the structure to expand or contract. Alternatively, a change in temperature affects the rate of water evaporation, thus indirectly inducing the contraction (increase in temperature) or expansion (decrease in temperature) of the structure. Such controlled shape change induces a modulation of the nanoscale CLC pitch in the ordered network, and results in a corresponding color change

## 3.3.3. Tuning of Mechanical Properties by Geometry

Geometry can play a prominent role in tuning the mechanical properties of microstructures to obtain specific functionalities, e.g., force sensing. Indeed, photosensitive resins are usually very

stiff ( E  GPa), but the design of specific architectures can give the structures an elastic behavior. For example, Alvo et al. [114] report the fabrication of microhelices (length 23 -25 μ m, pitch 4.5, diameter 4 -4.8 μ m, and thickness 0.6 μ m) with DLL by using IPG 780 (Nanoscribe, GmbH) photoresist. The helical microstructures show a very high stiffness (mean value nearly 0.82 N m ␀ 1 ) when subjected to tensile elongation test ( Figure 12 a); however, they can elongate up to 39% in the linear range (68% in one case) and sustain forces from 4.2 up to www.advancedsciencenews.com

<!-- image -->

12.8 μ N. Therefore, the microdevice is suitable for force sensing at the microscale as also demonstrated in other works where a spring design has been adopted. [60,114,115]

Noteworthy, in another example, [116] a spring design is used for a microgripper with integrated force sensing. The gripper (with 100 μ m length and width) is fabricated with DLL using IP-Dip photoresist (Nanoscribe GmbH) directly on the tip of an optical fiber for simultaneous sensing and actuation (Figure 12b(i)). A supercontinuum laser source is connected to the optical fiber (with 125 μ m diameter) for illuminating the sensing part of the gripper. The optical sensor is composed of a series of four circular thin (1 μ m) polymer platelets, arranged parallel along the vertical axis (with 10 μ m spacing), and supported by three springs (Figure 12b(ii)). At the end of the optical fiber, the broadband light is partially transmitted and reflected by the parallel plates, and the reflected light is collected back to a spectrometer. The obtained spectra are the readout of the compression state of the gripper, and thus, after a proper calibration it provides the force applied on the gripper. Indeed, when a normal force is applied, the springs compress causing changes in the distance between thin polymer plates and the subsequent change of the spectra. The design of the grippers with flexural hinges allows a compliant underactuated behavior; when an object approaches the palm of the grippers and applies a normal force the fingers close, leading to the gripping and holding of the object (Figure 12b(iii)). The force measurement error is minimal (0.79 μ N), revealing how the fine tuning of the geometry enables a compliant design and accuracy of the force microsensor.

Force sensing is also crucial in mechanobiology research, and Klein et al. [117] pioneered the use of DLL in the field. Indeed, they used a biocompatible photoresist (Ormocomp, Micro Resist Technology, GmbH) to build a 3D web-shaped microstructure via DLL, composed of vertical pillars (15 μ min height) connected by high aspect ratio horizontal beams with variable diameter www.advintellsyst.com

<!-- image -->

(0.66 -1.33 μ m) ( Figure 13 a). This specific design is used for sensing cellular traction forces. Unlike the pillars, the beams deform upon application of traction forces by cultured muscular cells (Figure 13b), which result in the range of tens of nN.

## 4. Conclusion

In this review, current trends in the DLL-based microfabrication of active microstructures are discussed. Taking DLL as a core enabling technology, the overall rationale is based on the different methodology to achieve active constructs, which is posited as indirect, when passive microstructures become active through postprocessing steps, or direct, when active structures are directly obtained by fabricating microstructures with active materials. In indirect methods, functionality is provided by the properties of the materials or biological components used in the postfabrication processing. Noteworthy, structures made out of nonphotosensitive materials can also be obtained by using passive structures as templates, molds, or masters. On the contrary, in direct methods functionality is given by the combination of two factors: the properties of the materials used for DLL (e.g., heterogeneous mechanical properties) and tuning of the laser writing parameters to create cross-linking gradients in stimuli-responsive materials. Here, postprocessing is usually not required.

However, in both cases, the design and fine control of geometrical parameters, enabled by DLL, play a fundamental role in controlling the functionality of the active structures. For example, in magnetically actuated microrobots, the material properties allow magnetic control, but choosing specific designs and dimensions enables a fine control of actuation parameters (e.g., velocity of microswimmers in biological fluids). [32,43] For sensing, among all cases the fine control on geometry is especially crucial in force microtransducers. Indeed, specific designs can be created only by www.advancedsciencenews.com www.advintellsyst.com DLL to achieve compliance by elastic structures at the microscale (e.g., microsprings). [114] The latter must suitably deform under the application of external forces, but need to be fabricated with stiff, reliable materials for avoiding collapsing when a force is applied. As reported in this review, unique spring-like force microsensors are obtained with both indirect and direct fabrication, e.g., by microsprings coated with a conductive material (i.e., CNTs) [49] and by optical-based sensing in a combined spring-plate microstructure, [116] respectively. In case of actuators, instead, soft materials are also used without compromising the efficiency of actuation but enhancing other properties, as in case of gelatin-based soft biodegradable hydrogel microstructures (i.e., GelMa microswimmers), [53,54] which provides a biocompatible substrate to support the neuronal cells growth, or multiple materials with very different mechanical characteristics (e.g., UDA and IPS) combined in the same structure are used integrated in a smart design for allowing complex actuation mechanisms. [101]

<!-- image -->

Indeed, in fabricating 3D active microstructures it is not always possible to clearly distinguish indirect and direct approaches, and in some cases their combination is needed to reach the desired functionality. For example, in the work of Hu, [112] microcages for the capture of microparticles are fabricated with pH -responsive hydrogel in a 4D printing approach (direct). However, targeted release is achieved only by deposition of a magnetic coating on the structures (indirect) and application of a magnetic rotating field.

Finally, in recent years researchers focalized more on the development and optimization of stimuli-responsive materials to be used with DLL for achieving structures with specific functionalities, and material swelling linked to cross-linking is used for wirelessly controlled microactuation, [105,108,110] or for sensing environmental changes (e.g., sensing ethanol vs water) at the microscale in a 4D-DLL approach. [113] However, at the best of our knowledge, mechanical microsensing with soft materials still represents an open challenge that requires investigation on both materials and transducing approaches at the microscale.

## Quantum Dots Facilitate 3D Two-Photon Laser Lithography

Ye Yu, Anatol Prudnikau, Vladimir Lesnyak,* and Robert Kirchner*

In the past two decades, direct laser writing (DLW) technologies have seen tremendous growth. However, strategies that enhance the printing resolution and the development of printing material with assorted functionalities are still sparser than expected. Herein, a cost-effective method to tackle this bottleneck is presented. Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are selected to carry out this task, most importantly via surface chemistry modification to enable their copolymerization with themonomers, resulting in transparent composites. The evaluations indicate that the QDs show great colloidal stability and their photoluminescent properties are well-preserved. This allows further exploration of the printing characteristics of such composite material. It is shown that in the presence of the QDs, the material provides a much lower polymerization threshold with faster linewidth growth, indicating that the QDs form a synergetic relationship with the monomer and the photoinitiator, widening the dynamic range of the material and thus increasing the writing efficiency for broader fields of applications. Lowering the polymerization threshold reduces the minimum achievable feature size by ≈ 32%, which is well-matched with STED-based (i.e., stimulated-emission depletion microscopy) methods in writing 3D structures. The study further elucidates the mechanism of the synergetic behavior, further guiding the future development of functional materials for DLW-related printing technologies.

## 1. Introduction

In the past two decades, 3D direct laser writing (DLW) based on two-photon polymerization (TPP) has developed from a scientific

Kirchner Center for Advancing Electronics Dresden (cfaed) TechnischeUniversität Dresden 01062Dresden,Germany A. Prudnikau, V. concept to a reliable technology with a great potential. [ 1-3] It generally utilizes a femtosecond laser with a central wavelength in the near-infrared range as the 'writing tool' and a UV-sensitive photoresist as the 'writing material'. The TPP process grants spatial addressability along the propagation direction of the laser and thus realizes the true 3D direct writing possibility. TPP-DLW is considered to be a disruptive technology in many cutting-edge technological fields. For example, in the field of optics, the 3D addressability of the technique has been exploited to create free-form refractive microlenses, [4-6] flatlenses/metalenses, [ 7,8] and other advanced micro-optics; [9,10] complex bio-inspired micro/nanostructures were also made possible in cell behavior, wettability, and drug delivery studies. [ 11-14] However, despite the vast development of the technology, certain challenges remain, such as developing functional photopolymerizable materials, reaching smaller feature sizes, higher resolution and throughput, to meet far broader requirements from both academic research and further industrialization.

In order to address the current bottlenecks, much innovation has been shown from various perspectives. For example, in the front line of material engineering, incorporating various functionalities in DLW, [ 15,16] or additive manufacturing in general, has been demonstrated, such as conductivity, [17] piezoelectricity, [ 18] or magnetic properties, [ 19] providing 'writing materials' with better performance and more diverse functionalities. More specifically, DLW of nanocomposites, with embedded optically active nanoparticles, such as semiconductor quantum dots (QDs), can be of particular interest for producing materials for a range of telecommunication applications and photonics. However, one of the main issues in manufacturing of such nanocomposites with superior optical properties is nanoparticle aggregation and their non-uniform distribution within the matrix, which are caused by the poor compatibility between QDs and photoresist that significantly worsens the optical characteristics of the final composite. In the field of wet chemical synthesis, surface modification of colloidal nanoparticles using ligand exchange method is a long-attested strategy to tune their compatibility with various solvents or media. For example, functionalization of low-toxic Cu-Zn-In-S QDs with 4-vinylaniline and zinc methacrylate was shown to provide efficient co-polymerization of nanoparticles with styrene, resulting in transparent composites with homogeneously distributed QDs. [20] In addition, grafting of ligands containing oligomeric chains of polyisobutylene onto www.advancedsciencenews.com Cu-Zn-In-S QDs or CdSe nanoplatelets enables uniform incorporation of these nanoparticles in linear or cross-linked polyisobutylene matrices. [ 21,22] Nevertheless, this strategy has yet to be further adopted into material development in DLW technology, resulting in limited exploration of the functional composite photoresist so far.

<!-- image -->

On the other hand, much effort has been made to advance the frontiers of the TPP technology. For example, in order to reach higher throughput, faster scanning speed is generally required, which calls for materials that are more photosensitive, and have a faster polymerization speed. Fourkas group has demonstrated a special type of polymer that increases the polymerization kinetics with increasing scanning speed. [23] While it could potentially increase the throughput of the DLW technique, more attempts on engineering the TPP-DLW apparatus to enhance the resolution as well as reduce the feature size even further, have been made. These approaches can include resolution augmentation through photoinduced deactivation (RAPID) lithography, [24] two-color photoinitiation/inhibition lithography, [ 25,26] and so on. Among them, one of the most widely employed methods is stimulated-emission depletion microscopy (STED). [27] For example, Wegener group has reported the lateral feature size, which can be reduced from ≈ 220 to 120 nm at optimal conditions. [ 28,29] Here, we would like to caution the readers regarding the comparability of feature sizes across literatures. For example, the minimum line width of 55 nm reported in ref. 29 was obtained only on isolated lines on the substrate, which is inherently smaller than that of the 3D structures. Furthermore, the wavelength of the working laser, the objective used in the system, as well as the refractive index of the photoresist used, are all crucial factors to consider. Our results shown in this study primarily focus on the DLW conditions for 3D structures, as we believe it applies to a much wider perspective in this field of technology. Despite the high effectiveness of these strategies, the prerequisite of two perfectly-aligned, shape-controlled laser beams has severely limited the practicality of aforementioned techniques that are based on various spatially-selected depletion methods, rendering it to be time-consuming, of high maintenance effort, and costly. Additional approaches for increasing throughput, such as parallel processing, e.g., by beam multiplying, will directly benefit from material innovations.

Herein, we provide a cost-effective strategy to realize an efficient feature size reduction by incorporating co-polymerizable InP-based QDs into the photosensitive material. QDs are widely used in many fields, yet in 3D two-photon laser lithography systems, QDs are mostly incorporated by physical mixing, [30-32] resulting in an unavoidable aggregation, causing low loading capacity and severe quenching of their photoluminescence (PL) as well as an increased consumption of the photoinitiator. First, we demonstrate a reliable route to chemically modify the QD surface to realize co-polymerization, enabling a high loading capacity and retaining strong PL of InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS core/shell/shell QDs upon TPP at the same time. Furthermore, we conducted systematic evaluation of the effectiveness in feature size reduction, confirming that high concentrations of QDs do enable feature size reduction that is on par with that induced by STED-DLW. We further studied the mechanism of such effect and confirmed the synergetic interaction between the QDs and the photoinitiator, which includes lowering the polymerization threshold by co-initiating

<!-- image -->

www.advmat.de

polymerization and enhancing the absorption cross-section, reducing the diffusion coefficient as well as potentially increasing the polymerization kinetics. We believe our strategy not only provides a unique opportunity to reduce the feature sizes and thus push the technological limitation further, but also offers great potential in direct printing QD-functionalized, high-quality microarchitectures.

## 2. Results

In this study, we used mono-2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl succinate (MMES) as a surface ligand providing the compatibility between photoluminescent InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS QDs and the photosensitive acrylate resist consisting of pentaerythritol triacrylate (PETA) as a cross-linkable tri-functional monomer and phenylbis(2,4,6trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide (BAPOs) as a photoinitiator ( Figure 1 A). MMES has a carboxylic functional group that forms a strong bond with zinc atoms on the QD surface and methacrylate end-group that is capable of co-polymerization with PETA. In addition, both PETA and MMES are esters with a similar structure providing high solubility of MMES-functionalized QDs in PETA. As shown previously, MMES-capped QDs are soluble in polar solvents like ethanol, isopropyl alcohol, or diethylene glycol monoethyl ether acetate and are able to co-polymerize with Bisphenol A ethoxylate diacrylate-based photoresist for conducting negative-tone photolithography of QD films. [ 33] This rationale is illustrated in Figure 1B, followed by a simplified depiction of the principle of TPP-DLW in Figure 1C.

To assess the ability of MMES-capped QDs solution in PETA to form 3D luminescent microstructures via DLW, we synthesized greenand red-emitting InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS core/shell/shell QDs with PL maxima at 537 nm (referred to as G-QDs) and 622 nm (referred to as R-QDs), respectively. Among various colloidal QDs explored to date, InP-based QDs attract increasing attention as promising alternatives to Cd-containing QDs, owing to an advantageous combination of their low toxicity, high stability, and emission tunability from visible to near-infrared region. [ 34,35] For the QD synthesis, we used a hot-injection approach with tris(trimethylsilyl)phosphine as a phosphorus precursor. [ 36,37] Since the polymerization of PETA is accompanied by the formation of free radicals, which can damage the QDs and thus lead to PL quenching, the InP QDs were covered with a thick ZnSe x S1x /ZnS shell. The as-synthesized InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS QDs with sizes of 7.4 and 11.9 nm (for G-QDs and R-QDs, correspondingly) have a non-spherical shape (Figure S1, Supporting Information) caused by the irregular shell growth due to the lattice mismatch between InP and ZnSe. [38] The resulting core/shell/shell QDs were capped with fatty carboxylic acids and were soluble in non-polar organic solvents, such as hexane, chloroform, or toluene. All attempts to dissolve them in PETA resulted in the formation of scattering dispersions with low concentrations of primarily aggregated particles, which can be seen in Figures S2 and S3 (Supporting Information). This situation is depicted in Figure 1B (left).

To functionalize the QDs with MMES, a surface modification through the ligand exchange was performed via the treatment of the purified particles in chloroform solution of MMES within 24 h. After the treatment, the QDs became insoluble in hexane, which evidences that MMES replaced the original ligand on the www.advmat.de QD surface and shows that this solvent can be used to precipitate MMES-capped QDs from the solution for their purification after the ligand exchange. The efficiency of ligand exchange with MMES is confirmed by FTIR spectra of extensively purified InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS QDs before and after the ligand exchange, shown in Figure 2 .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 1. A) Chemical structure of MMES employed for the functionalization of QDs, PETA and BAPOs used as a monomer and a photoinitiator in TPP, respectively. B) Schematic illustration of QDs functionalization with methacrylate end-groups and the influence of QDs modification on their distribution in a cross-linked polymer. C) Illustration of the principle of DLW, showing a set of galvo mirrors deflecting the laser beam along two directions. Note the immersive oil in between the objective and the cover slip is omitted for clarity.

<!-- image -->

Both initial and new ligands have carboxylic anchoring groups attached to the QDs surface in anion (carboxylate) form (Xtype ligand), [ 39] evidenced by a characteristic doublet at 15301540 cm -1 and 1430-1440 cm -1 in the FTIR spectra of the QDs before and after the ligand exchange. These features result from the splitting of asymmetric C = O stretching vibration into two bands (corresponding to the asymmetric and symmetric stretching modes) due to the interaction of carboxyl groups with metal atoms on the QDs surface. [40] In the case of the as-synthesized QDs, a group of highly intensive bands in the range of 28003000 cm -1 confirm the presence of the ligands with long alkyl chains. These bands can be attributed to the symmetric and asymmetric vibrations of methylene units (2848-2850 cm -1 and 2915-2917 cm -1 ) and asymmetric vibrations of methyl groups

(2952 cm -1 ). Despite the fact that MMES molecules also have methylene units, they exhibit extremely weak signals compared to the molecules having long hydrocarbon chains, since the intensity of vibrations of these units is proportional to their amount in the molecule. In addition, the intensity of these vibrations is further reduced by the chemical bonding of methylene units with heteroatoms. [41] The absence of bands in the range of 28003000 cm -1 in the FTIR-spectra of MMES-treated QDs provides an evidence of complete replacement of the initial ligand. In addition, after treatment with MMES the FTIR-spectra exhibit another group of bands at 1700 and 1144 cm -1 attributable to the stretching of carbonyl and (O = )C-O units of the ester moiety. [ 42] As can be concluded from the analysis of the FTIR-spectra, the treatment of InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS QDs with MMES leads to the efficient replacement of the initial ligands. It is worth pointing out that efficient functionalization of QDs by MMES can be ensured only in the case of certain surface properties of nanoparticles. Since MMES is an X-type ligand and has a strong affinity to cations, QDs used for the functionalization with MMES should have a high proportion of cationic facets on the surface and the

15214095, 2023, 29, Downloaded from https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adma.202211702 by National Institute Of Technology, Wiley Online Library on [14/03/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License www.advancedsciencenews.com initial ligands should not exhibit stronger affinity to these facets than carboxylates (for example, phosphonates or thiolates).

Figure 2. FTIR spectra of the as-synthesized InP/ZnSe x S 1 -x /ZnS QDs (GQDs, R-QDs) and after the ligand exchange with MMES (G-QDs-MMES and R-QDs-MMES). As a reference, the FTIR spectrum of MMES is provided in the middle panel.

<!-- image -->

After the ligand exchange, MMES-capped green- and redemitting InP/ZnSe x S1 -x /ZnS QDs demonstrate an excellent solubility in PETA, forming transparent colloidal solutions hereafter referred to as G-QDs@PETA and R-QDs@PETA, correspondingly (see insets in Figure 3 C,D). As one can see in Figure 3A,B, no significant changes in absorption and PL spectra of QDs occur after the ligand exchange and dissolution in PETA indicating the preservation of their optical properties.

The effect of the ligand exchange and transfer into PETA on the optical properties of QDs was also examined by time-resolved PL measurements. From the decay curves in Figure 3C,D, one can see that the PL lifetime values of the QDs before and after the ligand exchange and dispersing in PETA only show a minute change. This further confirms that both the surface modification and the dissolution of the QDs in PETA do not have any noticeable negative impact on their photophysical properties. Upon 780 nm laser exposure, as first demonstrated in Figure 4 A, the composite material can indeed photopolymerize through twophoton process. A simplified depiction of the writing process is shown in Figure 1C. Our results show that the addition of QDs with well-preserved photoluminescent properties and colloidal stability could provide a possibility of direct printing of functional microstructures and devices for optical and/or electronic applications. [ 43-45]

Given the semiconductive nature of the QDs, it would be reasonable to presume that their presence could potentially alter the polymerization behavior, when interacting with the photons with matching energy level during laser exposure. The presumption was corroborated by the smaller feature size in the direct comparison between QD-modified material and the one without. The www.advmat.de minimum achievable feature size of such system can be affected by many aspects. In order to properly evaluate the true minimum achievable feature size, careful selection of the test structure and its parameters is essential. In our experiments, we chose to focus on 3D woodpile structure (the illustration is shown in Figure S4, Supporting Information), since it reflects a wider applicability when employing extremely small feature sizes. Furthermore, the minimum feature size is evaluated ignoring the laser power required to achieve this particular size, thus we refer to it as an 'achievable minimum feature size'. A representative SEM image of the woodpile is shown in Figure 4A, along with both fluorescence and optical microscopy images (Figure 4B). The fluorescence microscopy images reveal that the distribution of the QDs in the PETA matrix is highly homogeneous and printed features exhibit high fluorescence intensities, as a result of the successful MMES-functionalization of the QD surface described above. Conversely, the use of dispersion of the as-synthesized QDsinPETAleads to the non-uniformly distributed QDs, shown in Figure S2 (Supporting Information), where high inhomogeneity and severe aggregation of QDs are clearly visible. Further SEM characterization indicates that many QD agglomerates directly precipitated onto the substrate prior to polymerization, shown in Figure S3 (Supporting Information), leading to severe quenching of the fluorescence signal. This is also evidenced by the significantly lower PL intensity of the poorly-distributed QDs. This result proves that in functionalization of photoresists with nanoparticles, their surface chemistry is crucial for incorporating high concentrations of the nanomaterials, homogeneous distribution, and thus preserving their functionality in the final composite materials.

<!-- image -->

The structural parameters of the woodpiles were also carefully chosen, so that the lateral pitch-the horizontal separation in between two adjacent lines-was large enough to avoid proximity effect, an example of which can be found in Figure S5 (Supporting Information); and the slicing distance-the vertical separation in between two adjacent layers-was large enough to reveal the true waist of the oval-shaped line. The oval-shaped crosssection is the result of the larger axial diffraction limit a z , which is directly influenced by the working wavelength /u1D706 , the refractive index of the medium n , and the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective: [ 2]

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

In our DLW system, with /u1D706 = 780 nm, n = 1.45, and NA = 1.4, we arrive at a z = 727 nm. Based on this value, we chose a relatively large slicing distance of 500 nm, to ensure that the waist of the voxel is always properly exposed for the linewidth measurements, as illustrated in Figure 4C. Consequently, the topmost layer of lines only has very little support at the base, resulting in lines leaning over, which can be observed from the thicker appearance of the horizontal lines in Figure 4D,E. However, the morphology of the lines from lower layers shows good integrity and consistency, which will facilitate the accurate evaluation of the minimum achievable linewidth. Directly from the SEM images showninFigure 4D,E, one can already observe, that the linewidth of woodpiles printed by the QD-modified PETA (Figure 4E,

15214095, 2023, 29, Downloaded from https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adma.202211702 by National Institute Of Technology, Wiley Online Library on [14/03/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License www.advancedsciencenews.com www.advmat.de being 140 nm on average) is smaller than that of the pristine PETA (Figure 4D, being 230 nm on average). A wider screening of the minimum achievable linewidths under various laser doses and scanning speeds were then carried out, the scatter plots of the corresponding data are shown in Figure 4F-H. In detail, an orthogonal screening of the laser power and the scanning speed were designed, ranging from a laser power of 20 to 60 mW, and a scanning speed of 16 to 32 mm s -1 . Examining the woodpiles from low laser dose to high laser dose, the linewidths from the first mechanically stable woodpiles were all statistically evaluated. From these three scatter plots, it is evident that in the presence of both green and red QDs, the linewidths of the first mechanically stable woodpiles are all significantly narrower than those from the pristine PETA. From the statistical data presented in Figure 4, the maximum feature size reduction is ≈ 32%, which is on par with that obtained from woodpile structures written by STED-DLW system. [28] We emphasize again that the minimum feature size obtained from 2D line structures is not comparable with that obtained from 3D structures. Furthermore, note that in Figure 4G,H, the achievable minimal linewidths were obtained under much smaller laser dose, as compared to that in Figure 4F. This suggests that with our material, the smaller feature size is achieved through lowering the polymerization threshold as opposed to lowering the polymerization efficiency, i.e., prematurely quenching radicals.

A-D) Absorption and PL spectra (A,B) and PL decay curves (C,D) of solutions of green- and red-emitting InP/ZnSe x S 1 -x /ZnS QDs with the initial ligands in CHCl 3 (G-QDs, R-QDs) and with MMES-capping in PETA (G-QDs@PETA, R-QDs@PETA). <!-- image -->

Progressing from the results presented in Figure 4, we further evaluated the polymerization behavior of the materials over a wide range of laser exposure conditions, as shown in Figure 5 . Unlike the vast majority of the nanostructuring technologies, such as electron beam lithography, photolithography, etc., which only have spatial addressability on 2D planes, 3D TPP-DLW is a volumetric process. When evaluating the www.advmat.de www.advancedsciencenews.com performance of a material in 3D TPP-DLW technology, a wide dynamic range, i.e., the ability to cover a larger volume within a shorter period of time, is equally if not more important than the pursuit of a smaller linewidth. In Figure 5, we identified three sections with distinctive polymerization behaviors, which we marked with color blocks: polymerization sections below the threshold (no polymerization, light orange), unstable structure (blue), and stable structures with measurable lines (green). It is evident that the light orange area where the laser dose is below the polymerization threshold, is largely narrowed in the presence of QDs; and the blue area, representing the unstable structure section, becomes smaller. In other words, the QDs lowered the polymerization threshold of the mixture and further enlarged the operation window. It is especially worth noting, that with relatively higher scanning speed, such as the top-most rows in Figure 5A,B, the impact that the QDs bring appears to be more prominent, which indicates that the polymerization kinetic could be accelerated. We further evaluated the linewidths of individual woodpiles in the SEM images, the scatter plots of which are shown in Figure 5C,D. From this comparison, it becomes apparent that not only the polymerization threshold is significantly lowered by the QDs, but the linewidths of QD@PETA are generally larger as compared to those from pristine PETA under identical writing conditions. The latter suggests that the effective voxel size for QD@PETA is larger. These phenomena facilitate a wider operation window, allow a faster scanning speed, while reducing the minimum achievable linewidth via lowering the polymerization threshold, indicating that our strategy provides a facile and costeffective alternative to enhance the performance of the material in TPP-based 3D laser lithography system.

## 3. Discussion

In order to understand the TPP behavior of our system more comprehensively, we continue the evaluation from various perspectives. It is widely accepted that the presence of QDs not only changes the optical properties of the photoresist, being the immersion medium at the focus spot of the laser; but also potentially creates more complex interactions with the photoinitiator, altering the polymerization behavior. For example, Peng et al. [ 32] reported that the presence of semiconductor QDs dispersed in PETA improves the spatial resolution of structures obtained by DLW based on TPP. The effect was attributed to the additional photon absorption by the QDs during writing and thus the decreased number of photons absorbed by the photoinitiator, which, in turn, led to the reduction of the voxel size and enhanced resolution; Later, Momper et al. [ 46] also demonstrated that the addition of CdSe/ZnCdS nanoplatelets functionalized by thiol-terminated poly(methyl methacrylate) in a commercial acrylate-based resin can be exploited to increase TPP-based 3D printing resolution. In this case, other than reducing the photon absorption by the photoinitiator, the effect was further attributed www.advmat.de to the radical quenching caused by the nanoplatelets. Both led to smaller linewidths achieved in the QD-modified composite, as compared to the pristine one, under identical writing conditions over a wide range of exposure conditions. However, our results present contradictive information, indicating that an in-depth study is still elusive and case-to-case investigation is needed, as discussed below.

<!-- image -->

## 3.1. Polymerization Threshold

Analyzing the data from Figure 4, it is evident that the polymerization threshold, i.e., the minimum power required to trigger polymerization ( P th ), is significantly lower in the presence of the QDs, as compared to that in the pristine PETA. From previous reports, we know that under identical instrumental configuration, the value of P th is always determined by not only the exposure time, but also the concentration and efficiency of the initiator, as well as the choice of the monomer. [ 47] In our study, the addition of QDsfirst leads to changes in the optical properties of the composite, which functions as the photoresist and the immersion media simultaneously. The QDs increase the refractive index of the photoresist by ≈ 0.1, calculated from the concentration of the QDs in PETA (2 wt%). As a result, the laser beam can be focused more tightly, which converts to higher power density under the same laser power output. Second, the high extinction coefficient of the QDs induces large absorption cross-section of the QDs@PETA composite, increasing the actual efficiency of the photoinitiator.

Apart from the reasons discussed above, another essential contribution of the QDs is their active participation in the polymerization process. The QDs exhibit PL upon exposure to 780-nm laser (Figure S6, Supporting Information), indicating that they experience two-photon absorption process and can directly initiate the radical photopolymerization (Figures S7 and S8, Supporting Information). Given that the overall size of the QDs is relatively small, being 7.4 and 11.9 nm for the green and red QDs, respectively, it is likely that the initiation of the polymerization occurred via charge or energy transfer from the QD core to the ligands on the surface.

This is further corroborated by our results shown in Figure S8 (Supporting Information), that a much lower P th in QDs@PETA without the photoinitiator is observed, similar to the photoresist QDs@PETA with the photoinitiator (such as samples shown in Figure 4B,D) and pristine PETA with the photoinitiator. Namely, under the same scanning speed of 16 mm s -1 , the laser power of the polymerization threshold was 20 mW for the QD-initiator pair and 35.7 mW for the photoinitiator. Thus, one can conclude, that the P th is primarily dominated by the presence of the QDs. It is also worth noting, that the morphology of the lines in QD@PETA without the photoinitiator is always poorly defined, as compared to those written in the presence of the photoinitiator. Clear highly localized polymerization sites (Figure S8,

## 3.2. Diffusion Coefficient

Another significant aspect that affects the minimum achievable linewidth is the diffusion coefficient of the active species for photopolymerization. The diffusion coefficient of the QDs can be calculated from the Stokes-Einstein equation:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where k B is the Boltzmann constant, T is the temperature (293 K), /u1D702 is the dynamic viscosity of the material mea- sured to be 812 mPa · s, and R 0 is the solvodynamic radius of the QDs, i.e., the sum of the radius of the QDs measured from transmission electron microscopy images in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), and the length of the ligand estimated to be 1.6 nm. Calculations result in a diffusion coefficient D (G-QDs) = 2.9366 × 10 -14 m 2 s -1 , D (RQDs) = 1.9578 × 10 -14 m 2 s -1 , and D (BAPOs) = 5.0729 × 10 -13 m 2 s -1 , respectively. This confirms that the diffusion coefficient of the QDs is significantly smaller than that of the photoinitiator, which is not unexpected. However, judging from the chemical composition of the QD ligand, which allows copolymerization between the QDs and the monomers, one can deduct that the mobility of the QDs and the active radical chains should be reduced further during the polymerization. The smooth texture of the lines presented in Figure 4E suggests that the photoinitiator was cleaved into radicals and participated in the polymerization process, even when the exposure condition was significantly lower than the polymerization threshold for the photoinitiator. Furthermore, it is well-

15214095, 2023, 29, Downloaded from https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adma.202211702 by National Institute Of Technology, Wiley Online Library on [14/03/2026]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License www.advancedsciencenews.com known that for peroxide-type initiators, chain transfer to such initiator is relatively prominent, and could potentially accelerate the generation of initiating radicals. [ 48] Thus, it stands to conclude, that in the QDs@PETA with photoinitiator, the polymerization is initiated by the QDs via charge/energy transfer, creating radicals at the end of the ligand. The radicals further the chain growth around the QDs and trigger the chain transfer to the photoinitiator molecules, which in turn promotes further polymerization.

<!-- image -->

## 4. Conclusions

We have demonstrated a cost-effective strategy to reduce the feature size in two-photon 3D DLW technique. We show that the QDs were successfully incorporated into the triacrylate material via ligand exchange, which enabled the co-polymerization of the QDs directly into the polymer matrix. This not only greatly improved the homogeneity of the composite, maintaining its transparency and optical properties of the pristine QDs, but also greatly increased their loading capacity. As a result, the refractive index of the composite material could reach a better match, facilitating a better focus. Additionally, the QDs provided a larger absorption cross-section, further enabling a higher absorption power at the focal spot, as compared to that in the pristine material. Further statistical analysis suggests no sign of radical quenching, but instead a larger voxel size and faster linewidth growth were confirmed. We believe that this is a result of a synergetic interaction between the three components in our composite material, namely the QDs, photoinitiator, and PETA, where the QDs initiate the polymerization via charge/energy transfer from the QD core to the ligand on its surface, creating free radicals and advancing the chain growth around the QDs. This further triggers the chain transfer from the PETA chains onto the photoinitiator, further promoting the polymerization at a higher radical concentration and faster kinetics. Our results show a significant feature size reduction of ≈ 32%, which is on par with the optimal result obtained by STED method. Moreover, this effect was achieved not only without exacerbating the asymmetrical voxel shape like in the STED methods, but also free of the hurdle of radical quenching as shown in other reports of nanocomposite materials used in DLW. We believe our method provides an applicable strategy to expand the boundaries of achievable minimum feature size, and also demonstrates a good approach to developing functional nanocomposite materials in 3D TPP-DLW technology and thus potentially enables the direct printing of functional devices in many application fields such as electronics, optoelectronics, and photonics.

## 5. Experimental Section

Materials : Pentaerythritol triacrylate (PETA, technical grade), mono2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl succinate (MMES), 3-(trimethoxysilyl)propyl methacrylate (TMSPMA, 98%), propylene glycol methyl ether acetate (PGMEA, 99.99%), bis-(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)-phenyl-phosphine oxide (BAPOs, 97%), isopropanol (IPA, 99.9%), methoxyperfluorobutane (MOPFB, 99%), chloroform ( ≥ 99%), n-hexane ( ≥ 95%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Acetonitrile (HPLC grade) was purchased from VWR Chemicals. All chemicals were used as received without further purification.

<!-- image -->

www.advmat.de

Circular glass cover slips with a diameter of 25 mm and a thickness of 160-170 µ m were used as substrates. Before usage, the substrates were thoroughly cleaned in IPA bath and blow-dried with compressed nitrogen.

Synthesis of QDs : InP/ZnSe x S 1 -x /ZnS QDs were synthesized using modified procedures, based on published approaches. [49,36] Adetailed description of the synthetic procedures can be found in the Supporting Information.

Ligand Exchange : To functionalize the QDs, 140 mg of MMES were added to the 1 mL of QDs solution in chloroform (30 mg mL -1 ). The solution was stirred on a hotplate at 30 ° C for 24 h in a closed vial protected from light, followed by precipitation using hexane as a nonsolvent with subsequent centrifugation. The obtained precipitate was dispersed in 1.18 g (1 mL) of PETA with intense mechanical mixing alternated with treatment in an ultrasonic bath.

Preparation of Pristine PETA Photoresist : 1 wt% of photoinitiator BAPOs was dissolved in PETA via sonication for 1-3 h at 30-40 ° C, until a pale-yellow viscose liquid was obtained.

Preparation of QD@PETA Photoresist : First, 5 wt% of BAPOs were dissolved in PETA through identical process as described in the previous paragraph. Then, 0.4 g of QDs and PETA (QDs concentration 30 mg mL -1 ) were mixed with 0.1 g of BAPOs@PETA (5 wt%). All photoresists were always kept at room temperature under yellow ambient light for long preservation.

3D Two-Photon Laser Lithography : The classic woodpile structures were chosen as the microstructures for investigation. Before printing, the glass substrates were treated in order to increase the adhesion between PETA and glass. The substrates were first treated by O 2 plasma (Oxford PLASMALAB 80PLUS) with an O 2 flow of 60 sccm and a forward power of 60 W for one minute to activate the glass surface for the silanization. The substrates were immediately transferred into an ethanol bath with TMSPMA concentration of 15 µ L mL -1 for 3 h to complete the silanization. The ethanol was always purged with nitrogen for 30 min before the TMSPMA solution was prepared, in order to minimize the oxidation. Immediately following the silanization, the substrates were rinsed with fresh ethanol and dried with a nitrogen stream. The silanized substrates were always used within a few days and were always kept in a nitrogen box to protect the surface.

The printing was done using a 3D two-photon laser lithography system Photonic Professional GT2 (Nanoscribe GmbH and Co. KG). The system was equipped with a laser with central wavelength of 780 nm, average laser power of 50 mW, repetition rate of 80 MHz. Single laser pulse duration is 100 fs. The naturally linearly-polarized laser beam was converted into circular polarized beam via passing it through a quarterlambda waveplate, then delivered to a beam expander, before it reached the objective. All prints were done using the 'conventional' writing mode, where an index-matching immersion oil was used to bridge the objective and the bottom of the substrate. A set of galvo mirrors were used to deflect the laser beam in x and y directions, combining with a piezo-controlled stage movement along z direction, with which the 3D prints were realized. During the DLW experiments, the laser power was calibrated every two hours, to ensure a constant, reliable exposure condition.

Characterization Methods : The characterization of the morphology of the printed structures was carried out with a scanning electron microscope (SEM) (S4700 Hitachi). Due to the polymeric nature of the samples, all the images were taken under a low acceleration voltage of 2 kV and an extraction current of 10 µ A. For the evaluation of linewidths, an open-source software ImageJ [50] was used. All statistical values were averaged from 15 to 30 measurements across multiple samples to ensure a high accuracy of the data. Correspondingly, the minimum and maximum values from the measurements were shown as error bands, as opposed to the standard deviation. Fluorescence microscopy images, as well as the optical microscopy images were both taken via an inverted optical microscope (Leica DM IRB) equipped with a UV-lamp for the fluorescence imaging, and a halogen lamp for the optical imaging. For the fluorescence imaging of the printed QDs@PETA structures, two bandpass filters were placed in the emission pathways, allowing only the fluorescence from the QDs reaching the camera. All fluorescence images were taken under the www.advancedsciencenews.com identical camera settings, ensuring a straightforward qualitative comparison of fluorescence intensity across various samples.

<!-- image -->

Optical absorption and emission spectra were recorded at room temperature using a Cary 60 UV-vis spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies) and a fluorescence spectrometer Fluoromax 4 (Horiba Jobin Yvon Inc), respectively. Time-resolved PL measurements were performed at room temperature using a Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorocube-01-NL. The samples were excited with a NanoLED-405 pulsed laser diode ( /u1D706 = 403 nm). Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was performed on a Nicolet 8700 FTIR spectrometer using the attenuated total reflectance (ATR) method. Prior to FTIR-measurements InP/ZnSe x S 1 -x /ZnS QDs were purified through precipitation and redispersion (five times) using chloroform as a solvent and acetonitrile (for as-synthesized QDs) or hexane (for MMES-capped QDs) as a nonsolvent. After the final precipitation, QDs were dried under vacuum overnight and the obtained powder was ground and placed onto the ATR crystal.

## Advances in display technology: augmented reality, virtual reality, quantum dot-based light-emitting diodes, and organic light-emitting diodes

<!-- image -->

Jihoon Kang a , Geun Woo Baek b , Jun Yeob Lee a,c , Jeonghun Kwak b and Jae-Hyeung Park d

<!-- image -->

a School of Chemical Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Republic of Korea; b Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Inter-University Semiconductor Research Center, and Soft Foundry Institute, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea; c SKKU Institute of Energy Science and Technology, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Republic of Korea; d Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

## ABSTRACT

Virtual reality, augmented reality, quantum dot light-emitting diodes, and organic light-emitting diodes have progressed over the last two years. Key achievements in these displays are discussed in terms of device performance.

## 1. Introduction

Augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), quantum dot light-emitting diode (QLED), and the organic light-emitting diode (OLED) are next-generation display technologies with remarkable progressive device performances during the last two years. OLEDs are the current leader in the display market, and the device performances of the high-efficiency blue OLEDs were dramatically improved by developing stable blue emitters and device architecture harnessing the excitons with little loss. QLEDs are still behind OLEDs in terms of efficiency and device lifetime, but the rapid advance of QLEDs shines a light on their commercialization in real products through the ink-jet printing process. AR and VR have emerged as the practical display although the market size is still quite small. Apple launched Vision Pro ® using VR technology and triggered the commercialization of VR and AR technologies. It may take time to expand the AR and VR market, but there is no doubt that they will be dominant displays in the future.

In this progress report, recent developments and progress of the AR, VR, QLED, and OLED displays are summarized and the prospect of them is proposed based on the technology and market trend.

<!-- image -->

## KEYWORDS

Augmented reality; virtual reality; quantum dot light-emitting diode; organic light-emitting diode

## 2. Recent advances in augmented reality and virtual reality

AR and VR are emerging fields that provide a new way for users to interact with other people and digital information. From a display technology perspective, the neareye display (NED), also called a head-mounted display (HMD), is the main device that enables many AR and VRapplications. For an ideal VR experience, NEDs need to provide high-resolution immersive virtual images with a wide field of view (FoV) that covers the entire human visual field. For the AR experience, NEDs should present virtual images along with the real scene in front of the user. In AR and VR NEDs, a slim form factor and a wide eye box are also required for a comfortable viewing experience.

In the traditional display sectors, which include the mobile phone, monitor, and TV sectors, the digital image on the display panel is directly seen by the user; thus, the display system's performance is solely determined by the display panel. In AR and VR NEDs, however, the digital image on the display panel is observed through an optics that forms the virtual image of the display panel far from the eye. Therefore, the performance of AR and VR NEDs depends on not only the display panel itself

but also on the associated optics of the NEDs. Hence, various NED display panel techniques, including liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS), organic light-emitting diode on silicon (OLEDoS), micro-LED (also called light-emitting diode on silicon, LEDoS), and laser beam scanning display (LBS) should be mated with proper optics and cooptimized according to the specific AR and VR applications to realize a high-performance system [1-3].

Recently, we have observed progress in AR and VR NED technologies. In the subsections that follow, we briefly review the major advances made in 2022 and 2023, focusing on the display panel and optics together. Along with the status of the micro-display panel, novel optical techniques that reduce the VR NED form factor and enhance the AR NED waveguide are discussed. Advances in focus cue support and foveated display are also reviewed. Finally, the recently emergent digital passthrough AR NED is compared with optical see-through AR NED. Table 1 shows the features of recently reported or commercialized NEDs.

## 2.1. Micro-display panel

A micro-display panel is placed inside the NED that presents virtual images to the user through magnifying optics. In VR, the micro-display panel must have a high resolution to support a wide FoV with a high angular resolution ( ∼ 60 pixels per degree, ppd). The luminance must also be high ( &gt; 1 K nit) to compensate for the optical efficiency loss of polarization-based path folding VR optics, also called pancake lenses, which have recently become popular. In AR, the micro-display panel needs to support integration into a small projection module and have very high luminance ( &gt; 1M nit) to ensure high image visibility during outdoor use, even with the low optical efficiency of the AR optical combiners. Currently, the available micro-display panels include LCoS, OLEDoS, micro-LED (or LED on Silicon), and LBS [26].

LCoS is a mature display technique. Although it requires an additional light source and illumination optics, the luminance can be readily increased with a high-power light source, addressing the high luminance requirement of AR. The polarized light output of the LCoS matches well with diffraction-based waveguide couplers, such as surface relief grating (SRG) and holographic optical element (HOE), which increase optical efficiency. The etendue of the illumination optics also enhances the optical efficiency by projecting all the LCoS light into the waveguide without loss [27]. Therefore, LCoS remains a viable option for waveguide-type AR NEDs. The OLEDoS display is an emerging display type. As it is an emissive display, the OLEDoS does not require an additional light source, which is an advantage in terms of form factor. Recent advances in high-resolution and high-ppi OLEDoS also make it attractive, especially in VR NEDs [28]. However, the maximum luminance of the currently available OLEDoS is approximately 10,000 nits [28], which is insufficient for diffraction-coupler waveguide-type AR NEDs. Therefore, OLEDoS is mainly considered for VR NEDs. For AR, OLEDoS is usually mated with optical combiners having high optical efficiency, such as a Birdbath or reflection-coupler waveguide [26]. Micro-LED is self-emissive and extremely bright ( &gt; 1Mnit), making it ideal for VR and AR. However, a full-color red, green, and blue (RGB) micro-LED panel is still being developed, and many problems with the monolithic full-color LED fabrication process remain [29]. The current option is to combine three mono-color R, G, and B panels using an x-cube, which increases the system volume and makes it difficult to match pixels between the individual panels [26]. Therefore, despite its potential advantages, the micro-LED panel has yet to become a mainstream technique for AR and VR. LBS has a small form factor and high luminance. The narrow linewidth of the laser light source is also beneficial for obtaining high optical efficiency in the diffractionbased couplers. However, scanning optics that uses 1D or 2D micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) mirrors is complex, and the coherence noise coming from the laser is also problematic [1,26]. Currently, LBS is usually applied to AR with free-space optical combiners.

## 2.2. VRNEDformfactor

A slim and lightweight form factor is key to making VR NEDs comfortable to wear. It will enhance the popularity of VR NEDs and expand their application from gaming to the recently emerging spatial computing. The form factor for the VR NED is mainly determined by the gap between the micro-display panel and the collimation lens. To form virtual images at a distance from the eye, the micro-display panel is placed at the focal length of the collimation lens. As the focal length of the collimation lens cannot be reduced arbitrarily at a given aperture size, the current VR NEDs have at least a few tens of millimeters thickness, which is far from a glasses-like compact form factor.

Current efforts to reduce the thickness of VR NEDs include using micro-lens arrays (MLAs) [21], pinhole arrays [30], and pancake lenses [31-33]. In the MLAbased approach, the display panel is placed at the focal length of the MLA. The MLA forms the intermediate virtual image of the display panel, which is magnified and collimated by the collimation lens to form the final virtual image at a far distance. Because the MLA can have a much shorter focal length than a large-aperture collimation lens, the overall thickness of conventional VR NEDs can be reduced to the short focal length of the MLA, thereby achieving a thin form factor. In the pancake lens approach, polarization-based path folding is used. The polarized light from the display panel undergoes double reflection inside the pancake optics, effectively reducing the physical gap between the display panel and the optics. Although the concept of pancake optics is quite old [32], pancake optics has recently become a mainstream approach to achieving a thinner form factor for VR NEDs [31,33].

AlthoughtheMLAandpancakelensapproacheseffectively reduce the thickness of the system, they still pose problems. For instance, in the MLA approach, the loss of resolution is problematic. The display panel is first imaged into the intermediate virtual image by the MLA at magnification m MLA = f collimation\_lens / f MLA, and then it is imaged again into the final virtual image by the collimation lens at magnification m collimation\_lens = dfi nal\_image / f collimation\_lens. Therefore, the overall system magnification is given by m = m MLA m collimation\_lens = dfi nal\_image / f MLA, which is significantly larger than the magnification used in conventional VR, i.e. m = m collimation\_lens = dfi nal\_image / f collimation\_lens. This increased magnification results in a coarser angular resolution of the final image, which requires the display panel to have higher pixel density and resolution for its compensation. When a pinhole array is used instead of the MLA, the displayed images do not have a uniform brightness, which is problematic [30]. In terms of the pancake lens approach, the light efficiency loss and ghost image are problematic [31,33]. For a polarized display panel, the pancake lens only outputs at most 25% of the incident light, wasting the rest 75%. For a non-polarized display panel, the optical efficiency drops even further to 12.5%. Ghost images that are due to nonideal polarization optics can also degrade the image quality [34]. Hence, recent research on pancake lenses has attempted to overcome these limitations by recycling polarized light [33] and enhancing broadband characteristics of the polarization optics on curved surfaces [34] (Table 2).

## 2.3. ARNEDoptical combiner

In AR NEDs, the optical combiner that adds light from the display panel to the light of the see-through view of the real scene is the main optical component that determines the form factor and the performance of the AR NEDs. Among the many optical combiners, including the Birdbath, free-space combiner, and waveguide [1], the waveguide has become a mainstream configuration because of its glasses-like compact form factor and easy 2D exit pupil expansion, which give a wide eye box. For the waveguide optical combiner, couplers that in - and out-couple the light into and out of the waveguide are crucial to obtaining adequate FoV and optical efficiency. Waveguide couplers can be classified as diffraction-based, including the SRG and the HOE, and reflection-based couplers, which use partial mirror arrays and are also called light optical elements (LOEs).

Table 2. Slim VR NED techniques reported in 2022, 2023, and 2024.

| Type          | Feature                                                                | Ref.   |
|---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------|
| Pinhole array | Image non-uniformity compensation by multiplexed retinal projection    | [30]   |
| Pancake       | Stray light analysis and suppression of pancake optics                 | [31]   |
| Pancake       | Optical efficiency enhancement by recycling polarized light            | [33]   |
| Pancake       | Stray light suppression by optimizing the broadband quarter-wave plate | [34]   |
| Metasurface   | Bi-facial metasurface for implementing the pancake lens                | [35]   |

Table 3. AR NED optical combiners reported in 2022 and 2023.

| Combiner Type    | Feature                                                                                                                                      | Ref.    |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| Waveguide + HOE  | 2D exit pupil expansion with enhanced uniformity                                                                                             | [37]    |
| Free space + HOE | HOE recording with off-axis aberration compensation using a freeform mirror. Full color by a single HOE                                      | [38]    |
| Free space + HOE | Chromatic and off-axis aberration compensation using dual HOEs and projection optics with a freeform mirror. Full color by a stack of 3 HOEs | [39]    |
| Waveguide + LOE  | 2D exit pupil expansion, < 2mm thickness                                                                                                     | [40,41] |

The diffraction-based couplers have advantages in form factor, as they are micrometer-thick components attached to or embedded inside the waveguide and they support a sub-millimeter waveguide slab. However, the diffraction-based operation inevitably results in significant wavelength dependency. It reduces the optical efficiency, especially when the linewidth of the display panel light is broad and requires a stack of multiple waveguides of individual colors [36-39]. Reflection-based couplers achieve good image quality free from these limitations, but they usually require a thicker waveguide for embedding the partial mirrors inside the waveguide, and the expansion of the 2D exit pupil is not trivial.

Past approaches commonly used diffraction-based couplers. But, recently, the reflection-based couplers are gaining new attention due to their superior image quality [26]. The recent development of the reflection-based couplers reduced the overall thickness of the waveguide to less than 2 mm and led to the expanded 2D exit pupil [40,41] (Table 3).

## 2.4. Focus cue support

Focus cue support is critical to providing visual comfort to AR and VR NEDs users. Conventional stereoscopic NEDsoffer depth perception only through binocular disparity, which introduces vergence-accommodation conflict (V AC) to the user. VAC is the main cause of visual fatigue in AR and VR experiences. VAC becomes especially severe when the 3D images are at arm's distance from the user. Because this arm's distance is important in AR and VR applications for the interaction between the user and the image, solving the VAC is vital.

Studies that address the VAC issue in AR and VR NEDs have included the Maxwellian view display, multifocal display, varifocal display, light field display, and holographic display. In recent years, all of those display techniques have been actively studied. The Maxwellian display alleviates VAC by presenting always-focused images regardless of the focal power of the eye lens, which is achieved by limiting the effective beam width that enters the eye pupil [42]. Although it is simple to configure, its reduced eye box is problematic. To solve this problem, various techniques, including multiple beam spot formation [42] and dynamic steering of beam spots with eye pupil tracking [23,43-45], have recently been recommended. The varifocal display dynamically controls the virtual image distance according to the eye's gaze direction. A notable recent study in this field is the work of META, which achieved a varifocal display by dynamically shifting the display panel's axial position using a mechanical system [46]. For multifocal displays, techniques using a stack of fast switchable diffusers [47] or an electrically controllable split-Lohmann lens array [24] have been reported, gaining wide attention. Light field displays that use a high refresh rate display panel and steering optics have also been studied [48,49] and have shown progress.

Among the technologies that mitigate VAC, holographic displays have made the most significant advances in recent years. Holographic displays are considered to be a promising solution to the VAC problem because they can provide natural 3D images with per-pixel continuous depth to users. However, they still have problems such as low image quality due to the coherent noise of the light source, small etendue that stems from the insufficient space - bandwidth product (SBP) of the SLM, and complicated system configuration required to remove the DC and conjugate images. Fast-developing deep learning techniques have been applied to the synthesis of hologram content and have enabled high-quality and high-speed optimization of SLM modulation patterns [25,50,51]. The active feedback from the displayed holographic images to the SLM pattern further enhances the 3D image quality [52], compensates for the nonideal operations of the optical components in the holographic displays, and suppresses the coherent noise from the light source. Optimization techniques that consider eye pupil size and position present a wide FoV holographic image in a large eye box and overcome the conventional SBP limitation of the SLM [53,54]. The ability of holographic displays to directly reconstruct wavefronts has even led to the highly compact waveguide-type holographic AR NEDs without lenses [25]. The advancements in 2022 and 2023 are expected to further accelerate the development of holographic display techniques in the coming years (Table 4).
