## Sub-wavelength patterned pulse laser lithography for ef fi cient fabrication of large-area metasurfaces

Received: 15 April 2022

Accepted: 20 September 2022

<!-- image -->

Lingyu Huang 1,3 , Kang Xu 1,3 , Dandan Yuan 1 , Jin Hu 1 , Xinwei Wang 2 &amp; Shaolin Xu 1

Rigorously designed sub-micrometer structure arrays are widely used in metasurfaces for light modulation. One of the glaring restrictions is the unavailability of easily accessible fabrication methods to ef fi ciently produce largearea and freely designed structure arrays with nanoscale resolution. We develop a patterned pulse laser lithography (PPLL) approach to create structure arrays with sub-wavelength feature resolution and periods from less than 1 μ mto over 15 μ mon large-area thin fi lms with substrates under ambient conditions. Separated ultrafast laser pulses with patterned wavefront by quasibinary phase masks rapidly create periodic ablated/modi fi ed structures by high-speed scanning. The gradient intensity boundary and circular polarization of the wavefront weaken diffraction and polarization-dependent asymmetricity effects during light propagation for high uniformity. Structural units of metasurfaces are obtained on metal and inorganic photoresist fi lms, such as antennas, catenaries, and nanogratings. We demonstrate a large-area metasurface (10 × 10 mm 2 ) revealing excellent infrared absorption (3 -7 μ m), which comprises 250,000 concentric rings and takes only 5 minutes to produce.

Check for updates

Recently, metasurfaces for light modulation have attracted signi fi cant attention due to the increasing demand for miniaturized ultra-thin optical systems 1 -4 with functions such as beam shaping (de fl ection, focusing, vortex modulation) 2,5 -8 , electromagnetic cloak 9 -11 , polarization control 12 , perfect absorption 5,13 -15 , and precise achromatization 8,16 -18 . Various structural units on metasurfaces perform crucial functions such as H shapes for directional surface wave coupling to absorb the light or modulate the wavefront 19 -22 , cross shapes to adjust the chromatic dispersion or absorption 23 -25 , and catenary shapes to offer high diffraction ef fi ciency and linear proportion between period and phase delay 26,27 . A combination of several units with continuous phase modulations is a critical type of metasurface for light splitting and de fl ection, including split rings with various directions 28,29 , antennas with multiple angles of spinning or opening 4,28,30,31 , squares or circles with various sizes 32 -34 . It is also helpful to achieve broadband modulation by integrating several structures with different scales or shapes 15 . Structural units with tens-of-micrometer scale period usually have long responded wavelength from mid to far-infrared wavelength (such as THz frequency), which have received great attraction on surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) spectroscopy, cloaking, and THz communication 10,25,28,32,35 .

The development of fabrication methods, especially mass production and easily accessible methods of metasurfaces, falls behind their designs. Electron beam lithography and extreme ultraviolet lithography with outstanding sub-10-nm resolution are general approaches with high freedom in achievable structures to verify the metasurface design for different light modulation abilities. Recently, direct laser writing as a maskless lithography method has been gradually applied in micro-/nanofabrication, whose resolution achieves hundreds of nanometers and is mainly restricted by the diameter of the laser spot and the sensitivity of the photoresist. The manufacturing speed and graphic precision of maskless lithography by direct writing depend entirely on the velocity and precision of the motion stage 36 . Referring to practical research and applications of metasurfaces, it is needed to develop a low-cost, highly ef fi cient, and easily accessible method to fabricate large-area metasurfaces with various rigorously designed arrayed structures. Nanoimprinting has been applied in large-area metasurface processing, which hugely relies on the resolution of the mask and may lose the precision of the structures due to defects generated during duplications 37 -39 .

1 Department of Mechanical and Energy Engineering, Southern University of Science and Technology, 1088 Xueyuan Avenue, Shenzhen 518055, China. 2 Department of Mechanical Engineering, Iowa State University, Ames, IA 50011, USA. 3 These authors contributed equally: Lingyu Huang, Kang Xu.

[e-mail: xusl@sustech.edu.cn](mailto:xusl@sustech.edu.cn)

Besides maskless lithography and mask-dependent duplicating methods, a modulated laser beam with one-step patterning ability has attracted researchers ' concentration. The computer-generated hologram (CGH) is a commonly used phase diagram for wavefront modulation of light through an SLM, usually calculated by the iterative Fourier transform algorithm, also called the Gale-Shapley algorithm 40,41 . Whereas CGH makes it challenging to produce microscale structures with sub-wavelength scale features and several micrometers period. The disordered phase distribution in the wavefront modi fi ed by CGH would highly disturb the energy distribution during light propagation (with comparison shown in Supplementary Fig. 1) 42,43 . Direct phase masks with binary gratings to remove the background show similar limitations due to strong diffraction at the boundary and uneven intensity inside the wavefront 44,45 . Simple binary masks with polarizers to modulate the wavefront intensity are concise and capable of generating a wavefront with consistent phase distribution, which is still not good enough in ablation performance on the bulk materials because intense ablation would amplify the shortcoming of energy unevenness in the wavefront 46 .

In this work, we propose a patterned pulse laser lithography (PPLL) method under ambient conditions to realize the highly ef fi cient production of large-area metasurface composed of periodic units with a period from sub-micrometer to tens of micrometers, highly alterable shapes, and uniform morphology with sub-wavelength featuresize. We duplicate the same pattern in the wavefront by separating pulse ablation on substrates which enables the ef fi cient fabrication under a high laser repetition frequency. Metal and inorganic photoresist fi lms with ablated or phase-modi fi ed patterns could form metasurfaces or act as masks for fabricating structural units on metasurfaces. The critical step is to modulate the pulse with a uniform patterned appearancewith circular polarization following the pixeled phase delays from a spatial light modulator (SLM) with gradient-grayscale boundaries. The phase masks with gradient-grayscale boundaries result in more uniform energy distributions at the wavefront by weakening diffraction during light propagation, which helps to reach smaller feature sizes simultaneously. The circular-polarized wavefront is employed to improve the consistency of patterns ' linewidth in different directions, especially for near-diffraction-limit width. Compared with existing methods, PPLL could be applied to various materials such as metals and create the unit pattern with sub-wavelength feature size in one step, ensuring consistency and accuracy.

## Results and discussion

## The principle of the PPLL process

As shown in Fig. 1a, a linear polarized femtosecond laser with a center wavelength of 520 nm and a repetition frequency of 10 kHz is modulated with the polarization distribution and then fi ltered to remain the homogeneous linear polarization, which would be turned to circular polarization by a QWP, and achieve a tailored patterned light intensity fi nally (with illustrations of beam pro fi les in Fig. 2a -e). The phase delay does the modulation through a re fl ection-type phase-only SLM with patterned quasi-binary phase masks, which comprise two major phase delay values with gradient boundary (Fig. 1c). Patterned pulses are continuously imposed into the samples and spatially separated during the high-speed scanning, as shown in Fig. 1b to fabricate structural arrays with sub-wavelength feature size and fi ne recast layers on boundaries, as illustrated in Fig. 1c -e. The fi lm ' s ablation thickness and modi fi cation depth depend on pulse energy and material properties. The relationship between desired scanning speed, period, and laser repetition frequency can be written as follows:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where v is the scanning speed, D is the pattern period, and f is the laser pulse repetition frequency. Every pulse or group of pulses results in an ablation or phase-modi fi cation region following the shape of the tailored intensity.

## Grayscale gradation of phase mask boundary to improve ablation precision

Patterned pulse with gradient intensity boundary achieved by the phase mask with gradient grayscale boundary on SLM can improve the precision and linewidth resolution of the ablated shape.

The gradation is created by polarization fi ltering due to gradient phase delay from phase mask with processing schematic in Fig. 2a -e that corresponds to the positions 1 -6inFig. 1a (with a detailed process in Supplementary Fig. 2). The pattern information is transferred from the phase mask on SLM to the polarization distribution of the wavefront, which is then transferred into intensity amplitude by the polarization fi lter. It is noticed that the elliptical polarization delivers the information of gradient boundary. Further theoretical calculation and analysis are stated in the supplementary information ' s second section. A50×objective(NA = 0.55) is applied to produce triangles (Fig. 2) and L shapes (Fig. 3) to study the related effects on a larger scale with a more obvious phenomenon. Heavy diffraction happens when geometric patterns with sharp angles are imposed (Fig. 2f4). Thus, pure binary phase masks such as triangles result in a rough ablated pattern boundary (Fig. 2f2). The strong diffraction comes from an abrupt changeinlightintensity at the boundary due to Fresnel approximation. Speci fi cally, the Fresnel approximation derived from the fi rst RayleighSommerfeld diffraction with a paraxial situation that is given by 47 :

Signi fi cantly, the U 0( x 1 , y 1, 0) denotes the original input light, namely the superposition of a Gaussian beam and the phase masks in our cases. Here, 6 pixels of gradient grayscale (with approximate sine distribution) at every boundary of the phase masks are suitable, which could form ef fi cient grayscale gradation but not affect the structural precision of the shape. Comparing experimental results and propagation calculation results in Fig. 2f1, f4, 2g1,g4, the addition of grayscale gradation could smooth the change of phase and intensity to weaken the diffraction, which helps achieve the patterns with straight boundaries and sharp angles. The curvature radius of the sharp angle could decrease from 367 nm to 119 nm, namely a sharper shape, as showninFigs.2f2, g2. It is noticed that the slight asymmetry of two 45° angles comes from comprehensive errors due to the spherical aberration of the SLM surface, imperfect Gaussian distribution of incident light, and the error in center misalignment, which cannot be completely avoided.

In addition to regulating the pattern appearance, gradient grayscales along the mask boundary can reduce the linewidth even beyond the diffraction limit. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 3, a sharp L shape with a width of 12 pixels cannot be ablated completely. Under the same laser pulse energy, a sharp L shape with a width of 20 pixels could be ablated totally. By comparison, the 20-pixel line with 6-pixel gradation on each boundary is feasible to achieve smaller line width than a 20pixel sharp one.

Stronger ablation (in the area with high light intensity) happens along the rod perpendicular to the polarization leading to a larger linewidth, which is evident in the SEM images (Fig. 3a,c). By comparison, the results ablated by laser with 45° and circular polarization show equal width along both rods of two directions. This slight difference becomes more evident when the linewidth is relatively small, especially when the linewidth is close to the diffraction limit. Thus, the circular polarization (Fig. 2e) would be more suitable for random patterns due to the same polarization components in all directions. In contrast, linear polarization could be applied for unique patterns such as 1D gratings.

In addition, isotropic shapes such as ring shapes reveal excellent shape stability during light propagation, keeping ablated structures uniform. As shown in Fig. 3g -j, the ultra-uniform wavefront with harmless concentric diffraction for structural regulation, could result in isotropic structures with regular shapes and relatively smaller feature sizes of 303nm, approximately 76% of the diffraction limit (397 nm under NA of 0.8).

## Linewidth-pixel relationship and sub-diffraction-limit resolution of PPLL

We could predict the linewidth of structures fabricated by PPLL through magni fi cation analysis. As shown in Fig. 4a, the ablated linewidth is nearly proportional to the pixel numbers in phase masks. We fabricate all the single lines with pulse energy just above the ablation threshold. Referring to Supplementary Fig. 4 and the corresponding analysis, the ablated linewidth L follows the following equations:

We obtain the k with around 0.96, and the k under higher NA reveals higher amplitude due to a more intense laser focus.

## Demonstrations and applications of patterned structures

The PPLL method could produce rigorously designed patterns on fi lm samples (with demonstrations in Supplementary Figs. 4, 5, 7, 8). Furthermore, the nanopatterned fi lms on substrates processed by PPLL canactas masksforfurther etching to fabricate structures with a larger depth-to-width ratio on metasurfaces for better light modulation ef fi ciency.

The white arrows indicate the polarization direction. The applied pulse energy is 0.15 μ J. Wedemonstrate several fundamental nanostructure arrays for metasurfaces by PPLL with additional plasma and chemical etching, as shown in Fig. 5. In Fig. 5b -g and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6, we illustrated structure arrays after inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etching with the laser patterned Cr fi lms as masks on SiO2 samples (Fig. 5a). Figure 5b shows an H shaped structure array after reverse H shaped pulse laser ablation and plasma etching, which is generally applied to manipulate phase response under microwave even THz 19,22 . Figure 5d shows classical V-shaped antennas for regulating electromagnetic waves by resonance 49 . Each group of four V-shaped antennas with different orientations is obtained by single patterned pulse ablation. Figure 5e reveals regular concentric rings with high uniformity. Catenaries and gratings are also demonstrated in Fig. 5f, g, which are common structures for metasurface offering high diffraction ef fi ciency 26,27,50 -54 . Supplementary Fig. 5 exhibits catenaries and gratings with smaller linewidth, periods, and larger height-to-width ratio and 2D gratings. When the reverse patterned pulse laser is imposed to create the male structural arrays (Fig. 5b -d and Supplementary Figs. 6a, b, d), a slight overlap between pulses is required. Remarkably, the sub-wavelength resolution has been achieved in the linewidth of all the structural units.

Scale bar: 2 μ m. g , h The simulated propagation results and detected beam pro fi les of concentric rings without and with gradient boundary. i concentric ring arrays by pulse energy of 0.23 μ J. j Single rings with a width of 303 nm by pulse energy of 0.09 μ J. The samples are composed of 10 nm Au, 3 nm Cr on SiO2 substrate.

Apart from the direct laser ablation, phase change material Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) is available to fabricate stereoscopic structures by chemical etching after patterned laser modi fi cation, which could offer an excellent performance of the wavefront modulation due to structural depth up to hundreds of nanometers and a high refractive index of GST 55 . The GST material has been widely applied for tunable metasurfaces owing to its phase-dependent optical property, robust reproducibility, and quick crystal-phase changing 56,57 . It is also a frequently used inorganic phase-change photoresist for micro-/nanofabrication due to the different etching rates between amorphous (GSTa) and crystallized (GSTc) phases (Fig. 5h) 58 . As illustrated in Fig. 5i -l, we demonstrate four types of common three-dimensional structures on GST fi lms (the original samples with 250 nm GST fi lm deposited on SiO2 substrates). As shown in Fig. 5i, we fabricate an array of a combined unit composed of ring and cross structures with different dimensions resulting in a combination of different resonance frequencies, which is helpful for broadband absorbers 15 . Furthermore, we demonstrate chiral structures, which are always utilized to adjust the wavefront because of their selective response to the left or right circular polarization (Fig. 5j) 59 . Besides, concentric structures with open ends are produced with excellent uniformity and precision, which are great resonant antennas for absorbers (Fig. 5k, l) 28,60 .

Fig. 4 | Line-shaped pulse laser ablation with different pixel numbers of linewidth. a , b Statistics of ablated linewidth under various pixel numbers with diffraction-limit at 397 nm (purple dashed line) and wavelength at 520 nm (green solid line). The error bars represent the standard deviation of measured linewidth.

<!-- image -->

Above all, the PPLL can produce various types of metasurface units directly or by combining with etching processes with high ef fi ciency that reveals excellent potential in the fabrication of practical large-area metasurfaces. The structure size of one unit can be precisely controlled from less than1 μ m up to tens of micrometers by the zooming out mechanism. The depth-to-width ratio can even reach around 7:1 under a linewidth of 92 nm (Supplementary Fig. 5f).

It is noticed that the high resolution and positioning accuracy of the displacement stage are signi fi cant for large-area repeatability. Under a stable device condition, we can slightly adjust scanning speed to modulate the period distribution and alignment (Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8), revealing further controllability in the spatial distribution of structural units. The gratings in Fig. 5g come from the seamless join between line pulse scanning with a proper scanning speed.

According to the results in Fig. 3, the PPLL is quite suitable for fabricating uniform concentric rings, which could be structural units for electromagnetic resonance forming metasurface. We design two concentric rings by the Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method (inserted in Fig. 6d) to achieve absorbers with different absorption wavelengths on the mid-infrared wavelength of 3 -7 μ m (3333 -1429 cm -1 ), which can be further applied in SEIRA for biology detection. As shown in Fig. 6a, a classical sandwich structure was designed to improve the absorption ef fi ciency on the resonant wavelength. We use the evaporated SiO2 layer with a thickness of 50nmastheinsulatorlayer,theAulayerwitha thicknessof 70 nmfor the re fl ective metal layer at the bottom, and patterned GST with a total thickness of 250 nm for the resonant structures. The resulting structure depth reaches ~200 nm after PPLL and chemical etching, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 9, providing ef fi cient resonance conditions for metasurface.

c Beamprofi le of the line pulse modulated by a phase mask with 14-pixel linewidth. d , e Gratings produced by PPLL with a period of 453 nm and remaining linewidth of 54nm (laser-ablated linewidth is 399 nm) by pulse energy of 0.07 μ J.

According to the sectional electric fi eld distribution in Fig. 6d, the light intensity accumulates in the SiO2 insulator layer under a TMpolarization mode excitation. And the double-valley re fl ectance of small concentric rings mainly comes from resonance in the center circle and two outer rings, respectively. The large concentric rings only exhibit a single resonance in the center circle. After processing with the PPLL method and further chemical etching, we produced two concentric rings with different dimensions (Fig. 6c), whose absorption peaksmatchourdesignwithlessthan300nmshiftofspectrumvalleys with excellent peak absorbance over 98%.

In summary, we developed a patterned pulse laser lithography (PPLL) to produce metasurfaces composed of sub-wavelength structural units with high ef fi ciency and low cost at ambient conditions. The principles of PPLL have been studied, and the fabrication processes have been optimized. Boundary gradation of quasi-binary phase masks andcircularpolarization can help weaken wavefront deformation from diffraction and polarization-dependent asymmetricity effect during light propagation, resulting in uniform structures and sub-wavelength feature size. We obtained various patterns containing classical subwavelength structures for metasurface with the minimum feature size beyond the diffraction limit. Combining with etching processes, we demonstrate an ef fi cient large-area metasurface as a mid-infrared absorber that achieves peak absorption over 98% under the wavelength of 3 -7 μ m. This novel fabrication technique is highly feasible to obtain rigorously designed patterns with nanoscale feature size and high ef fi ciency on various materials. The consistency and accuracy of the designed patterns are highly guaranteed by the one-step separated modulated pulse energy deposition by direct high-speed laser scanning. Patterns with higher resolution would be achieved by further adoption of shorter laser wavelength (smaller diffraction limit), SLM with smaller pixel size ( l ), 4 f system for beam narrowing (larger f 1 / f 2 ), and photoresist samples with smaller ablation/modi fi cation threshold. The PPLL method promises broad applications for large-area metasurface to achieve perfect absorption, polarization fi ltering, and beam de fl ection.

## Data-driven optimization of maskless grayscale laser lithography

Adrian H. A. Lutey 1  , David Kuhness 2 , Seyyedhossein Mckee 3 , Vincenzo Ferraro 1 , Marco Negozio 1 , Walter Belardi 3 , Luca Romoli 4 , Markus Postl 2 &amp; Barbara Stadlober 2

A data-driven optimization algorithm is described for maskless grayscale laser lithography (MGLL), providing effective correction for topography errors deriving from the non-linear response of the photoresist to exposure dose, proximity effects and sharp dose transitions near edges and vertices. The algorithm employs an artificial neural network (ANN) to represent the physical process, with the MGLL virtual photomask and its radial averages as input variables and the predicted surface topography as the output. Virtual photomask optimization is achieved by predicting the surface topography obtained with a given virtual photomask and implementing corrections based on the predicted error. An elaborate training model with a range of different surface features is employed to acquire a comprehensive dataset comprising approximately one million rows of data for training the ANN. Hyperparameter optimization with an independent test set sees greatest accuracy and ability to generalize achieved with a simple ANN comprising a Sigmoid activation function and a single hidden layer with 15 neurons. Optimized virtual photomasks are calculated for the training model and an ultrathin free-form micro-optical element (FFMO), with the average Euclidean distance between the experimental and target surfaces reduced from 3.6 μm with an experimental contrast curve to 1.0-1.2 μm with the optimization algorithm in a single build. The developed approach provides an effective, versatile and adaptable pathway towards first time right MGLL.

Keywords Grayscale laser lithography, Data-driven optimization, Artificial neural networks, Micro-optical elements

Maskless grayscale laser lithography (MGLL) has emerged as a key enabling technology for the production of  micro-optical  elements,  micro-electromechanical  systems  (MEMS)  and  functional  surfaces  via  direct manufacturing of continuous-relief structures down to the sub-micrometer scale or fabrication of masters for replication over large areas via roll-to-roll processes 1-5 .  Large-scale fabrication of ultrathin free-form microoptical  elements  (FFMOs)  via  MGLL  is  expected  to  see  widespread  uptake  in  compact  and  high-efficiency lighting and detection systems, personal electronics and augmented and virtual reality headsets 6-8 . In contrast to physical mask-based lithography, maskless or direct-write grayscale lithography offers greater flexibility and control via variation of the light dose during writing in low contrast photoresists by varying the power of the light  source  or  using  an  acousto-optic  modulator  (AOM) 9 .  Cost-effective  production  of  large  and  complex geometries can therefore be achieved by employing a grayscale exposure image, gray value distribution (GVD) or 'virtual photomask' calculated via computer aided design (CAD) software and a contrast curve assigning laser parameters to given geometric characteristics. Process parameter optimization in MGLL typically requires several iterations for each build due to the non-linear response of the photoresist to exposure dose, as well as proximity effects (variations in the geometry of a feature as a function of proximity to other nearby features) and sharp dose transitions near edges and vertices leading to non-uniform laser exposure and consequent deviations from the target geometry 10 . Additional experiments can be expensive and time-consuming due to the lengthy steps involved, including photoresist deposition, laser exposure, sample development, topography acquisition, data analysis and revision of the virtual photomask. To reduce the number of iterations and ultimately achieve first time right MGLL, new process models must be developed that are capable of predicting surface topography over a sufficiently wide parameter range to be of use in production, high-quality experimental data must be

1 Dipartimento di Ingegneria dei Sistemi e delle Tecnologie Industriali, Università degli studi di Parma, 43124 Parma, Italy. 2 Joanneum Research Forschungsgesellschaft, 8160 Weiz, Austria.  3 Dipartimento di Ingegneria e Architettura, Università degli studi di Parma, 43124 Parma, Italy.  4 Dipartimento di Ingegneria Civile e Industriale, Università di Pisa, 56122 Pisa, Italy.  email: adrian.lutey@unipr.it available  for  calibrating  or  training  such  models,  and  effective  optimization  algorithms  must  be  capable  of updating the virtual photomask based on actual or predicted outcomes to obtain the highest possible build accuracy for a given optical setup.

A consolidated approach to modeling MGLL is through the development of physics-driven representations predicting variations in converted initiator and photoresist solubility based on the absorbed energy dose 11-14 . These typically calculate the total energy dose within each region based on the intensity distribution of the incident beam and scanning strategy, simulating free-radical polymerization and photoresist development 15 . Such  models  form  the  basis  of  proximity  and  process  correction  in  commercial  software  packages  such  as GenISys BEAMER 3D-PEC 12 . Optimization of virtual photomasks can be performed by correcting dose values within regions subject to proximity effects and sharp dose transitions 16 , which has been shown to be fast and accurate but sensitive to experimental calibration and photoresist stability 12 .  Despite reducing the number of experiments,  physics-based  models  require  careful  calibration  of  process  constants  and  material  properties, while also presenting barriers in terms of complexity and access to specialized software.

Artificial  intelligence  (AI)  and  machine  learning  (ML)  are  currently  receiving  renewed  attention  across all  facets of manufacturing, from defect detection to process optimization based on outcome prediction and route cause analysis 17,18 .  ML  models are effective at handling high dimensional problems to discover causal relationships within data that are not necessarily accounted for in physics-driven models 19 . ML finds widespread application in traditional  lithography 20 for  hotspot  detection 21 ,  optimization 22 and  photomask synthesis 23,24 . Of particular relevance are artificial neural networks (ANNs), which currently provide a good combination of performance, efficiency and ease of implementation with standardized toolboxes for applications across a range of scientific fields. Recent works have employed ANNs to generate free-form physical photomasks for grayscale lithography 25 . ANNs have also been applied to MGLL for the definition of virtual photomasks based on inverse models using U-Net convolutional neural network-based modification methods defining the surface topography as an input and the laser intensity distribution as an output 26 . Despite reducing the number of experiments, this approach requires the design of complex ANNs that still do not achieve accuracy up to physical limits of the process in a single build.

A critical aspect of developing AI and ML process models is the availability of high-quality datasets representing the physical process taking place. Ideally, a single experiment should provide a complete dataset for calibrating or training models that can predict process outcomes across the full range of foreseeable conditions. In the field of laser lithography, this is typically performed by producing elementary forms such as lines, pillars, dimples, ramps or steps with various levels of laser exposure and subsequently quantifying geometric parameters such as surface elevation and line width with a scanning electron microscope (SEM), optical profiler or atomic force microscope (AFM) 5,9,27 . The period and depth of sub-micrometric periodic structures can also be determined via diffraction-based methods 28 . The main limitation of these techniques lies in the low volume of data acquired and the range of geometric parameters considered, which may not be representative of complex asymmetrical multiscale objects leading to proximity effects and sharp dose transitions during exposure 12 . There is currently scope for improving approaches to data collection in grayscale laser lithography, taking inspiration from other additive manufacturing (AM) processes employing benchmark artefacts for evaluation of build accuracy and process characterization 29-31 .

Physics-driven  models  continue  to  represent  the  current  state  of  the  art  for  optimization  of  process parameters in MGLL, despite their complexity and sensitivity to calibration 12 .  While data-driven approaches have also been implemented, these have achieved only moderate improvements in build accuracy compared to experimental optimization by implementing sophisticated inverse models to predict the virtual photomask required for a given build geometry 26 . There is currently potential for the development of data-driven models that directly predict the resulting geometry obtained with a specific virtual photomask, thus representing the physical process. This approach exploits the advantages of ML in terms of ease of implementation and capturing causal relationships that are not necessarily accounted for in physics-driven models, while also yielding higher accuracy  than  inverse  models  through  the  implementation  of  optimization  algorithms.  The  present  work therefore provides a complete methodology for data-driven optimization of MGLL with the aim of facilitating first  time  right  fabrication,  employing  a  direct  ANN  representation  of  the  physical  process.  The  developed approach comprises three key elements: (i) acquisition of high-quality training data via the production of an elaborate training model, (ii) training of a direct ANN representation of the process, including hyperparameter optimization, to predict the resulting geometry achieved with a given virtual photomask, or map of the acoustooptic modulator (AOM) voltage employed to control the transmitted laser power at each point, and (iii) iterative optimization of virtual photomasks for the production of new objects based on predictions obtained with the trained ANN. The presented approach requires a single experiment to be performed to obtain training data, after which optimized virtual photomasks for any number of objects can be obtained with the same setup and photoresist,  requiring  no  further  experimental  calibration.  The  versatility  and  effectiveness  of  the  approach is  demonstrated by building an ultrathin FFMO with a new photoresist, with and without the optimization algorithm, demonstrating the magnitude of improvement in surface accuracy that can be achieved through data-driven optimization. The overall objective is to demonstrate that first time right manufacturing is feasible through data-driven optimization, providing additional instruments to manufacturers and users of maskless laser  writers  during  calibration  and  use  of  new  MGLL  equipment  and  photoresists,  allowing  faster  and  less resource-intensive process optimization.

## Materials and methods Optimization algorithm

The developed optimization algorithm was based on an ANN model of the MGLL process capable of predicting the geometry obtained with a given virtual photomask. To acquire such predictions, it was firstly necessary to  train  the  ANN  with  experimental  data  deriving  from  a  training  model  and  perform  hyperparameter optimization to maximize the accuracy of predictions. Once this had been completed, the trained ANN was employed to perform iterative optimization of virtual photomasks for production of a target object. This was achieved by predicting the geometry obtained with a given virtual photomask, comparing this geometry with the target object model, and iteratively updating the virtual photomask until the lowest possible predicted error was achieved. The various steps involved in the process are presented in Fig. 1.

During the training phase (upper part of Fig. 1), a training model, z model ( ① in Fig. 1), comprising elevation data z model,ij for  points ( x i , y j ) , i = 1 , . . . , n , j = 1 , . . . , m ,  was  employed  to  obtain  a  training  virtual photomask, E ( ③ ), or map of the AOM voltage employed to control the transmitted laser power at each point. Values of the virtual photomask at each point were calculated based on a training contrast curve, f ( z model,ij ) ( ② ), defining the AOM voltage as a function of the model elevation. The training virtual photomask, E , together with radial averages representing the radial distribution function of E at  each  point, g E ( r ) ,  where r is  the  local radial distance from each point, were considered as inputs for training the ANN ( ⑥ ), while the experimentally acquired surface topography, z exp ( ⑤ ), was considered the output ( ⑧ ). This approach therefore considered the virtual photomask value at a given point, E ij , and its radial distribution function, g E ( r ) ij , as yielding a specific value of elevation at the same point, z exp,ij .  In  practice, the radial distribution function was represented by radial averages, denoted g E ( r lower -r upper ) for r lower &lt; r ≤ r upper , to reduce the number of input variables provided to the ANN and thus limit its complexity (see Fig. 3), facilitating robust generalization to unseen data. This approach grouped virtual photomask values in adjacent regions at similar radial distances from the point of interest into discrete average values to account for their contribution to the effective absorbed energy dose.

For the employed experimental setup with a focused laser spot size of approximately 2 μm (see 'Grayscale laser  lithography  setup  and  sample  preparation'),  six  radial  averages  of E were  evaluated  over  the  ranges 0 µm &lt; r ≤ 2 µm , 2 µm &lt; r ≤ 4 µm , 4 µm &lt; r ≤ 8 µm , 8 µm &lt; r ≤ 16 µm , 16 µm &lt; r ≤ 32 µm and 32 µm &lt; r ≤ 64 µm ,  performing  two-dimensional  convolutions  of  weighted  Boolean  masks  for  each  radial interval and the virtual photomask matrix with a calculation resolution of 1 μm. These radial averages were referred to as g E (0 -2) , g E (2 -4) , g E (4 -8) , g E (8 -16) , g E (16 -32) and g E (32 -64) , respectively. The number of radial averages and their intervals were chosen as a compromise between limiting the number of  input  variables  provided  to  the  ANN  to  achieve  robust  generalization  and  adequately  accounting  for  the physical phenomena taking place to achieve accurate predictions. While it was found to be important to include relatively large radial averages compared to the focused laser spot size, division of the same area into many different radial averages with smaller intervals was found to be of little benefit. As such, the intervals over which radial averages were calculated were increased exponentially from the point of interest to the largest distance considered to be of influence. In this way, rapid changes in laser intensity and chemical reactions taking place close to the point of interest could be accounted for with high resolution while still enabling a large area to be considered. Figure 2 provides a representation of regions considered for calculation of radial averages at a generic point, ( x i , y j ) , together with a schematic of the MGLL process for a single laser scanning pass employing an  experimental  contrast  curve.  The  latter  illustrates  how  the  obtained  surface  (after  positive  photoresist development) is a non-linear function of not only the laser power at each point but also that in adjacent regions, leading to deviation of the obtained surface from the target near edges.

Fig. 1 .  Flow diagram of data-driven optimization algorithm for MGLL.

| Hyperparameter                                 | Tested range                                                     | FinalANN   |
|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|
| Activation function for fully connected layers | Rectified linear unit (ReLU); Hyperbolic tangent (tanh); Sigmoid | Sigmoid    |
| Number of fully connected layers               | 1-2                                                              | 1          |
| Number of neurons per layer                    | 1-25                                                             | 15         |

Data pre-processing was undertaken by performing a series of elementary transformations on experimental data  to  calculate  process  parameters  and  outcomes  at  common  coordinates.  Model,  virtual  photomask  and experimental topography data for a single build were imported and cropped as required, after which horizontal leveling of the experimental profile and vertical alignment with the model were performed based on selected regions and markers outside the build area. In-plane alignment of the experimental profile with the model and virtual  photomask was carried out by performing a Procrustes transformation without scaling or mirroring based on least-squares alignment of a least three features. Noisy and missing data were removed, with the final dataset standardized.

Training of a feedforward fully connected ANN for regression was performed in MATLAB using the fi trnet function. The Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno quasi-Newton algorithm (LBFGS) was employed to minimize the training loss, defined as the mean squared error (MSE) of the predicted surface topography. To maximize the accuracy of the trained ANN, grid hyperparameter optimization was performed over the ranges indicated in Table 1 to determine the effects of the activation function, number of fully connected layers and number of neurons in each layer. In all cases, layer weights were initialized with the Glorot initializer and initial layer biases were set to zero. Based on the outcomes of hyperparameter optimization, the final ANN configuration comprised a Sigmoid activation function and one fully connected layer with 15 neurons. A schematic of this configuration is shown in Fig. 3. With the final training dataset, comprising approximately one million rows of data, hyperparameter optimization required approximately 24 h on a Dell workstation running an 18-core Intel i9 processor. Training of the final ANN with the same dataset required three minutes on an Apple MacBook Air running an M2 processor.

During the optimization phase (lower part of Fig. 1), the target object to be fabricated was defined by its model, z model ( ⑨ in Fig. 1). The trained ANN ( ⑦ ) was employed to predict the surface topography obtained with  a  given  virtual  photomask E k ( ⑪ )  for  iteration k , z k pred ( ⑫ ).  The  initial  virtual  photomask  ( k = 0 ) could either be set to zero across the entire region or determined based on an experimental contrast curve, f ( z model,ij ) ( ⑩ ).  In  the  present  work,  the  initial  photomask was set to zero for simplicity. For subsequent iterations, z k pred was compared with the model geometry, z model , to determine the predicted error for iteration k , ε k pred ( ⑰ ).  The  predicted  error, ε pred ,  together  with  radial  averages  representing  the  radial  distribution function of ε pred at each point, g ε pred ( r ) , were then used to update the virtual photomask for the subsequent iteration ( ⑬ ) with the objective of minimizing the predicted error. Virtual photomask correction was managed by introducing a proportionality constant, β , multiplied by the predicted error at each point, ε pred,ij , together with another proportionality constant, κ , multiplied by the mean value of radial averages representing the radial distribution function of the predicted error, g ε pred ( r ) ij . Correction was based on the local and regional error in this way to avoid error accumulation, penalizing local error correction where this was detrimental to accuracy in surrounding regions. An example of where this behavior was required was along edges, where laser power could be increased up to system limits within regions of high power but could not be reduced below zero in adjacent regions, leading to uncontrolled widening of the former. Correction terms were multiplied by a nonlinear function of the model height to account for differences in photoresist sensitivity in regions of low and high elevation. For virtual photomask optimization with the employed experimental setup, coefficients β and κ were set to 2 × 10 -5 and 2 × 10 -4 . The function h ( z model,ij ) = 1 + z 2 model,ij was chosen to apply correction more aggressively in regions of high elevation, in line with experimental observations, while still allowing correction to take place where z model,ij = 0 . Finally, virtual photomask values were limited to the useable laser power range with the employed experimental setup, leading to convergence towards a solution with constant error due to inherent physical limitations. The optimization procedure was stopped once the difference between the average predicted error of two subsequent iterations was below a given value, ∇ ε cut ( ⑭ ), after which the object was produced with the optimized photomask and analyzed to obtain the acquired surface topography, z exp ( ⑯ ) . With appropriate selection of β and κ , ∇ ε cut &lt; 10 nm could typically be achieved within 30 iterations. Optimization of the virtual photomask for the ultrathin FFMO (see 'Models and test cases'), comprising approximately 1 million points, required less than two minutes on an Apple MacBook Air running an M2 processor.

Fig. 3 .  ( a ) Schematic of ANN configuration employed for the MGLL optimization algorithm.

Code availability

Custom  MATLAB  code  developed  to  train  the  ANN  model  of  the  MGLL  process  and  perform  iterative optimization of virtual photomasks is available in the Supplementary Material.

## Grayscale laser lithography setup and sample preparation

Experiments were performed with an MGLL setup employing a 500 mW continuous-wave diode laser with emission wavelength of 405 nm. A series of absorption filters was employed prior to focusing optics to achieve a maximum laser power of 1 mW on the sample, with an AOM employed to actively control the transmitted laser power over the range 0-1 mW based on the virtual photomask matrix. A 0.25 N.A. (10 ×) objective was employed to achieve a focused laser spot size of approximately 2 μm on the target surface. Samples were held on a high-precision xy translation stage with a travel range of 160 mm × 160 mm, with the focusing lens attached to a vertical stage. Accurate positioning of the laser focus on the sample was achieved with a confocal laser microscope setup. Serial laser lithography was performed with a scanning speed of 40 mm/s and a hatch spacing of 1 μm.

Borosilicate glass wafers of diameter 4 ″ were spin-coated with mr-P 22G\_XP positive photoresist supplied by micro resist technology GmbH at 1000 RPM for 20 s. Baking was performed for 30 min at 30 °C, 15 min at 50 °C, 60 min at 80 °C and 360 min at 90 °C, with a relaxation time of 360 min. A final photoresist thickness of 50 μm was chosen for fabrication of structures with a maximum nominal height of 20 µm and base offset of 11 µm (total height of 31 µm), leaving adequate space for diverse experimental outcomes while minimizing the risk of influence from the underlying substrate. Use of a positive photoresist required inversion of the model surface and correction of the virtual photomask based on the surface depth. Room temperature and humidity were held constant at 21 ± 1 °C and 44 ± 3%, respectively, during all phases of the process. After MGLL experiments, samples were developed for 30 min with TMAH-based ma-D 532/S provided by the same supplier, rinsed with deionized water and blow dried with nitrogen gas. To allow comparison between the developed optimization algorithm and existing standard procedures, as well as generate data for training the ANN representation of the process, an experimental contrast curve was obtained by writing lines with various levels of laser power, evaluating the resulting depths and fitting an exponential curve defining grayscale values and corresponding AOM voltages as functions of surface depth. Two iterations of this process were performed to improve results obtained with the experimental contrast curve, with the final version chosen based on the best outcomes achieved for the targeted depths.

## Models and test cases

The models displayed in Fig. 4 were employed to generate datasets to train and test the ANN representation of  the  process  and  assess  the  performance  of  the  developed  optimization  algorithm.  The  training  model 32 (Fig. 4a) was developed with the aim of combining a wide range of representative geometric features such as flat and inclined planes, cylinders, semi-cylinders, semi-spheres, cones, prisms, steps and free-form elements with different dimensions, slope, curvature, aspect ratio, orientation and position on the build platform into a single object. The overall dimensions of the training model were 500 μm (l) × 500 μm (w) × 20 μm (h), with a maximum aspect ratio of 7. While most regions could be produced with the employed experimental setup, those with highest aspect ratio could not be accurately reproduced, thus providing data relating to process limits. For acquisition of a comprehensive training dataset, the model was fabricated in both upright and inverted positions in a single build with virtual photomasks calculated based on both the experimental contrast curve described in 'Grayscale laser lithography setup and sample preparation' and a linear contrast curve defining AOM voltages proportionally to the surface elevation over the entire operating range. By combining virtual photomask and experimental topography data for the resulting objects, this approach provided training data comprising approximately one million rows, representative of the full range of potential operating conditions, including at low laser power below the threshold for material transformation and at high laser power where the photoresist was relatively insensitive to changes in intensity. Data obtained from production of the training model were randomly partitioned into training (80%) and test (20%) datasets for assessment of ANN accuracy.

The test model 31 was developed by Minetola et al . as a benchmark artefact for evaluating build accuracy in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). Within the present study, the model was rescaled for production via MGLL (Fig. 4b), with the final object comprising a range of simple geometric elements of various sizes with overall dimensions of 165 µm (w) × 165 µm (l) × 20 µm (h). The test model was built in upright and inverted positions with  the  aforementioned  experimental  contrast  curve,  providing  an  independent  test  dataset  for  evaluating ANN model performance during hyperparameter optimization.

Finally, the effectiveness of the developed optimization algorithm was assessed by building both the training model (Fig. 4a) and an ultrathin FFMO (Fig. 4c) with virtual photomasks obtained via optimization with the developed algorithm. To allow a comparison of results obtained with and without the developed optimization methodology, the same objects were also built with the experimental contrast curve described previously with a base offset of 11 µm to limit the AOM voltage to 0.5-2.8 V in order to minimize the risk of threshold effects and allow room for subsequent optimization of the virtual photomask over the entire operating range of the system. While characterized by simpler geometry than the training and test models, the FFMO represented a real use case with unique challenges due to variable radial distances between inclined elements, leading to variable dose transitions and proximity effects from the central axis to the outer edge. All models were built with a resolution (pixel size) of 1 μm.

Fig. 4 .  Geometry of ( a ) training model, ( b ) test model and ( c ) ultrathin FFMO employed for experiments.

<!-- image -->

## Sample characterization and data acquisition

Characterization and analysis of all fabricated structures was performed with a Keyence LSCM and a JEOL scanning electron microscope (SEM). Prior to measurements, samples were sputter coated with a 30 nm thick Au-Pt layer to enable adequate laser reflection during LSCM and avoid local charge accumulation during SEM. LSCM measurements were carried out with a 50 × objective in double scanning high precision mode. A filter was applied using bright and dark cut levels (BCL/DCL) to remove saturated pixels and replace them with interpolated values. Data were subsequently exported as clouds of points for pre-processing.

Full datasets acquired for models and test cases employed within the study, including model geometry, virtual photomasks and experimental topography, are available in the Supplementary Material.

## Results and discussion ANN hyperparameter optimization

The results of ANN hyperparameter optimization were assessed separately for test data deriving from partitioning of the training model dataset (Fig. 4a) into 80/20% training/test sets and independent test data deriving from the entire test model dataset (Fig. 4b). For each combination of hyperparameters, an ANN was therefore trained with the training dataset and the loss evaluated for both the partitioned and independent test sets. The results are presented in Fig. 5 for the partitioned test set and Fig. 6 for the independent test set. In the former case, values of MSE generally decreased with increasing number of neurons for all activation functions in 1- and 2-layer configurations.  ReLU,  Sigmoid  and  tanh  activation  functions  performed  similarly;  however,  lowest  loss  and variability were achieved with a Sigmoid activation function. An MSE of approximately 2.3 µm 2 was achieved with a single hidden layer containing 20-25 neurons, while a loss of 2.1 µm 2   was achieved with two hidden layers containing 20-25 neurons each. While exhibiting some similar characteristics, results obtained with the independent test dataset highlighted the risk of increasing ANN complexity based on partitioned test data alone. With independent test data, the MSE decreased rapidly with increasing number of neurons for low values before oscillating and subsequently increasing for all activation functions in both 1- and 2-layer configurations. ANNs with 2 layers exhibited greater sensitivity to increases in the number of neurons in the first layer than in the second. Lowest loss and variability were again achieved with a Sigmoid activation function, obtaining an MSE of approximately 1.4 µm 2 with both a single layer containing 15 neurons and two layers containing 8 neurons each. Lower values of MSE were achieved for the independent test set than for the partitioned test set due to the simpler geometry and lower aspect ratio in the former case (Fig. 4). Based on these outcomes, a simple ANN comprising a Sigmoid activation function and a single hidden layer with 15 neurons was chosen for implementation within the optimization algorithm to ensure robust generalization to unseen data.

## Final ANN performance and feature importance

A comparison of actual and predicted values in the test set obtained by partitioning training model data into 80/20% training/test sets is provided in Fig. 7 for the final ANN configuration, together with the permutation importance of each input variable. The absolute percentage error was highest for low absolute values of elevation due to threshold effects and high sensitivity to changes in laser power at low values; however, outcomes were considered acceptable for production, as the absolute error was similar to other regions and a vertical base offset is generally introduced in MGLL to avoid threshold effects. The permutation importance, a machine learning explainability metric providing an indication of how strongly the model depends on each input variable, was highest  for  radial  averages  over  the  range 0 µm &lt; r ≤ 8 µm ,  suggesting  that  chemical  reactions  leading  to photoresist solubility took place over a larger area than the focused laser spot size of 2 μm. The same radial averages were also found to be of greater importance than the virtual photomask value itself ( E ), a result of the larger area covered by the radial averages (Fig. 2a) and the marked influence of the incident laser intensity near each point, highlighting the importance of correctly accounting for the effective absorbed energy dose within MGLL models. Radial averages greater than 8 μm were instead found to be of lesser significance.

## Virtual photomask optimization

Virtual  photomasks  were  calculated  with  the  optimization  algorithm  based  on  the  final  ANN  for  both  the training model (Fig. 4a) and the ultrathin FFMO (Fig. 4c). Stable convergence of the algorithm to ∇ ε cut &lt; 10 nm was achieved within 30 iterations in both cases. Figure 8 compares virtual photomasks obtained with the experimental contrast curve and optimization algorithm for the training model in both upright and inverted positions. Noting the axial symmetric geometry of the ultrathin FFMO, a comparison of a single quadrant of the virtual photomasks obtained with the experimental contrast curve and optimization algorithm is provided in Fig. 9, together with radial cross-sections of both. Virtual photomasks were inverted with respect to the model due to the use of a positive photoresist.

For the training model with upright geometry, the optimization algorithm (Fig. 8c) assigned lower AOM voltages to edges and vertices of raised features than to adjacent regions having the same elevation in order to compensate for the higher energy dose in nearby base regions between features. Analogously, higher AOM voltages were assigned to nearby base regions to compensate for the lower energy dose employed to produce the features. The opposite took place for the training model with inverted geometry, where the optimization algorithm (Fig. 8d) assigned higher AOM voltages to edges and vertices of sunken features than to adjacent regions having the  same elevation, and lower AOM voltages to nearby base regions. The degree to which proximity effects and sharp dose transitions were compensated for varied continuously depending on the severity of changes in geometry and the characteristics of surrounding features. Such corrections were completely absent from virtual photomasks generated with the experimental contrast curve (Fig. 8a and b), with each feature characterized by sharp edges reflecting the model geometry. Further to correction of proximity effects and sharp dose transitions, the optimization algorithm automatically defined the AOM voltage within flat regions, implementing higher values  than  the  contrast  curve  for  deeper  regions  based  on  the  dataset  employed  for  ANN  training.  Such differences were particularly evident for the upright geometry (Fig. 8a and c), where the optimization algorithm assigned base regions an AOM voltage approximately 1 V higher than that with the contrast curve.

For the ultrathin FFMO (Fig. 9), the optimization algorithm implemented both macroscopic corrections for overall improvement of build accuracy and fine corrections to compensate for proximity effects and sharp dose transitions near ridges and valleys. The AOM voltage was increased in regions of high depth and decreased in adjacent regions of low depth to improve the inclination of vertical walls and the accuracy of edges, as well as minimize in-plane expansion of high-depth regions. Such corrections led to variable gradient of the AOM voltage over the entire useable range (0-5 V).

Fig. 8 .  Comparison of virtual photomasks for training model with experimental contrast curve ( a ) upright and ( b ) inverted, and with optimization algorithm ( c ) upright and ( d ) inverted.

## Performance evaluation

The  acquired  surface  profile  and  minimum  Euclidean  distance  between  experimental  and  target  surfaces obtained  with  the  experimental  contrast  curve  and  optimization  algorithm  are  displayed  in  Fig.  10  for  the training model. For correct interpretation of the acquired profiles, it must be noted that the geometry of the training model was deliberately designed to achieve an aspect ratio going beyond values that could be achieved with the experimental setup in some regions to ensure that training data contained information relating to process limits. Regions in which the MGLL setup was not able to reproduce model geometry with acceptable accuracy were generally limited to square and rectangular column arrays, where the aspect ratio was as high as 7 (Fig. 4a). Some features also appeared to be missing or incomplete in optimized profiles acquired via LSCM, including small cones and pyramids; however, SEM images (Fig. 12a and b) confirmed that all features were in fact present and intact. These regions of relatively high apparent error were therefore the result of LSCM acquisition.

Despite  the  aforementioned  issues,  the  build  accuracy  was  nonetheless  significantly  higher  with  the optimization  algorithm  than  with  the  experimental  contrast  curve,  leading  to  a  reduction  in  the  average minimum Euclidean distance between the experimental and target surfaces from 3.6 to 1.2 μm. By comparing Fig. 10b and f (upright geometry) and Fig. 10d and h (inverted geometry), part of this improvement was due to the greater accuracy of base regions surrounding each feature. Form accuracy improved in regions of higher aspect ratio up to process limits, including stair structures, rectangular prisms and curved and free-form surfaces. The width of individual features was also closer to the original model, with the width of protruding and sunken 'S' features more closely representing the model geometry than those produced with the experimental contrast curve. Peak error values for optimized structures were concentrated around vertical walls, where process limits led to some level of inclination of the surfaces and therefore relatively large differences between the target and actual topography within these regions. While the same regions appear to have lower error in profiles obtained with the contrast curve, this was simply due to the base region being shallower. For the same reason, some of the features obtained with the contrast curve appear to be more accurate than the surrounding base region; however, the height of such features relative to the base plane is ultimately incorrect. SEM images of the optimized surfaces presented in Fig. 12a and b exhibit small ridges around some edges, which are not present in LSCM profiles. These features appear to be the result of overcompensation for sharp dose transitions in regions of high slope, where data acquired via LSCM was of lower quality.

While the training model was essentially a combination of complex surface features, some of which were difficult or impossible to produce via MGLL, the ultrathin FFMO instead represented a realistic use-case scenario where the  process  could  be  employed  for  production.  A  comparison  of  the  resulting  geometry  for  a  single quadrant of the ultrathin FFMO produced with the experimental contrast curve and optimization algorithm is provided in Fig. 11, together with radial cross-sections of the experimental and target profiles. The higher aspect ratio achieved with the optimization algorithm led to distinct measurement artefacts in some regions of the Elevation (μm)

profile obtained via LSCM; however, SEM analysis (Fig. 12c and d) confirmed that such artefacts were not present on the surface itself. Radial cross-sections (Fig. 11c) were therefore chosen in correspondence with the red lines shown in the elevation profiles. Overall build accuracy improved significantly with the optimization algorithm compared to the experimental contrast curve, with the average Euclidean distance between the experimental and target surface decreasing from 3.6 to 1.0 μm in the cross-sections presented in Fig. 11c. Peak heights and valley depths with the optimized virtual photomask were generally accurate to within 1-2 μm of target values, while sloped surfaces exhibited similar alignment. The experimental contrast curve instead exhibited relatively large differences between the experimental and target surfaces of 7-8 μm within the deepest parts of valleys. Improvements in build accuracy of this magnitude would be expected to have an important impact on FFMO performance, yielding improved optical functions such as anti-reflection, focusing and transmission, as well as increased focusing efficiency, lower distortion, fewer aberrations and better image resolution 33,34 .

Although improvements in accuracy could also be achieved iteratively with an experimental contrast curve for a single object, the process would be lengthy and characterized by complexities relating to threshold effects and  differences  in  sensitivity  to  changes  in  laser  intensity  over  the  entire  useable  process  parameter  range. Derivation of the contrast curve for a new photoresist is itself a complex process that can involve several iterations, with two iterations performed in the present study to improve results with the experimental contrast curve prior to comparison with the data-driven optimization algorithm. It must be noted, however, that subsequent iterations could also be performed with data-driven optimization by feeding results from optimization or other experiments into data used to train the ANN. More sophisticated approaches to determining the contrast curve, taking into consideration lateral resist effects and the Gaussian intensity distribution of the incident laser beam, would also undoubtably lead to greater alignment between results obtained with current approaches and the data-driven optimization algorithm; however, the objective of the present study was to compare realistic first attempts at defining the virtual photomask for a new photoresist and demonstrate that data-driven optimization can effectively be employed to achieve first time right fabrication with a single training dataset.

The  main  limitation  of  the  developed  methodology  is  instead  related  to  data  quality  for  training  of  the ANN, particularly in regions of high inclination where surface acquisition techniques such as LSCM struggle to provide reliable measurements. These regions are often the same as those subject to proximity effects and sharp dose transitions, further accentuating the issue. This limitation is evident to some extent around the edges of features in Fig. 12a and b, where overcompensation for sharp dose transitions appears to have taken place despite not being evident in LSCM measurements. Measurement artifacts must be removed from training data to avoid anomalous outputs from the trained ANN, which in the present study was performed within the LSCM instrument software itself. Data acquisition issues of this nature represent important limitations in terms of data quality affecting both physics- and data-driven models, which must be addressed as best as possible with the available instrumentation to ensure adequacy in representing the MGLL process within optimization software.

## Conclusion

While data-driven models for optimization of MGLL must be evaluated more extensively, outcomes achieved in the present study with a simple ANN representation and optimization algorithm suggest that this approach has the potential to reduce time and resource requirements for fabrication of new devices. A fundamental part of this approach is the acquisition of high-quality datasets that adequately represent the process, including in conditions that would normally exceed acceptable process limits in terms of accuracy and aspect ratio. This element was addressed in the present study by employing an elaborate training model combining a wide range of representative geometric features into a single object; an approach that could potentially be applied to different process configurations and photoresists with minimal changes. Acquired surface data was employed to train an ANN for predicting surface topography based on the virtual photomask, or map of the AOM voltage employed to  control  the  transmitted  laser  power  at  each  point.  This  approach  was  found  to  be  effective  at  accurately representing the process while maintaining a relatively limited number of input variables. Robust generalization to unseen data was therefore obtained with a simple configuration comprising a Sigmoid activation function and a single hidden layer with 15 neurons. Optimization of virtual photomasks for the training model and an ultrathin FFMO led to a reduction in the Euclidean distance between the experimental and target surfaces from 3.6 μm to 1.0-1.2 μm compared to outcomes achieved with an experimental contrast curve.

Though the presented methodology provides a fundamental approach for developing data-driven models and optimization algorithms for MGLL, a number of challenges remain. The performance of data-driven models is inherently linked to the quality of training data, which in turn depends on the training model geometry and quality of topography acquisition. While the former was addressed within the present study, LSCM acquisition of surface topography represented a limitation in terms of data quality for regions of high slope, which ultimately led to minor defects near the edges of optimized structures due to overcompensation for sharp dose transitions. While  it  may  not  always  be  possible  to  resolve  this  aspect  due  to  limitations  in  available  instrumentation, attention must be paid to the influence of acquisition quality on model performance. Further to this aspect, the developed approach is essentially capable of correcting for systematic errors deriving from the laser energy dose in a single experimental configuration in terms of scanning speed, scanning direction, number of scanning passes,  photoresist,  photoresist  thickness  and  optical  setup.  For  different  configurations,  this  implies  either training individual ANNs for each or introducing these parameters as inputs to the ANN. Development of more complete representations of MGLL comprising the full range of process parameters and multiple photoresists therefore remains a future challenge not only for algorithm development but also for systematic data collection, as extensive training data would be required over the entire foreseeable parameter range. The approach presented within this study nonetheless represents a starting point for relatively quick deployment, providing optimized virtual photomasks for any number of objects over the full range of achievable geometries with a given MGLL setup and photoresist.
